from typing import Generic, TypeVar, Optional, Generator
import collections.abc

T = TypeVar('T')

class Graph(Generic[T]):
    __slots__ = ("_adj_list", "_is_directed")

    def __init__(self, is_directed: bool = False):
        # We use a set for neighbors for O(1) edge lookups and removals!
        self._adj_list: dict[T, set[T]] = {}
        self._is_directed = is_directed

    @property
    def vertex_count(self) -> int:
        return len(self._adj_list)

    @property
    def edge_count(self) -> int:
        count = sum(len(neighbors) for neighbors in self._adj_list.values())
        return count if self._is_directed else count // 2

    def __contains__(self, vertex: T) -> bool:
        """Enables 'if vertex in graph:'"""
        return vertex in self._adj_list

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        kind = "DirectedGraph" if self._is_directed else "UndirectedGraph"
        return f"{kind}(Vertices: {self.vertex_count}, Edges: {self.edge_count})"

    def add_vertex(self, vertex: T) -> None:
        """Adds a vertex to the graph in O(1) time."""
        if vertex not in self._adj_list:
            self._adj_list[vertex] = set()

    def add_edge(self, src: T, dst: T) -> None:
        """Adds an edge between src and dst in O(1) time."""
        # Ensure both vertices exist
        self.add_vertex(src)
        self.add_vertex(dst)
        
        self._adj_list[src].add(dst)
        if not self._is_directed:
            self._adj_list[dst].add(src)

    def remove_edge(self, src: T, dst: T) -> None:
        """Removes the edge between src and dst in O(1) time."""
        if src in self._adj_list and dst in self._adj_list[src]:
            self._adj_list[src].remove(dst)
            
        if not self._is_directed:
            if dst in self._adj_list and src in self._adj_list[dst]:
                self._adj_list[dst].remove(src)

    def remove_vertex(self, vertex: T) -> None:
        """Removes a vertex and ALL its connected edges in O(V) time."""
        if vertex not in self._adj_list:
            return
            
        # 1. Remove the vertex completely from the adjacency list
        del self._adj_list[vertex]
        
        # 2. Iterate through all other vertices and remove this vertex from their sets
        for neighbors in self._adj_list.values():
            neighbors.discard(vertex)  # discard removes without throwing KeyError

    def get_neighbors(self, vertex: T) -> set[T]:
        """Returns the neighbors of a vertex in O(1) time."""
        if vertex not in self._adj_list:
            raise KeyError(f"Vertex {vertex} not found in graph.")
        return self._adj_list[vertex]

    def get_vertices(self) -> list[T]:
        """Returns all vertices in the graph."""
        return list(self._adj_list.keys())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Testing Undirected Graph...")
    graph: Graph[str] = Graph(is_directed=False)
    
    # Add vertices and edges
    graph.add_edge("A", "B")
    graph.add_edge("B", "C")
    graph.add_edge("C", "A")
    
    assert graph.vertex_count == 3
    assert graph.edge_count == 3
    assert "B" in graph.get_neighbors("A")
    assert "A" in graph.get_neighbors("B")
    print("✅ Add Edges passed!")

    # Remove Edge
    graph.remove_edge("A", "B")
    assert "B" not in graph.get_neighbors("A")
    assert "A" not in graph.get_neighbors("B")
    assert graph.edge_count == 2
    print("✅ Remove Edge passed!")

    # Remove Vertex
    graph.remove_vertex("C")
    assert "C" not in graph
    assert graph.vertex_count == 2
    assert graph.edge_count == 0  # C held the last two edges
    print("✅ Remove Vertex passed!")
    
    print("\nTesting Directed Graph...")
    di_graph: Graph[int] = Graph(is_directed=True)
    di_graph.add_edge(1, 2)
    
    assert 2 in di_graph.get_neighbors(1)
    assert 1 not in di_graph.get_neighbors(2)  # One-way street!
    assert di_graph.edge_count == 1
    print("✅ Directed Edges passed!")

    print("\n🎉 All Graph tests passed successfully!")

Engine 013 - Union-Find (Disjoint Set)
▶

🌲 Union-Find (Disjoint-Set Union): The Dynamic Connectivity Engine

"Union-Find answers the fundamental question of network topology: 'Are these two entities connected?' in near-instantaneous $O(\alpha(N))$ time — practically indistinguishable from $O(1)$ across the entire known universe."

📍 Level 100 — The Napkin Sketch (30 Seconds)

The Real-World Analogy: Feudal Kingdoms & Paved Highways

Imagine a continent of 1,000 independent villages. Each village starts as its own tiny kingdom with its own Mayor:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
[ Village A ] (Mayor A)       [ Village B ] (Mayor B)
  1. The Alliance (union(A, B)):

Village A and Village B sign a mutual defense pact. They do not hold a chaotic election among all 500 citizens. Mayor A simply pledges allegiance to Mayor B. Now, Mayor B is the Supreme Leader of both villages.

  1. The Verification (connected(X, Y)):

To check if Citizen X and Citizen Y are allies, you ask both: "Who is your Supreme Leader?" If both answer "Mayor B", they belong to the same alliance. This is find(X) == find(Y).

  1. The Paved Highway (Path Compression):

When Citizen X travels across 5 intermediate villages to visit the Supreme Leader, she lays down a paved highway directly from her home to the capital:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Before Path Compression (Winding path):
X ──> Village 1 ──> Village 2 ──> Village 3 ──> Supreme Leader

After Path Compression (Flattened):
X ──────────────────────────────────────────> Supreme Leader

The next time Citizen X needs the Supreme Leader, the trip takes 1 step instead of 4. The tree permanently flattens!

The Core Invariant

The Canonical Root Invariant: Every set is represented by a rooted, directed tree where each node points to its parent. The set's canonical representative is the unique root whose parent pointer points to itself (parent[root] == root). Two elements $x$ and $y$ belong to the same set if and only if find(x) == find(y).

🎯 Level 200 — Street Fundamentals (5 Minutes)

🧠 Mental Model Card
- Core Superpower: Dynamic connectivity in $O(\alpha(N)) \approx O(1)$ time per operation.
- The Kryptonite: Does not support directed edges, edge weights, edge deletions, or finding the actual path between nodes.
- When to Reach for It:
- "Do these two nodes share a connected component?"
- Cycle detection in an undirected graph (if find(u) == find(v) before adding edge $(u, v)$, a cycle exists!).
- Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree (MST).
- Number of connected components after dynamic edge additions.
- When to Run Away:
- Directed graphs $\to$ Reach for Tarjan's or Kosaraju's SCC algorithm.
- Finding the shortest path $\to$ Reach for BFS or Dijkstra.
- Edge deletions $\to$ Reach for Euler Tour Trees or Link-Cut Trees.
- Complexity Budget: Find: $O(\alpha(N))$ | Union: $O(\alpha(N))$ | Space: $O(N)$.

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [1] * n

    def find(self, i: int) -> int:
        if self.parent[i] != i:
            self.parent[i] = self.find(self.parent[i])  # Path compression
        return self.parent[i]

    def union(self, i: int, j: int) -> bool:
        root_i, root_j = self.find(i), self.find(j)
        if root_i == root_j:
            return False  # Already connected (Detected a cycle!)
        # Union by rank: attach smaller tree under taller tree
        if self.rank[root_i] < self.rank[root_j]:
            self.parent[root_i] = root_j
        elif self.rank[root_i] > self.rank[root_j]:
            self.parent[root_j] = root_i
        else:
            self.parent[root_j] = root_i
            self.rank[root_i] += 1
        return True

⚙️ Level 300 — Working Professional (15 Minutes)

Real-System Architecture: Production Applications

  1. Kruskal's Minimum Spanning Tree:

Sort all $E$ edges by weight. Iterate through edges: if dsu.union(u, v) returns True, include the edge in the MST. Stop when $V - 1$ edges are selected. Total time: $O(E \log E)$ (dominated by the initial sort; DSU operations take total $O(E \alpha(V))$).

  1. Computer Vision (Connected Component Labeling):

In binary images (e.g. medical MRI scans, OCR text recognition), Union-Find connects adjacent foreground pixels in a single streaming pass to identify distinct tumors or letter glyphs.

  1. Hex & Percolation Games:

Simulating fluid percolation through porous materials: DSU tracks if top surface fluid connects to bottom floor cells.

Complete Implementation: Production Union-Find with Component Tracking

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
"""
Production Union-Find (Disjoint-Set Union) Implementation.
Includes path compression, union-by-size, component counting, and maximum cluster size.
"""

from typing import List, Tuple

class UnionFind:
    """Disjoint-Set Union supporting O(alpha(N)) operations."""

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        self._n = n
        self.parent: List[int] = list(range(n))
        self.size: List[int] = [1] * n  # Union by size
        self.num_components: int = n
        self.max_component_size: int = 1 if n > 0 else 0

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        """Finds representative with two-pass full path compression."""
        root = x
        while root != self.parent[root]:
            root = self.parent[root]

        # Path compression: point all ancestors directly to root
        curr = x
        while curr != root:
            nxt = self.parent[curr]
            self.parent[curr] = root
            curr = nxt

        return root

    def union(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Merges sets containing x and y. Returns True if merged, False if already connected."""
        root_x = self.find(x)
        root_y = self.find(y)

        if root_x == root_y:
            return False

        # Union by size: attach smaller tree under larger tree
        if self.size[root_x] < self.size[root_y]:
            root_x, root_y = root_y, root_x

        self.parent[root_y] = root_x
        self.size[root_x] += self.size[root_y]
        self.num_components -= 1

        if self.size[root_x] > self.max_component_size:
            self.max_component_size = self.size[root_x]

        return True

    def connected(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Checks if x and y belong to the same component."""
        return self.find(x) == self.find(y)

    def get_component_size(self, x: int) -> int:
        """Returns the number of elements in x's component."""
        return self.size[self.find(x)]

Critical Edge Cases & Failure Modes

  1. Recursion Limit on Path Compression:

If you implement find with recursion on a skewed tree of size $N = 50,000$ without union-by-rank, the first find call will exceed Python's recursion limit. The iterative two-pass implementation above is 100% immune to recursion limit errors.

  1. Forgetting Path Compression: If you implement Union-by-Rank without Path Compression, operations take $O(\log N)$ instead of $O(\alpha(N))$. If you omit both, trees degrade to linked lists taking $O(N)$ per operation!

🔬 Level 400 — Staff & Senior Engineer (30 Minutes)

Tarjan's Proof & The Inverse Ackermann Function $\alpha(n)$

Why is the complexity $O(\alpha(N))$ rather than $O(1)$?

Robert Tarjan (1975) analyzed the exact behavior of Union-Find:

  • The Ackermann Function $A(i, j)$ grows unimaginably fast:
$$A(0, n) = n + 1$$
$$A(1, n) = n + 2$$
$$A(2, n) = 2n + 3$$
$$A(3, n) = 2^{n+3} - 3$$
$$A(4, n) = 2^{2^{\cdot^{\cdot^2}}} - 3 \quad (n+3 \text{ towers of 2})$$
  • $A(4, 2) = 2^{65536} - 3$, which has over 19,728 decimal digits (far exceeding the number of atoms in the observable universe $\approx 10^{80}$).
  • The Inverse Ackermann Function $\alpha(N)$ is defined as:
$$\alpha(N) = \min \{ k : A(k, 1) \ge N \}$$
  • For all practical values $N \le 10^{80}$, $\alpha(N) \le 4$.
  • Therefore, for any physical computer system, $\alpha(N)$ is effectively a small constant $\le 4$.

(For the potential function $\Phi$ amortized proof breakdown, see Ch 04: Amortized Analysis).

🎓 Level 500 — Researcher's Corner (Collapsible)

<details>

<summary><b>📜 Fredman & Saks Cell-Probe Lower Bound (Click to expand)

The Impossibility of Strict $O(1)$ Dynamic Connectivity

Could a brilliant engineer invent an alternative disjoint-set data structure that runs in strict $O(1)$ worst-case time without Ackermann's function?

No. It is mathematically impossible.

In 1989, Michael Fredman and Michael Saks proved the Cell-Probe Lower Bound:

On a Word RAM model with cell size $W = O(\log N)$, any data structure maintaining disjoint sets under arbitrary union and find operations must satisfy:

$$\text{Average Time per Operation} = \Omega(\alpha(M, N))$$

Tarjan's Union-Find algorithm with path compression and union-by-rank achieves this lower bound with zero waste. It is universally optimal.

⚙️ union_find.py
from typing import List


class UnionFind:
    """Disjoint-Set Union supporting near-constant time operations.

    Complexity:
        - find(x): O(alpha(N)) amortized
        - union(x, y): O(alpha(N)) amortized
        - connected(x, y): O(alpha(N)) amortized
        - Space: O(N)
    """

    def __init__(self, n: int) -> None:
        """Initializes DSU with N disjoint singleton sets [0 ... N-1]."""
        self._n = n
        self.parent: List[int] = list(range(n))
        self.size: List[int] = [1] * n
        self.num_components: int = n
        self.max_component_size: int = 1 if n > 0 else 0

    def find(self, x: int) -> int:
        """Finds representative of x's set with iterative path compression."""
        root = x
        while root != self.parent[root]:
            root = self.parent[root]

        # Path compression: update ancestors to point directly to root
        curr = x
        while curr != root:
            nxt = self.parent[curr]
            self.parent[curr] = root
            curr = nxt

        return root

    def union(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Merges sets containing x and y.

        Returns:
            True if elements were in separate sets and merged.
            False if elements were already in the same set (detected a cycle!).
        """
        root_x = self.find(x)
        root_y = self.find(y)

        if root_x == root_y:
            return False

        # Union by size: attach smaller tree under larger tree
        if self.size[root_x] < self.size[root_y]:
            root_x, root_y = root_y, root_x

        self.parent[root_y] = root_x
        self.size[root_x] += self.size[root_y]
        self.num_components -= 1

        if self.size[root_x] > self.max_component_size:
            self.max_component_size = self.size[root_x]

        return True

    def connected(self, x: int, y: int) -> bool:
        """Returns True if x and y share the same component root."""
        return self.find(x) == self.find(y)

    def get_component_size(self, x: int) -> int:
        """Returns the number of elements in the component containing x."""
        return self.size[self.find(x)]


def test_union_find() -> None:
    """Unit tests verifying UnionFind correctness and component tracking."""
    uf = UnionFind(6)
    assert uf.num_components == 6
    assert uf.max_component_size == 1

    # Merge {0, 1}
    assert uf.union(0, 1) is True
    assert uf.connected(0, 1) is True
    assert uf.connected(0, 2) is False
    assert uf.num_components == 5
    assert uf.get_component_size(0) == 2

    # Merge {1, 2} -> component becomes {0, 1, 2}
    assert uf.union(1, 2) is True
    assert uf.connected(0, 2) is True
    assert uf.num_components == 4
    assert uf.get_component_size(2) == 3

    # Redundant connection (cycle detection test)
    assert uf.union(0, 2) is False  # Already connected!
    assert uf.num_components == 4

    # Merge {3, 4} and {4, 5}
    assert uf.union(3, 4) is True
    assert uf.union(4, 5) is True
    assert uf.num_components == 2

    # Final bridge between {0, 1, 2} and {3, 4, 5}
    assert uf.union(2, 5) is True
    assert uf.num_components == 1
    assert uf.max_component_size == 6
    assert uf.connected(0, 5) is True

    print("✅ All UnionFind tests passed successfully!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_union_find()
Engine 014 - Bit Manipulation
▶

⚡ Bit Manipulation: The Silicon-Level Speed Engine

"High-level languages offer abstractions; hardware offers bits. When you manipulate bits directly, your code runs at the raw speed of physical CPU silicon transistors — zero overhead, zero allocation, 1 clock cycle."

📍 Level 100 — The Napkin Sketch (30 Seconds)

The Real-World Analogy: 8 Light Switches on a Wall Panel

Imagine a wall panel in a smart home with 8 toggle switches:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Switch:  [ 7 ] [ 6 ] [ 5 ] [ 4 ] [ 3 ] [ 2 ] [ 1 ] [ 0 ]
State:     0     0     1     0     1     0     0     1
Meaning:        (Heater)       (Garage)            (Front Door)

To record whether 8 household appliances are ON or OFF:

  • You do not allocate 8 strings or a heavy dictionary with 8 keys.
  • You store a single tiny number: 0b00101001 = 41.
  • To check if the Garage (Switch 3) is open, you slide a stencil over Switch 3 (x & (1 << 3)).
  • To flip the Garage switch, you toggle it (x ^ (1 << 3)).

The Two's Complement Invariant

The Two's Complement Law: In modern computer hardware, negative numbers are represented by inverting all bits and adding 1:
$$-x = (\sim x) + 1$$
Because of this mathematical symmetry, bitwise ANDing a number with its negative instantly isolates its lowest set bit (rightmost 1-bit):
$$\text{Lowest Set Bit} = x \ \& \ (-x)$$
This single formula powers Fenwick Trees, bitmap scans, and high-speed graph traversals.

🎯 Level 200 — Street Fundamentals (5 Minutes)

🧠 Mental Model Card
- The Core Superpower: 32 or 64 independent boolean flags stored in a single integer register, manipulated in 0.25 nanoseconds.
- The Kryptonite: Operator precedence bugs (bitwise operators bind looser than addition/subtraction) and language integer overflows.
- When to Reach for It:
- "Find the unique element when all others appear twice" $\to$ XOR cancellation.
- "Check if integer is a power of 2" $\to$ x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0.
- Generating all $2^N$ subsets $\to$ Count from $0$ to $2^N - 1$.
- State-space DP with $N \le 20$ elements (TSP, Hamiltonian path).
- When to Run Away: When flags exceed 64 bits and change dynamically $\to$ Use bitarray or Python's set().
- Complexity Budget: Every standard bit operation runs in strict $O(1)$ Time and $O(1)$ Space.

The 6 Primitive Bitwise Operators

OperatorSyntaxDescriptionExample (A = 5 0101, B = 3 0011)
ANDA & B1 only if both bits are 15 & 3 = 1 (0001)
ORA | B1 if either bit is 15 | 3 = 7 (0111)
XORA ^ B1 if bits differ ($x \oplus x = 0$, $x \oplus 0 = x$)5 ^ 3 = 6 (0110)
NOT~AInverts all bits (in two's complement: $\sim x = -(x+1)$)~5 = -6
Left ShiftA << kShifts bits left by $k$ positions (multiplies by $2^k$)5 << 1 = 10 (1010)
Right ShiftA >> kShifts bits right by $k$ positions (integer divides by $2^k$)5 >> 1 = 2 (0010)

The 7 Golden Street Tricks Cheat Sheet

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# 1. Test if k-th bit is set (0-indexed from right)
is_set = (x >> k) & 1 == 1

# 2. Set k-th bit to 1
x |= (1 << k)

# 3. Clear k-th bit to 0
x &= ~(1 << k)

# 4. Toggle k-th bit (0 -> 1, 1 -> 0)
x ^= (1 << k)

# 5. Clear lowest set bit (Brian Kernighan's trick)
x &= (x - 1)  # e.g., 01100 -> 01000

# 6. Isolate lowest set bit
lowest = x & (-x)  # e.g., 01100 -> 00100

# 7. Check if x is a power of 2
is_pow2 = x > 0 and (x & (x - 1)) == 0

Street Code Snippets: 2 Core Interview Workhorses

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# 1. Brian Kernighan's Algorithm: Count Set Bits (Hamming Weight)
# Runs in O(Set Bits) time, NOT O(32) — skips all 0-bits instantly!
def count_set_bits(n: int) -> int:
    count = 0
    while n:
        n &= (n - 1)  # Clears rightmost 1-bit
        count += 1
    return count


# 2. Single Number (XOR Cancellation) — O(N) Time, O(1) Space
# Given an array where every element appears twice except one:
def single_number(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    unique = 0
    for x in nums:
        unique ^= x  # x ^ x = 0; 0 ^ unique = unique
    return unique

⚙️ Level 300 — Working Professional (15 Minutes)

Real-System Architecture: Production Applications

  1. Linux POSIX File Permissions:

A 9-bit bitmask determines file access rights:

rwxr-xr-- $= (111 \ 101 \ 100)_2 = 0754$ in octal.

Checking read permission takes a single mode & S_IRUSR CPU instruction.

  1. Bloom Filters & Bitmaps:

High-throughput databases (Cassandra, Redis, RocksDB) check if a key exists among 100 million rows by testing $k$ bit positions in a compact shared 128 MB bit array.

  1. Bitmask Dynamic Programming ($N \le 20$):

In the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) or job scheduling, representing the visited subset of $N$ cities as a Python frozenset creates huge hash overhead. An integer mask in range $[0, 2^N - 1]$ fits in a CPU register and indexes DP arrays directly: dp[mask][curr_city].

Complete Implementation: BitHacks Production Suite

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
"""
Production Bit Manipulation Library.
Includes Brian Kernighan popcount, two non-repeating numbers, and submask iterator.
"""

from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple

class BitHacks:
    """Production suite of silicon-level bit manipulation algorithms."""

    @staticmethod
    def count_set_bits(n: int) -> int:
        """Counts set bits using Brian Kernighan's algorithm in O(K) where K = set bits."""
        count = 0
        while n > 0:
            n &= (n - 1)
            count += 1
        return count

    @staticmethod
    def two_single_numbers(nums: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
        """Finds the two unique numbers in an array where all other elements appear twice.

        Time: O(N)
        Space: O(1)
        """
        # Step 1: XOR all elements -> gives xor_all = a ^ b
        xor_all = 0
        for x in nums:
            xor_all ^= x

        # Step 2: Find any bit where a and b differ (isolate lowest set bit)
        diff_bit = xor_all & (-xor_all)

        # Step 3: Partition all numbers into two groups based on diff_bit
        a = b = 0
        for x in nums:
            if x & diff_bit:
                a ^= x
            else:
                b ^= x

        return (min(a, b), max(a, b))

    @staticmethod
    def enumerate_submasks(mask: int) -> Iterator[int]:
        """Iterates through all submasks of a given mask in descending order.

        Complexity:
            Iterating over submasks of all masks takes O(3^N) total time, not O(4^N)!
        """
        sub = mask
        while sub > 0:
            yield sub
            sub = (sub - 1) & mask
        yield 0  # Empty submask

Critical Edge Cases & Operator Precedence Traps

  1. The Python Precedence Trap (HIGH SEVERITY):

In Python, addition and subtraction have higher precedence than bit shifts!

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# ❌ BUG: Evaluates as 1 << (2 + 1) = 1 << 3 = 8!
   val = 1 << 2 + 1

   # ✅ FIX: Explicit parentheses
   val = (1 << 2) + 1  # Equals 5
  1. The == vs & Precedence Trap:

== binds tighter than &:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# ❌ BUG: Evaluates as x & (1 == 0) -> x & False -> 0!
   if x & 1 == 0: ...

   # ✅ FIX: Always wrap bitwise expressions in parentheses!
   if (x & 1) == 0: ...
  1. Python Arbitrary-Precision Sign Extension:

In C/Java, an integer is fixed at 32 or 64 bits. In Python, integers have arbitrary precision. Therefore, ~0 is not 0xFFFFFFFF (all 1-bits), but -1. To simulate 32-bit two's complement in Python:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
MASK_32 = 0xFFFFFFFF
   val_32 = x & MASK_32

🔬 Level 400 — Staff & Senior Engineer (30 Minutes)

SWAR Parallel Bit Counting (Hamming Weight in $O(1)$)

How does hardware POPCNT count 1-bits in a 32-bit integer in constant time without any loops?

Using SIMD Within A Register (SWAR):

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def popcount_32(x: int) -> int:
    """Computes number of set bits in a 32-bit int in 5 clock cycles using SWAR."""
    x = x - ((x >> 1) & 0x55555555)  # Sum 2-bit pairs
    x = (x & 0x33333333) + ((x >> 2) & 0x33333333)  # Sum 4-bit nibbles
    x = (x + (x >> 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F  # Sum 8-bit bytes
    x = x + (x >> 8)  # Sum 16-bit words
    x = x + (x >> 16)  # Sum 32-bit full register
    return x & 0x0000003F

The $O(3^N)$ Submask Enumeration Proof

When solving Bitmask DP (e.g. partition an array into $K$ subsets), we iterate over every mask, and for each mask, iterate over all its submasks:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
sub = mask
while sub:
    sub = (sub - 1) & mask

How many total operations occur?

A mask with $k$ set bits has exactly $2^k$ submasks.

By the Binomial Theorem:

$$\sum_{k=0}^N \binom{N}{k} 2^k = (1 + 2)^N = 3^N$$

Instead of naive nested loops taking $O(2^N \times 2^N) = O(4^N)$, submask enumeration takes strictly $O(3^N)$! For $N = 15$, $4^{15} \approx 10^9$ (TLE), but $3^{15} \approx 14 \times 10^6$ (passes within 0.05 seconds).

🎓 Level 500 — Researcher's Corner (Collapsible)

<details>

<summary><b>📜 De Bruijn Sequences & Branchless Log2 (Click to expand)

Branchless $\lfloor \log_2 x \rfloor$ via De Bruijn Sequences

How do you find the most significant bit (MSB) of an integer in 3 assembly instructions without hardware BSR (Bit Scan Reverse)?

Using a De Bruijn Sequence $B(2, 5)$ of length $2^5 = 32$:

A cyclic sequence where every possible 5-bit pattern appears exactly once as a contiguous substring.

The magic 32-bit constant is 0x077CB531:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
DE_BRUIJN_LOOKUP = [
    0, 1, 28, 2, 29, 14, 24, 3, 30, 22, 20, 15, 25, 17, 4, 8,
    31, 27, 13, 23, 21, 19, 16, 7, 26, 12, 18, 6, 11, 5, 10, 9
]

def floor_log2(v: int) -> int:
    """Returns floor(log2(v)) in 3 operations without branches or loops."""
    # Round down to power of 2
    v |= v >> 1
    v |= v >> 2
    v |= v >> 4
    v |= v >> 8
    v |= v >> 16
    v = (v >> 1) + 1
    # Multiply by De Bruijn constant and shift
    return DE_BRUIJN_LOOKUP[(v * 0x077CB531 & 0xFFFFFFFF) >> 27]

⚙️ bit_manipulation.py
from typing import Iterator, List, Tuple


def count_set_bits(n: int) -> int:
    """Counts set bits using Brian Kernighan's algorithm.

    Complexity: O(K) where K is number of set bits (skips zero bits entirely).
    """
    count = 0
    while n > 0:
        n &= (n - 1)
        count += 1
    return count


def is_power_of_two(n: int) -> bool:
    """Determines whether n is a positive power of 2 in O(1) time."""
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0


def single_number(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    """Finds the single unique number where all others appear twice.

    Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) space.
    """
    unique = 0
    for x in nums:
        unique ^= x
    return unique


def two_single_numbers(nums: List[int]) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Finds the two unique numbers where all others appear twice.

    Complexity: O(N) time, O(1) space.
    """
    xor_all = 0
    for x in nums:
        xor_all ^= x

    # Isolate lowest set bit where a and b differ
    diff_bit = xor_all & (-xor_all)

    a = b = 0
    for x in nums:
        if x & diff_bit:
            a ^= x
        else:
            b ^= x

    return (min(a, b), max(a, b))


def enumerate_submasks(mask: int) -> List[int]:
    """Enumerates all submasks of a mask in descending order."""
    submasks: List[int] = []
    sub = mask
    while sub > 0:
        submasks.append(sub)
        sub = (sub - 1) & mask
    submasks.append(0)
    return submasks


def test_bit_manipulation() -> None:
    """Unit tests verifying bit manipulation functions."""
    # 1. Brian Kernighan count set bits
    assert count_set_bits(0) == 0
    assert count_set_bits(1) == 1
    assert count_set_bits(7) == 3   # 0b111
    assert count_set_bits(16) == 1  # 0b10000
    assert count_set_bits(255) == 8 # 0b11111111

    # 2. Power of two check
    assert is_power_of_two(1) is True
    assert is_power_of_two(2) is True
    assert is_power_of_two(16) is True
    assert is_power_of_two(18) is False
    assert is_power_of_two(0) is False
    assert is_power_of_two(-8) is False

    # 3. Single Number
    assert single_number([4, 1, 2, 1, 2]) == 4
    assert single_number([2, 2, 1]) == 1

    # 4. Two Single Numbers
    assert two_single_numbers([1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5]) == (3, 5)
    assert two_single_numbers([-1, 0]) == (-1, 0)

    # 5. Submask enumeration
    # mask = 0b101 = 5. Submasks: 5 (101), 4 (100), 1 (001), 0 (000)
    assert enumerate_submasks(5) == [5, 4, 1, 0]

    print("✅ All Bit Manipulation tests passed successfully!")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    test_bit_manipulation()

Chapter 1: What Is a Tree? 🌳

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine your family tree hanging on the wall at Grandma's house.

At the very top is Great-Grandma. She has two children — Grandpa Joe and Grandpa Sam.

Grandpa Joe has three children. Grandpa Sam has one child.

Those children have their own children, and so on.

Notice two very important things:

  1. Everyone has exactly one parent (except Great-Grandma at the top — she has none).
  2. There are NO loops. You can't follow the "parent" chain and end up back where you started. Your grandmother cannot also be your granddaughter!

That's a Tree. It's a group of things (nodes) connected by relationships (edges), with one single starting point (the root), where every connection flows downward and loops are strictly forbidden.

🎯 Formal Computer Science Definition

A Tree is a connected, acyclic, undirected graph with N nodes and exactly N − 1 edges.

When we designate one specific node as the root, it becomes a rooted tree, and suddenly direction appears — every node has a parent (except the root) and zero or more children.

A Forest is a collection of zero or more disjoint trees (i.e., multiple disconnected trees grouped together).

[!TIP]
Memory trick for Depth vs Height:
- Depth = how deep in the water you are (measured from the surface/top = root, going down)
- Height = how tall something is (measured from the ground/bottom = leaf, going up)

📐 The 3 Fundamental Properties of Trees

These three properties are equivalent — if any one holds, the others follow. They uniquely characterize a tree.

Property 1: N Nodes → Exactly N−1 Edges

A tree with N nodes always has exactly N−1 edges.

Intuition: To build a tree, you start with 1 node (the root, 0 edges). Each new node you add brings exactly 1 new edge (the edge connecting it to its parent). So after adding N−1 more nodes, you have N−1 edges.

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
N = 8 nodes → 7 edges
(Count the arrows in the diagram above: 1→2, 1→3, 2→4, 2→5, 3→6, 4→7, 4→8 = 7 ✅)

Corollary: If a connected graph has N nodes and N−1 edges, it MUST be a tree.

Property 2: Exactly One Unique Path Between Any Two Nodes

Pick any two nodes in a tree. There is exactly one path connecting them.

  • More than one path → the graph has a cycle (not a tree)
  • Zero paths → the graph is disconnected (not a tree, maybe a forest)

Property 3: Removing ANY Single Edge Disconnects the Tree

Every edge in a tree is a bridge — critical to the tree's connectivity. Unlike graphs where you might have redundant paths, a tree has no redundancy. This is the direct consequence of having exactly N−1 edges.

🔁 The Recursive Nature of Trees

This is the most important mental model for writing tree algorithms:

A tree is either:
- Empty (null/None), OR
- A root node connected to zero or more subtrees, where each subtree is itself a tree.

This recursive definition is why virtually all tree algorithms are recursive. When you write dfs(node.left) and dfs(node.right), you are literally applying this definition — treating each child as the root of its own tree.

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Tree(root=1)
├── Tree(root=2)
│   ├── Tree(root=4)
│   │   ├── Tree(root=7) → Empty, Empty
│   │   └── Tree(root=8) → Empty, Empty
│   └── Tree(root=5) → Empty, Empty
└── Tree(root=3)
    └── Tree(root=6) → Empty, Empty

➕ Mathematical Properties Summary

PropertyFormula
Number of edges`E= N − 1`
Sum of all node degrees`Σ degree(v) = 2(N−1) = 2E` (since each edge contributes 2 to total degree)
Max edges in a graph with N nodes (without cycles)N − 1
Minimum edges to connect N nodesN − 1
Number of leaves in a Full Binary Treeinternal_nodes + 1
[!NOTE]
"Sum of degrees = 2|E|" is the Handshaking Lemma — it applies to all graphs, not just trees.
For trees: sum of all degrees = 2(N−1). This means average degree ≈ 2 for large trees.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Misconceptions

  1. "A tree must have a root with two children" → ❌ Wrong. Any number of children (including 0, 1, 3, 100...) is valid unless you're talking specifically about binary trees.
  1. "Depth and Height are the same thing" → ❌ Wrong. Depth is measured top-down from root. Height is measured bottom-up from leaves. Root has depth 0, leaves have height 0.
  1. "All leaves are at the same level" → ❌ Only true for perfect binary trees. An arbitrary tree can have leaves at many different levels.
  1. "A path must go from parent to child" → ❌ A path in a tree can go "up" through a common ancestor then "down". Example: The path from node 5 to node 7 is 5 → 2 → 4 → 7.
  1. "N nodes = N−1 edges, so a graph with those counts is always a tree" → ❌ Only if the graph is also connected. A disconnected graph can also have N−1 edges (it would be a forest).

Theory Chapter 2: Binary Trees 🌲

Chapter 2: Binary Trees 🌲

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

A Binary Tree is a tree where every single parent can have at most 2 children — a left child and a right child.

Think of it like a family of decisions. Every day you flip a coin:

  • Heads → Left
  • Tails → Right

After 3 flips, you've made 8 possible journeys through the tree, each ending at a different leaf. That branching structure — 2 choices at every step — is exactly what makes binary trees so powerful and so mathematically tractable.

⚠️ A Binary Tree is NOT a Binary Search Tree. A Binary Tree is just a structural constraint (≤2 children). A BST has an additional ordering property (left < root < right). Chapter 4 covers BSTs. This chapter is purely about the structure.

🏷️ Types of Binary Trees

These definitions appear constantly in interview problems. Know every single one.

1. Full Binary Tree (Proper / Strictly Binary Tree)

Every node has 0 or 2 children. Never exactly 1.

2. Complete Binary Tree

All levels are fully filled, except possibly the last level, which must be filled from left to right.

Why this matters: Heaps use this structure — storing a complete binary tree in an array is both memory-efficient and elegant.

3. Perfect Binary Tree

Every internal node has exactly 2 children AND all leaves are at the same level.

This is the "ideal" tree — maximum nodes for a given height.

Mathematical properties (for height h, where root is at height 0):

  • Total nodes: 2^(h+1) − 1
  • Leaves: 2^h
  • Internal nodes: 2^h − 1
  • Nodes at level k: 2^k

A perfect binary tree is simultaneously a full and a complete binary tree. The reverse is not always true.

4. Balanced Binary Tree

The height of the left and right subtrees of every node differs by at most 1.

Why it matters: A balanced tree guarantees O(log N) height. An unbalanced tree can degenerate to O(N) height (a linked list!), making all operations O(N).

[!IMPORTANT]
A "balanced" binary tree is NOT necessarily a "complete" or "perfect" tree. It just means no subtree is dramatically taller than its sibling.

5. Degenerate (Skewed) Binary Tree

Every node has only one child — the tree has become a linked list.

This is the worst case for binary trees.

This happens when you insert already-sorted data into a BST: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] → the BST becomes a right-skewed degenerate tree. Height = N−1 instead of log N. This is why balanced BSTs (AVL, Red-Black) were invented.

📐 Essential Mathematical Formulas

These formulas appear in complexity proofs and interview problems. Understand them, don't just memorize them.

PropertyFormulaIntuition
Height of perfect tree with N nodesh = ⌊log₂N⌋Each level doubles the count
Max nodes in perfect tree of height hN = 2^(h+1) − 1Sum of geometric series: 1+2+4+...+2^h
Leaves in perfect tree of height hL = 2^hBottom level only
Internal nodes in perfect treeN - L = 2^h - 1Everything except leaves
Height of complete tree with N nodes⌊log₂N⌋Same as perfect — within one level
Min nodes for tree of height hh + 1Degenerate/skewed tree
Max nodes at level k2^kBranching factor of 2
Full binary tree: leaves vs internalsL = I + 1Each internal node adds one more leaf than it "consumes"

Worked Example

Q: A perfect binary tree has 7 nodes. What is its height? How many leaves?
7 = 2^(h+1) − 1 → 2^(h+1) = 8 → h+1 = 3 → h = 2
Leaves = 2^h = 2^2 = 4
Internal nodes = 7 − 4 = 3
Check: Full binary tree property → L = I + 1 → 4 = 3 + 1 ✅

🗄️ Array Representation of Binary Trees

Complete binary trees have a beautiful property: they can be stored in a flat array with no pointers!

If a node is at index i (1-indexed):

  • Parent is at index ⌊i/2⌋
  • Left child is at index 2i
  • Right child is at index 2i + 1

Or with 0-indexed arrays (more common in Python):

  • Parent of node at i → ⌊(i−1)/2⌋
  • Left child of node at i → 2i + 1
  • Right child of node at i → 2i + 2
⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Tree:          Array (0-indexed):
     1          [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
   /   \         0  1  2  3  4  5  6
  2     3
 / \ / \
4  5 6  7

Parent of index 3 (value=4): ⌊(3-1)/2⌋ = 1 → value=2 ✅
Left child of index 1 (value=2): 2(1)+1 = 3 → value=4 ✅
Right child of index 1 (value=2): 2(1)+2 = 4 → value=5 ✅

This is exactly how Min-Heaps and Max-Heaps work. See Fundamentals 010 - Min and Max Heap.

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# Heap array navigation in Python
def parent(i):     return (i - 1) // 2
def left_child(i): return 2 * i + 1
def right_child(i):return 2 * i + 2

🐍 Python Representation: The Node Class

The standard way to represent a binary tree in Python interview problems:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    """Standard LeetCode-style binary tree node."""
    def __init__(self, val: int = 0,
                 left: Optional[TreeNode] = None,
                 right: Optional[TreeNode] = None):
        self.val   = val
        self.left  = left
        self.right = right

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"TreeNode({self.val})"


# Build the tree:   1
#                  / \
#                 2   3
#                / \
#               4   5
root = TreeNode(1,
    left=TreeNode(2,
        left=TreeNode(4),
        right=TreeNode(5)),
    right=TreeNode(3))

Important helpers used across many problems:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def height(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """Recursive height. O(N) time, O(H) space."""
    if not node:
        return -1  # Convention: empty tree has height -1; leaf has height 0
    return 1 + max(height(node.left), height(node.right))

def count_nodes(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """Count all nodes. O(N) time."""
    if not node:
        return 0
    return 1 + count_nodes(node.left) + count_nodes(node.right)

def is_leaf(node: TreeNode) -> bool:
    return node.left is None and node.right is None

🔑 The Heap Connection

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart LR
    BT["Binary Tree\n(structure only)"] -->|"+ complete\n+ heap-order"| H["Heap\n(Min or Max)"]
    BT -->|"+ BST property\nleft < root < right"| BST["BST"]
    BST -->|"+ self-balancing\nrotations"| AVL["AVL Tree"]
    BST -->|"+ 5 coloring rules"| RB["Red-Black Tree"]
State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

A Heap IS a Complete Binary Tree with one additional constraint: the heap-order property.

  • Min-Heap: every parent ≤ its children (root = minimum)
  • Max-Heap: every parent ≥ its children (root = maximum)

Because it's a complete binary tree, it stores perfectly in an array — no pointers needed.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls & Interview Traps

TrapReality
"Complete = Full"No! Complete = filled left-to-right. Full = every node has 0 or 2 children.
"Perfect = Complete"Perfect IS complete (and full). But complete is NOT necessarily perfect.
"Balanced = height log N"Yes — if balanced by the formal definition. But "visually balanced-looking" doesn't prove it.
"BST = Binary Tree"BST is a special binary tree. Not all binary trees are BSTs!
"Deleting from a complete tree is easy"No — you must maintain the "left-to-right" property. This requires finding the rightmost node at the last level.

🔗 Connections to Coding Patterns

Theory Chapter 3: Tree Traversals 🗺️
▶

Chapter 3: Tree Traversals 🗺️

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a giant treasure map that looks like a tree. The treasure is hidden at one of the leaves, and you need to visit every single room in the mansion to find it.

The question is: in what order do you visit the rooms?

You can visit rooms in four completely different orders, and each order is useful for a different goal:

  1. Level-Order (BFS): Start at the front door, visit every room on Floor 1 first, then every room on Floor 2, then Floor 3, etc. You see all rooms at the same depth before going deeper.
  1. Pre-Order: Enter a room, look around immediately, then go left, then go right. You see the current room before its children.
  1. In-Order: Go all the way left first, then look at the current room, then go right. In a BST, this visits everything in sorted order!
  1. Post-Order: Go left, go right, then look at the current room last. You process children before their parent — like demolishing a building floor by floor from the top down.

Order: Visit every node level by level, left to right, top to bottom.

Mechanism: Uses a Queue (FIFO). Process a node, add its children to the back of the queue.

Python Implementation

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional

def level_order(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[list[int]]:
    """Returns nodes grouped by level. O(N) time, O(W) space (W = max width)."""
    if not root:
        return []
    result = []
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)     # ← KEY: snapshot of current level's size
        current_level = []

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            current_level.append(node.val)
            if node.left:  queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right: queue.append(node.right)

        result.append(current_level)

    return result
# → [[1], [2,3], [4,5,6,7], [8,9]]

When to use: Finding shortest paths in unweighted trees/graphs, level-by-level processing, minimum depth.

Result for our tree: [1, 2, 4, 8, 9, 5, 3, 6, 7]

Recursive Implementation

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def pre_order_recursive(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[int]:
    """Root → Left → Right. O(N) time, O(H) space."""
    result = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        result.append(node.val)  # ① Process ROOT first
        dfs(node.left)           # ② Then LEFT subtree
        dfs(node.right)          # ③ Then RIGHT subtree
    dfs(root)
    return result

Iterative Implementation (with Stack)

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def pre_order_iterative(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[int]:
    if not root: return []
    result = []
    stack = [root]

    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        result.append(node.val)
        # Push RIGHT first so LEFT is processed first (LIFO)
        if node.right: stack.append(node.right)
        if node.left:  stack.append(node.left)

    return result

When to use: Serializing/copying a tree, creating a "prefix" representation, top-down computation where parent value is needed first.

Traversal 3: In-Order (Left → Root → Right) 🔤

Mnemonic: Left, Now, Right — "Visit everything to my left, THEN me, THEN everything to my right"

Result for our tree: [8, 4, 9, 2, 5, 1, 6, 3, 7]

⭐ CRITICAL INSIGHT: In-order traversal of a BST always yields elements in sorted (ascending) order. This is THE defining property — a BST guarantees that in-order traversal = sorted array.

Recursive Implementation

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def in_order_recursive(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[int]:
    """Left → Root → Right. Yields SORTED output for BST. O(N) time, O(H) space."""
    result = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        dfs(node.left)           # ① Dive ALL the way LEFT first
        result.append(node.val)  # ② Process ROOT (when left is done)
        dfs(node.right)          # ③ Then RIGHT subtree
    dfs(root)
    return result

Iterative Implementation (with Stack)

The iterative version reveals the true mechanics of DFS:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def in_order_iterative(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[int]:
    result = []
    stack  = []
    curr   = root

    while curr or stack:
        # Go as far LEFT as possible — push every node
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.left

        # Backtrack: process the node
        curr = stack.pop()
        result.append(curr.val)

        # Now explore its RIGHT subtree
        curr = curr.right

    return result

When to use: BST sorted-order operations, BST validation (check if in-order output is strictly increasing), k-th smallest element in BST.

Traversal 4: Post-Order (Left → Right → Root) 🏗️

Mnemonic: Left, Right, Now — "Deal with both my children BEFORE I deal with myself"

Result for our tree: [8, 9, 4, 5, 2, 6, 7, 3, 1]

This is a bottom-up traversal — leaves are processed first, root is processed last.

Recursive Implementation

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def post_order_recursive(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> list[int]:
    """Left → Right → Root. Bottom-up computation. O(N) time, O(H) space."""
    result = []
    def dfs(node):
        if not node: return
        dfs(node.left)           # ① LEFT subtree first
        dfs(node.right)          # ② RIGHT subtree second
        result.append(node.val)  # ③ Process ROOT LAST
    dfs(root)
    return result

When to use: Deleting a tree (can't delete parent before children), computing subtree heights/sizes from leaves up, expression tree evaluation, Tree Diameter and Maximum Path Sum problems (Pattern 12).

[!TIP]
Memory device for the 3 DFS traversals:
- Pre = parent before children (NLR)
- In = parent in-between children (LNR)
- Post = parent after children (LRN)
The only thing that changes is where you put the ROOT processing step relative to the recursive calls.

🧠 The Call Stack Visualization

This is the hardest thing to internalize. Here's what Python's call stack actually looks like during an in-order traversal of a simple 3-node tree (root=2, left=1, right=3):

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
in_order(2)
  │
  ├─► in_order(1)              ← Dive LEFT
  │     ├─► in_order(None)     ← Hit bottom, return
  │     ├─► PROCESS: append 1  ← ✅ Visit 1
  │     └─► in_order(None)     ← No right child, return
  │
  ├─► PROCESS: append 2        ← ✅ Visit 2 (after left subtree done)
  │
  └─► in_order(3)              ← Dive RIGHT
        ├─► in_order(None)     ← Hit bottom, return
        ├─► PROCESS: append 3  ← ✅ Visit 3
        └─► in_order(None)     ← No right child, return

Final result: [1, 2, 3] ← SORTED! ✅

The call stack IS the "backtracking trail" — when in_order(1) returns, execution picks up right where it left off in in_order(2), continuing to process node 2.

🐍 Python Generator Pattern

For large trees, Python generators are memory-efficient — they don't build the entire list upfront:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
from typing import Generator, Optional

def in_order_gen(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Generator[int, None, None]:
    """Lazy in-order traversal using generators. O(H) space at any moment."""
    if node:
        yield from in_order_gen(node.left)
        yield node.val
        yield from in_order_gen(node.right)

# Usage: only materializes one value at a time
for val in in_order_gen(root):
    if val == target:
        break  # Stop early — we don't need to traverse the rest!

State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

Counterintuitive insight: For a perfect tree, BFS uses O(N/2) = O(N) space because the last level alone has N/2 nodes in the queue simultaneously. DFS only uses O(log N) space. So for wide, balanced trees, DFS is more memory-efficient than BFS.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

PitfallExplanation
Forgetting the base caseif not node: return is mandatory in every recursive traversal. Without it, you'll hit a NullPointerException.
Mutating the shared path listWhen collecting root-to-leaf paths, always path.append(val) before recursion and path.pop() after. Without the pop(), the path "bleeds" into other branches.
Confusing in-order BST outputIn-order of a BST → sorted. But in-order of a generic binary tree is NOT sorted!
BFS without a visited setFor trees, BFS doesn't need a visited set (no cycles). For graphs, it's mandatory.
Level-order vs simple BFSLevel-order groups by level (using len(queue) snapshot). Simple BFS just processes in order without grouping.

Theory Chapter 4: Binary Search Trees (BST) 🔍
▶

Chapter 4: Binary Search Trees (BST) 🔍

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine a dictionary on your bookshelf. If you're looking for the word "Mango", you don't start from page 1 and read every single word! You open to the middle. If you're in the M's — great, search this half. If you're in the S's — search the first half.

A Binary Search Tree (BST) is a binary tree that works exactly like a dictionary. At every single node, a golden rule is strictly enforced:

🏆 The BST Property: Everything in the left subtree is LESS THAN the root. Everything in the right subtree is GREATER THAN the root. This rule applies at every node, not just the root.

This property lets you discard half the remaining tree at every step — just like a dictionary!

📜 The BST Property (Formally)

For every node N in a BST:

  • max(N.left subtree) < N.val
  • min(N.right subtree) > N.val

[!IMPORTANT]
The BST property must hold for ALL descendants, not just direct children!
A common trap: placing 35 as a right child of 30 — valid locally (35 > 30). But 35 < 50 means it should be in the LEFT subtree of 50. So 35 placed as the right child of 30 is ✅ valid in a BST rooted at 50.
But placing 55 as the right child of 30 is ❌ INVALID — 55 > 50, it belongs in the right subtree of 50, not left.

🔧 Core Operations Deep-Dive

Operation 1: Search — O(H)

Starting at root, at each node ask: "Is my target smaller, larger, or equal?"

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def search(root, target):
    curr = root
    while curr:
        if target == curr.val:   return True   # Found!
        elif target < curr.val:  curr = curr.left   # Go LEFT
        else:                    curr = curr.right  # Go RIGHT
    return False  # Fell off the tree — not found

Trace: Searching for 60 in the tree above:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
At 50: 60 > 50 → go RIGHT
At 70: 60 < 70 → go LEFT
At 60: 60 == 60 → FOUND! ✅
(Only visited 3 nodes out of 7)

Operation 2: Insert — O(H)

Search for where the value would be, then insert it there.

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def insert(root, val):
    if not root:
        return TreeNode(val)  # Base case: empty spot found
    if val < root.val:
        root.left  = insert(root.left, val)
    elif val > root.val:
        root.right = insert(root.right, val)
    # If val == root.val, ignore duplicates (or handle as needed)
    return root

Trace: Inserting 45 into the tree above:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
At 50: 45 < 50 → go LEFT
At 30: 45 > 30 → go RIGHT
At 40: 45 > 40 → go RIGHT
At None: INSERT 45 here as right child of 40 ✅

Operation 3: Delete — O(H) (The Tricky One)

Three distinct cases, and each requires different handling:

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    Start["Delete node N"] --> Check{"How many children?"}
    Check -->|"0 children\n(Leaf)"| Case1["CASE 1: Simple\nJust remove N.\nReturn None to parent."]
    Check -->|"1 child"| Case2["CASE 2: Bypass\nReturn N's only child\nto N's parent.\nN is bypassed."]
    Check -->|"2 children"| Case3["CASE 3: Successor\n① Find in-order successor\n(min of right subtree)\n② Copy successor val into N\n③ Delete successor from\nright subtree (recursively)"]

    style Case1 fill:#55EFC4,color:#333
    style Case2 fill:#FDCB6E,color:#333
    style Case3 fill:#FF7675,color:#fff
State convergence & algorithmic execution graph
⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def delete(root, val):
    if not root: return None

    if val < root.val:
        root.left  = delete(root.left, val)
    elif val > root.val:
        root.right = delete(root.right, val)
    else:
        # Found the node to delete!
        if not root.left:  return root.right  # Case 1 or 2 (no left child)
        if not root.right: return root.left   # Case 2 (no right child)

        # Case 3: Two children — find in-order successor
        successor = root.right
        while successor.left:
            successor = successor.left
        root.val   = successor.val             # Copy successor's value
        root.right = delete(root.right, successor.val)  # Delete successor

    return root

Trace: Deleting 50 (the root, which has 2 children):

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1. Find in-order successor of 50: min of right subtree {70, 60, 80}
   → Go right to 70, then go left to 60. 60 has no left child.
   → In-order successor = 60

2. Copy 60 into root's val. Tree root now holds value 60.

3. Delete 60 from right subtree:
   → 60 is a leaf there. Remove it.

Result: Root = 60, left subtree unchanged, right = {70, 80}

🏆 The In-Order Successor & Predecessor

These concepts appear constantly in BST interview problems.

TermDefinitionHow to Find
In-Order SuccessorThe next larger value after a given node in the BST. The node that would come right after this one in sorted order.If node has a right subtree: min(right subtree). If not: walk up ancestors until you find one where you came from the left.
In-Order PredecessorThe next smaller value before a given node.If node has a left subtree: max(left subtree). If not: walk up ancestors until you find one where you came from the right.

[!WARNING]
A plain BST gives NO guarantees on balance. If you insert [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] in sorted order, you get a linked list. This is why AVL Trees and Red-Black Trees were invented (Chapter 5). In Python, sortedcontainers.SortedList and in Java, TreeMap use Red-Black trees internally to guarantee O(log N).

💡 The BST ↔ Sorted Array Duality

This is THE fundamental insight about BSTs:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
In-order traversal of BST  ↔  Sorted array
BST insertion              ↔  Inserting into sorted array at correct position
BST search                 ↔  Binary search on sorted array
BST height                 ↔  log(N) iterations of binary search

The BST is essentially a dynamic sorted data structure — unlike a sorted array, you can insert and delete without shifting elements.

🎯 Key BST Interview Patterns

Validate a BST

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def is_valid_bst(root, min_val=float('-inf'), max_val=float('inf')):
    """Check if tree satisfies BST property at every node."""
    if not root: return True
    if not (min_val < root.val < max_val): return False
    return (is_valid_bst(root.left,  min_val, root.val) and
            is_valid_bst(root.right, root.val, max_val))

The trap: Don't just compare a node with its direct children. You must pass down the valid range (min_val, max_val) through the entire subtree.

K-th Smallest Element in BST

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def kth_smallest(root, k):
    """In-order traversal stops at the k-th element. O(H + k) time."""
    count = [0]
    result = [None]

    def in_order(node):
        if not node or result[0] is not None: return
        in_order(node.left)
        count[0] += 1
        if count[0] == k:
            result[0] = node.val
            return
        in_order(node.right)

    in_order(root)
    return result[0]

LCA (Lowest Common Ancestor) in BST

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def lca_bst(root, p, q):
    """The BST property makes LCA trivial. O(H) time."""
    while root:
        if p.val < root.val and q.val < root.val:
            root = root.left   # Both nodes are in left subtree
        elif p.val > root.val and q.val > root.val:
            root = root.right  # Both nodes are in right subtree
        else:
            return root  # We've diverged — this is the LCA!

⚠️ Common BST Pitfalls

PitfallCorrect Approach
Validating BST by only comparing parent-childPass min/max bounds down the recursion
Forgetting BST successor for deletionWhen deleting a 2-child node, find min(right subtree), not just right.val
Assuming BST is balancedNever assume! Height can be O(N). Always think about worst case.
Duplicate handlingClarify with interviewer: ignore duplicates, allow left≤root, or allow root≤right?

Theory Chapter 5: Balanced Trees ⚖️

Chapter 5: Balanced Trees ⚖️

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you're building a tower of blocks. A BST is like stacking blocks however they come — if all your blocks arrive in order from smallest to biggest, your tower gets super tall and skinny and falls over!

A Balanced Tree is like a smart robot that takes each block you hand it, and if the tower starts leaning too much to one side, it rearranges the blocks to keep the tower squat, wide, and sturdy.

That rearranging is called a rotation, and the rules that trigger it are what separate AVL trees from Red-Black trees from B-Trees.

🔥 The Problem: Why Plain BSTs Fail

Insert these values into a BST in order: [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

Solution: After every insertion or deletion, automatically rebalance the tree so the height stays O(log N).

🌿 AVL Trees

Named after inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis (1962). The first self-balancing BST ever invented.

The Balance Factor

Every node tracks its balance factor:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
balance_factor(node) = height(left subtree) − height(right subtree)

AVL invariant: Every node's balance factor must be −1, 0, or +1.

  • +1 → left-heavy (left subtree is 1 taller) ✅
  • 0 → perfectly balanced ✅
  • −1 → right-heavy (right subtree is 1 taller) ✅
  • ±2 → VIOLATION → trigger a rotation to fix it!

The 4 Rotation Cases

Rotations are local tree restructurings that preserve the BST property while fixing balance.

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    subgraph RR ["Right Rotation (for Left-Left case)"]
        direction TB
        RR1["    z (+2)\n   /\n  y (+1)\n /\nx\nRotate RIGHT at z\n↓\n  y\n / \\\nx   z"]
    end
    subgraph LR2 ["Left Rotation (for Right-Right case)"]
        direction TB
        LR1["z (-2)\n \\\n  y (-1)\n   \\\n    x\nRotate LEFT at z\n↓\n  y\n / \\\nz   x"]
    end
    subgraph LRCASE ["Left-Right Rotation (LR case)"]
        direction TB
        LRC["  z (+2)\n /\ny (-1)\n \\\n  x\n① Rotate LEFT at y → LL case\n② Rotate RIGHT at z"]
    end
    subgraph RLCASE ["Right-Left Rotation (RL case)"]
        direction TB
        RLC["z (-2)\n \\\n  y (+1)\n /\nx\n① Rotate RIGHT at y → RR case\n② Rotate LEFT at z"]
    end

AVL Complexity

OperationTimeSpace
SearchO(log N)O(log N)
InsertO(log N) — at most 1 rotationO(log N)
DeleteO(log N) — may need O(log N) rotationsO(log N)

AVL trees are more strictly balanced than Red-Black trees → faster lookups, but more rotations needed on insert/delete.

Used in: Python's sortedcontainers library (internally uses skip list actually), some database index implementations.

🔴⚫ Red-Black Trees

Invented by Rudolf Bayer (1972), popularized by Sedgewick. The most widely used self-balancing BST in practice.

The 5 Red-Black Properties

Every Red-Black tree must satisfy ALL five properties simultaneously:

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    P1["Property 1:\nEvery node is either RED or BLACK"] --> P2
    P2["Property 2:\nThe ROOT is always BLACK"] --> P3
    P3["Property 3:\nEvery LEAF (NIL node) is BLACK\n(sentinel null nodes are black)"] --> P4
    P4["Property 4:\nIf a node is RED, both its children\nmust be BLACK\n(no two consecutive red nodes)"] --> P5
    P5["Property 5:\nFor any node, ALL paths from\nthat node to any descendant NIL\nhave the SAME number of BLACK nodes\n(black-height is uniform)"]

    style P1 fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style P2 fill:#2c3e50,color:#fff
    style P3 fill:#2c3e50,color:#fff
    style P4 fill:#e74c3c,color:#fff
    style P5 fill:#8e44ad,color:#fff
State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

Why These Properties Guarantee O(log N)

Properties 4 and 5 together enforce that the longest path in the tree is at most 2× the shortest path.

  • Shortest path: all black nodes (black-height bh)
  • Longest path: alternating red-black nodes (2 × black-height)
  • Therefore: height ≤ 2 × bh ≤ 2 × log₂(N+1) → O(log N)

Red-Black vs AVL

CriterionAVL TreeRed-Black Tree
BalanceMore strictly balancedLess strictly balanced
Lookup speed⚡ Slightly fasterSlightly slower
Insert speedSlower (more rotations)⚡ Faster (at most 2 rotations)
Delete speedSlower (O(log N) rotations)⚡ Faster (at most 3 rotations)
Memory1 extra int (balance factor)1 extra bit (color)
Used inDatabases needing fast readsLinux kernel, Java TreeMap, C++ std::map
Best forRead-heavy workloadsMixed read-write workloads
[!TIP]
In interviews, you will almost never be asked to implement an AVL or Red-Black tree from scratch. But you WILL be asked:
- "Why does Python's SortedList / Java's TreeMap have O(log N) operations?"
- "What data structure would you use for a dynamic sorted set?"
- "Why is insertion into a sorted array O(N) but into a balanced BST O(log N)?"
The answer: Balanced BST (Red-Black tree) → guarantees O(log N) for all operations.

🗄️ B-Trees: The Database Tree

B-Trees are the self-balancing tree used by every major database and filesystem (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, SQLite, Linux ext4, NTFS, macOS HFS+).

Why Not Just Use Red-Black Trees?

Hard disks and SSDs read data in pages (typically 4KB or 16KB). A Red-Black tree node holds ONE key. To find a value in a million-node tree requires ~20 disk accesses (log₂ 1,000,000 ≈ 20) — and each disk access is painfully slow (milliseconds).

A B-Tree node holds HUNDREDS of keys and pointers. With branching factor ~1000, a million keys fit in a tree of height 2! Only 2-3 disk accesses instead of 20.

B-Tree Properties

A B-Tree of order m (minimum degree t):

  • Every node has at most 2t − 1 keys
  • Every node (except root) has at least t − 1 keys
  • All leaves are at the same level (perfectly balanced!)
  • Every internal node with k keys has k + 1 children

🐍 Using Balanced BSTs in Python

Python does NOT include a built-in balanced BST. Use these:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
# Option 1: sortedcontainers (pip install sortedcontainers)
from sortedcontainers import SortedList, SortedDict, SortedSet

sl = SortedList([5, 1, 3, 2, 4])
sl.add(0)           # O(log N)
sl.remove(3)        # O(log N)
sl[0]               # O(log N) — smallest element
sl.bisect_left(3)   # O(log N) — index of first element >= 3
# SortedList supports slicing: sl[2:5] is O(log N + k)

# Option 2: Use heapq for partial ordered access (only min/max)
import heapq
heap = [5, 1, 3, 2, 4]
heapq.heapify(heap)     # O(N)
heapq.heappush(heap, 0) # O(log N)
heapq.heappop(heap)     # O(log N) — always removes minimum

# Option 3: Use bisect for sorted list (no automatic rebalancing)
import bisect
arr = [1, 2, 4, 5]
bisect.insort(arr, 3)   # O(N) — but correct sorted insertion position is O(log N) to find

Theory Chapter 6: Special Trees 🌐

Chapter 6: Special Trees 🌐

Overview

So far we've covered binary trees (at most 2 children per node). The real world demands more:

  • A file system folder can have hundreds of subfolders
  • An autocomplete system needs to branch by every possible character
  • A database needs to answer "sum of values from index 3 to 97" in milliseconds

Each of these needs a specialized tree structure. This chapter maps each one, shows how they relate to binary trees, and connects them to the coding patterns in this repo.

1. N-ary Trees (General Trees)

What Is It?

An N-ary tree (also called a multiway tree or rose tree) allows each node to have any number of children — not just 2.

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100%

    D --> I(("9"))

State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

Node 1 has 3 children. Node 4 has 3 children. This is perfectly valid in an N-ary tree.

Python Representation

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
class NaryNode:
    def __init__(self, val: int, children: list['NaryNode'] = None):
        self.val      = val
        self.children = children or []

Traversals on N-ary Trees

Same concepts as binary trees, just iterate over all children:

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def n_ary_level_order(root):
    """BFS — identical logic to binary tree BFS."""
    if not root: return []
    result, queue = [], deque([root])
    while queue:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            queue.extend(node.children)   # Add ALL children, not just left/right
        result.append(level)
    return result

def n_ary_pre_order(root):
    """DFS pre-order — process root, then each child."""
    if not root: return []
    result = [root.val]
    for child in root.children:
        result.extend(n_ary_pre_order(child))
    return result

The Left-Child Right-Sibling Trick

Any N-ary tree can be encoded as a binary tree using this transformation:

  • Left child pointer → first child
  • Right child pointer → next sibling
⚡ TEXT Implementation 
N-ary tree:          Binary encoding:
    A                    A
  / | \                 /
 B  C  D               B
 |                      \
 E                       C
                          \
                           D
                          /
                         E

This is how Huffman coding trees and some recursive descent parsers work internally.

2. Trie (Prefix Tree / Radix Tree)

What Is It?

A Trie is an N-ary tree where edges represent characters. A path from root to any node spells out a prefix; a path to a marked node spells out a complete word.

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    ROOT(("ROOT")) --> C1(("c"))
    ROOT --> D1(("d"))
    C1 --> A1(("a"))
    A1 --> T1(("t✓\ncat"))
    A1 --> R1(("r✓\ncar"))
    D1 --> O1(("o"))
    O1 --> G1(("g✓\ndog"))
    O1 --> T2(("t✓\ndot"))

    style T1 fill:#00B894,color:#fff

State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

Green nodes are "end of word" markers. The trie above stores: cat, car, dog, dot.

Key Properties

  • Space: Shared prefixes are stored ONCE. "cat" and "car" both share the c → a path.
  • Search time: O(L) where L = length of search string. Completely independent of how many words are stored!
  • Alphabet size: Branching factor = alphabet size (26 for lowercase English, 128 for ASCII, 65536 for Unicode)

Operations

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children: dict[str, TrieNode] = {}
        self.is_end_of_word: bool = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()

    def insert(self, word: str) -> None:        # O(L)
        node = self.root
        for char in word:
            if char not in node.children:
                node.children[char] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[char]
        node.is_end_of_word = True

    def search(self, word: str) -> bool:         # O(L)
        node = self.root
        for char in word:
            if char not in node.children: return False
            node = node.children[char]
        return node.is_end_of_word

    def starts_with(self, prefix: str) -> bool:  # O(L)
        node = self.root
        for char in prefix:
            if char not in node.children: return False
            node = node.children[char]
        return True  # prefix exists even if no complete word ends here

4. Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree / BIT)

What Is It?

A Fenwick Tree is an implicit binary tree embedded in a flat array. It's a clever bit-manipulation trick that computes prefix sums in O(log N) time and supports point updates in O(log N).

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Index:  1   2   3   4   5   6   7   8
Array: [1] [3] [2] [5] [2] [8] [3] [4]
BIT:   [1] [4] [2] [11] [2] [10] [3] [28]

BIT[i] stores the sum of elements from (i - lowbit(i) + 1) to i
where lowbit(i) = i & (-i)  (the lowest set bit of i)

The Magic of lowbit

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def lowbit(i): return i & (-i)

# For i = 6 = 0b110:
# -i  = -6 = 0b...11111010 (two's complement)
# i & (-i) = 0b010 = 2
# So BIT[6] covers 2 elements: indices 5 and 6

# For i = 8 = 0b1000:
# lowbit(8) = 8
# BIT[8] covers 8 elements: indices 1 through 8
⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
class BIT:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n    = n
        self.tree = [0] * (n + 1)  # 1-indexed

    def update(self, i, delta):     # O(log N)
        while i <= self.n:
            self.tree[i] += delta
            i += i & (-i)           # Jump to next responsible node

    def prefix_sum(self, i):        # O(log N)
        total = 0
        while i > 0:
            total += self.tree[i]
            i -= i & (-i)           # Jump to parent
        return total

    def range_sum(self, l, r):      # O(log N)
        return self.prefix_sum(r) - self.prefix_sum(l - 1)

Segment Tree vs Fenwick Tree

CriterionSegment TreeFenwick Tree (BIT)
ComplexityO(log N)O(log N)
ConstantsSlower⚡ ~2-3x faster
Code lengthLonger⚡ Very concise
Memory4NN
Range updates✅ YesNeeds modification
Arbitrary ranges✅ YesPrefix sums only (range = prefix diff)
Functions supportedAny (min, max, GCD, XOR...)Only invertible functions (sum, XOR) — NOT min/max

5. Heap (Binary Heap)

Relationship to Binary Trees

A Heap is a Complete Binary Tree with a heap-order property:

  • Min-Heap: parent.val ≤ child.val for all nodes. Root = global minimum.
  • Max-Heap: parent.val ≥ child.val for all nodes. Root = global maximum.

It's stored as an array using the complete binary tree index formulas from Chapter 2.

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
Min-Heap tree:        Array representation:
       1               [1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 6, 4]
      / \               0  1  2  3  4  5  6
     2   3
    / \ / \
   5  7 6  4

Level-orderLevel by level"Floor by floor"1 2 3 4 5 6 7Shortest path, level queries
Mnemonics: Think of Pre/In/Post as where you put the Root relative to children:
- Pre: Root → Left → Right (root is BEFORE)
- In: Left → Root → Right (root is IN the middle)
- Post: Left → Right → Root (root is AFTER)

⚠️ Top 10 Tree Interview Traps

#TrapCorrect Knowledge
1"Complete = Full"Complete = left-to-right filled. Full = 0 or 2 children.
2"BST = Binary Tree"BST is a special binary tree with ordering.
3Validating BST only by parent-child comparisonPass (min_bound, max_bound) down the recursion.
4Forgetting to backtrack when building path listsAlways path.pop() after recursive calls.
5"Balanced = log N height"Only if formally balanced (AVL property).
6"BFS needs a visited set for trees"Trees have no cycles. Only graphs need visited sets.
7"Inserting sorted data into BST is O(log N)"Sorted insertion → skewed tree → O(N)!
8"Height and depth are the same"Depth: top-down from root. Height: bottom-up from leaves.
9"Post-order for height, pre-order for everything else"Understand WHY: post-order = bottom-up computation.
10"A heap gives O(log N) search"Heap gives O(1) min/max but O(N) search for arbitrary elements!

🏃 Interview Warm-Up Checklist

Before a tree problem, quickly ask yourself:

  • [ ] Is this a binary tree or BST or N-ary tree?
  • [ ] What traversal fits? (BFS for levels/shortest path, DFS for root-to-leaf, post-order for bottom-up)
  • [ ] Do I need to modify the tree? (Careful about mutating while traversing)
  • [ ] What's the base case? (if not node: return ...)
  • [ ] Am I building a path? (Need to backtrack — append before, pop after)
  • [ ] Is the tree balanced? (Affects space complexity of my recursive call stack)
  • [ ] Does the problem use a BST property? (Can I use it to eliminate half the tree?)

Theory Chapter 1: What Is a Graph? 🕸️

Chapter 1: What Is a Graph? 🕸️

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you're playing with a map of your city.

  • Every building (airport, school, house) is a dot.
  • Every road connecting two buildings is a line.

Now here's what makes a city map different from a family tree:

  1. Roads can go both ways — you can drive from school to home AND from home to school.
  2. Some roads are one-way — like a one-way street: you can go from A to B but not back.
  3. Some buildings are connected to many others — a highway interchange connects dozens of roads.
  4. You can go in circles — drive around the block and end up where you started!

That city map IS a graph. It's the most flexible and powerful data structure in computer science.

Trees are the "tidy" version of graphs — no loops, everything flows neatly top-down. Real-world problems (social networks, roads, web pages, dependencies) are messy graphs.

🎯 Formal Definition

A Graph G = (V, E) is a pair of:
- V — a set of vertices (also called nodes)
- E — a set of edges, where each edge connects a pair of vertices

Example: The graph of cities connected by flights.

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
V = {NYC, LAX, CHI, MIA, SEA}
E = {(NYC, LAX), (NYC, CHI), (CHI, MIA), (LAX, SEA), (CHI, SEA)}

🤝 The Handshaking Lemma

For any undirected graph: The sum of all vertex degrees equals 2 × |E|.
$$\sum_{v \in V} \deg(v) = 2|E|$$

Intuition: Every edge contributes exactly 2 to the total degree count — one for each of its two endpoints. When you shake hands, both people's "handshake count" goes up by 1.

Corollary: In any graph, the number of vertices with odd degree is always even. (Can you prove this? It follows directly from the lemma: if the sum is 2|E| — an even number — the odd-degree vertices must pair up.)

Example verification (from our diagram):

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
degree(A) = 3, degree(B) = 2, degree(C) = 3, degree(D) = 2, degree(E) = 1, degree(F) = 1
Sum = 3+2+3+2+1+1 = 12
|E| = 6 (edges: A-B, B-C, C-D, D-A, A-C, E-F)
2×|E| = 12 ✅

PropertyTreeGraph
ConnectedAlways ✅Not required

EdgesExactly N−10 to N(N-1)/2

Key insight: Because trees have no cycles, you never revisit a node during traversal. Graphs CAN have cycles — so without a visited set, you'll loop forever.

📐 Euler's Formula (Planar Graphs)

For a connected planar graph (a graph that can be drawn on a plane without edge crossings):

$$V - E + F = 2$$

Where:

  • V = vertices
  • E = edges
  • F = faces (regions, including the outer infinite region)

Example: A cube has V=8, E=12, F=6 → 8 - 12 + 6 = 2 ✅

For trees: Trees have no "enclosed" faces. F = 1 (just the outer region).

N - (N-1) + 1 = 2 ✅ (confirms our earlier formula E = N−1)

📊 Graph Density

Two important classes:

ClassDefinition
Sparse Graph`E≈V` — few edgesRoad networks, social graphs
Dense Graph`E≈V²` — many edgesComplete graphs, dense matrices
Complete Graph K_nEvery vertex connected to every other`E= N(N-1)/2`

This distinction matters for choosing representations:

  • Sparse → Adjacency List (wastes no space)
  • Dense → Adjacency Matrix (O(1) edge lookup pays off)

Chapter 2: Graph Types 🗂️

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Graphs come in many flavors. When you look at a real-world problem and ask "is this a graph?", the next question is always "what kind of graph?"

  • Twitter → Directed: you can follow someone without them following back.
  • Facebook → Undirected: friendships are mutual.
  • Google Maps → Weighted: roads have distances/travel times.
  • University courses → DAG: no circular prerequisites (you can't need a course that needs itself).
  • Checkerboard → Bipartite: black squares only connect to white squares.

Knowing the type of graph immediately tells you which algorithms apply!

The most fundamental distinction.

In-degree vs Out-degree (directed graphs):

  • In-degree of v = number of edges pointing into v
  • Out-degree of v = number of edges pointing out of v
  • Handshaking lemma for directed: Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|

2. Weighted vs Unweighted

Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Unweighted ["Unweighted"]
        A1((A)) --- B1((B))
        B1 --- C1((C))
        A1 --- C1

State convergence & algorithmic execution graph
  • Unweighted: All edges have equal "cost". Shortest path = fewest edges → BFS.
  • Weighted: Edges have costs/distances/capacities. Shortest path ≠ fewest edges → Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford.

Weights can be:

  • Positive (distances, costs) → Dijkstra's works
  • Negative (profits, gains) → Need Bellman-Ford
  • Zero (free to traverse) → 0-1 BFS or regular BFS

3. DAG — Directed Acyclic Graph

A DAG is a directed graph with no directed cycles.

Course prerequisites — a classic DAG. You can't take Algorithms without first taking both Data Structures and Calculus.

Key DAG properties:

  • Has at least one topological ordering (a valid processing order)
  • Has at least one source (in-degree 0, e.g. CS101) and one sink (out-degree 0, e.g. CS401)
  • Every tree is a DAG (trees are acyclic by definition)

Real-world DAGs:

  • Build systems (Makefile, Bazel, Gradle)
  • Package managers (pip, npm dependency resolution)
  • Git commit history
  • Excel spreadsheet formula dependencies
  • Neural network computation graphs

Pattern connection: Pattern 27 — Topological Sort

4. Bipartite Graph

A graph where vertices can be split into two disjoint sets U and V, such that every edge connects a vertex in U to a vertex in V (no edges within the same set).

State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

2-colorable = Bipartite: A graph is bipartite if and only if you can 2-color it (color each vertex Red or Blue) such that no two adjacent vertices share a color.

Detection: BFS/DFS with 2-coloring. If you ever need to assign the same color to two adjacent vertices → NOT bipartite (has an odd-length cycle).

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def is_bipartite(graph):
    color = {}
    for start in range(len(graph)):
        if start in color: continue
        queue = deque([start])
        color[start] = 0
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            for neighbor in graph[node]:
                if neighbor not in color:
                    color[neighbor] = 1 - color[node]  # Flip color
                    queue.append(neighbor)
                elif color[neighbor] == color[node]:
                    return False  # Same color → not bipartite
    return True

Real-world bipartite graphs:

  • Job assignments (people ↔ jobs)
  • Movie recommendations (users ↔ movies)
  • Course enrollment (students ↔ courses)
  • Dating apps (users ↔ potential matches)

8. Planar Graphs

Kuratowski's Theorem: A graph is planar if and only if it contains no subdivision of K₅ (complete graph with 5 vertices) or K₃,₃ (complete bipartite graph with 3+3 vertices).

For planar graphs, Euler's formula holds: V − E + F = 2

Interview use: Circuit board layout, geographic map coloring (4-Color Theorem: any planar map can be colored with 4 colors so no adjacent regions share a color).

⚠️ Common Misconceptions

MisconceptionReality
"A DAG is a tree"Not necessarily. A DAG can have multiple paths between nodes — it just can't have directed cycles.
"Bipartite = even number of nodes"No. Bipartite means 2-colorable. K₃ (triangle) has 3 nodes and is NOT bipartite. K₄ (square minus one edge) can be bipartite.
"Strongly connected = connected"Strongly connected is stricter — it requires directed paths in BOTH directions.
"A cycle means the graph isn't useful"Cycles are essential — they model things like "returning home", circular dependencies to detect, and Hamiltonian paths.
