🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N \log N)$. Sorting the jobs takes $O(N \log N)$. Iterating through the $N$ jobs and performing heap pushes/pops takes $O(\log N)$ per operation.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst-case scenario where all jobs overlap simultaneously, the min-heap will store $N$ tuples.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Exact boundary touching: e.g., [1, 2, load: 5] and [2, 3, load: 5]. The condition job.start >= min_heap[0][0] translates to 2 >= 2, which is True. The first job is popped, its load is subtracted, and then the new job is added. The current_load briefly drops to 0 and goes back up to 5. It never incorrectly spikes to 10.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
import heapq

class Job:
    def __init__(self, start, end, cpu_load):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end
        self.cpu_load = cpu_load

def find_max_cpu_load(jobs: list[Job]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the maximum CPU load at any time if all jobs run on the same machine.
    """
    if not jobs:
        return 0

    # 1. Sort the jobs by start time
    jobs.sort(key=lambda x: x.start)

    max_load: int = 0
    current_load: int = 0
    min_heap: list[tuple[int, int]] = [] # Stores (end_time, cpu_load)

    for job in jobs:
        # Remove all jobs that have ended
        while min_heap and job.start >= min_heap[0][0]:
            ended_job_end_time, ended_job_load = heapq.heappop(min_heap)
            current_load -= ended_job_load

        # Add the current job to the heap and to the current load
        heapq.heappush(min_heap, (job.end, job.cpu_load))
        current_load += job.cpu_load

        # Record the maximum load we've seen so far
        max_load = max(max_load, current_load)

    return max_load

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    jobs1 = [Job(1, 4, 3), Job(2, 5, 4), Job(7, 9, 6)]
    assert find_max_cpu_load(jobs1) == 7, "Test 1 failed: Overlap [1,4] and [2,5] -> 3+4=7"

    jobs2 = [Job(6, 7, 10), Job(2, 4, 11), Job(8, 12, 15)]
    assert find_max_cpu_load(jobs2) == 15, "Test 2 failed: No overlap, max is 15"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    jobs3 = [Job(1, 4, 2), Job(2, 4, 1), Job(3, 6, 5)]
    assert find_max_cpu_load(jobs3) == 8, "Edge 1: Multiple overlapping (2+1+5=8)"
    
    jobs4 = [Job(1, 2, 5), Job(2, 3, 5)]
    assert find_max_cpu_load(jobs4) == 5, "Edge 2: Exact boundary touching (does not sum)"
    
    assert find_max_cpu_load([]) == 0, "Edge 3: Empty list"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N log N) — Sorting takes O(N log N). Heap operations take O(log N) for N jobs. 💾 Space: O(N) — In the worst case (all jobs overlap), the heap stores N jobs.
Hard Employee Free Time
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Employee Free Time

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a team of 3 people. Each person gives you a list of the times they are busy working today.

You want to schedule a team-building pizza party, which means you need to find all the times when EVERYONE is free!

Since everyone is free when no one is working, this is the exact opposite of finding when people are busy.

If we take EVERY single working shift from ALL employees, dump them into a big pile, and sort them from morning to night, we just need to look for the "GAPS" between the shifts!

If the latest time anyone has worked so far is 3:00, and the next person doesn't start working until 4:00, then from 3:00 to 4:00, the whole team is free!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a clever inversion of the standard Merge Intervals pattern. Instead of merging overlapping intervals, we are looking for the empty space between merged intervals.

  1. Flatten the Schedule: Take the lists of intervals from all employees and combine them into one massive, flat list of intervals.
  2. Sort all the intervals in this massive list by their start time.
  3. Keep track of the max_end time we've seen so far. Initialize it to the first interval's end time.
  4. Iterate through the sorted intervals starting from the second one (index 1):
  5. Find the Gap: If the current interval's start time is STRICTLY GREATER than max_end, we found a gap where no one is working! Add the interval [max_end, current.start] to our free_time list.
  6. Update max_end: Regardless of whether we found a gap or not, we might have overlapping or extending shifts. Update max_end = max(max_end, current.end).
  7. Return the free_time list.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: schedule = [[[1, 3], [9, 12]], [[2, 4]], [[6, 8]]]

  1. Flatten: [[1, 3], [9, 12], [2, 4], [6, 8]]
  2. Sort: [[1, 3], [2, 4], [6, 8], [9, 12]]
  3. Initialize: max_end = 3, free_time = []
StepCurrent Shiftmax_end (Before)Gap Found? (start > max_end)Actionmax_end (After)free_time State
1[2, 4]32 > 3? No.Just update max_end.max(3, 4) = 4[]
2[6, 8]46 > 4? YES!Found gap! Add [4, 6].max(4, 8) = 8[[4, 6]]
3[9, 12]89 > 8? YES!Found gap! Add [8, 9].max(8, 12) = 12[[4, 6], [8, 9]]

Result: [[4, 6], [8, 9]]

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N \log N)$. $N$ is the total number of intervals across all employees. Flattening takes $O(N)$, sorting takes $O(N \log N)$, and the final iteration takes $O(N)$. The bottleneck is the sorting step.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. We create a new flat list containing all $N$ intervals, and the result array can also contain up to $N$ free time gaps.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Overlapping Chain: e.g., [[1, 3], [2, 4], [3, 5]]. max_end will smoothly update from 3 to 4 to 5 without ever triggering the gap condition, correctly recognizing that the team is continuously busy from 1 to 5.
  • Identical Hours: If everyone works [9, 5], sorting puts them together, and max_end stays 5 while no gaps are detected. Works perfectly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
class Interval:
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.start == other.start and self.end == other.end
        
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"[{self.start}, {self.end}]"

def find_employee_free_time(schedule: list[list[Interval]]) -> list[Interval]:
    """
    Finds the finite intervals of free time common to all employees.
    """
    # 1. Flatten the schedule
    all_intervals: list[Interval] = []
    for employee in schedule:
        all_intervals.extend(employee)

    if not all_intervals:
        return []

    # 2. Sort by start time
    all_intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x.start)

    free_time: list[Interval] = []
    
    # 3. Track the maximum end time seen so far
    max_end: int = all_intervals[0].end

    # 4. Find the gaps
    for i in range(1, len(all_intervals)):
        current = all_intervals[i]

        if current.start > max_end:
            # We found a gap where no one is working!
            free_time.append(Interval(max_end, current.start))
        
        # Always update the max_end
        max_end = max(max_end, current.end)

    return free_time

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    sched1 = [[Interval(1, 3), Interval(5, 6)], [Interval(2, 3), Interval(6, 8)]]
    res1 = find_employee_free_time(sched1)
    assert res1 == [Interval(3, 5)], f"Test 1 failed: {res1}"

    sched2 = [[Interval(1, 3), Interval(9, 12)], [Interval(2, 4)], [Interval(6, 8)]]
    res2 = find_employee_free_time(sched2)
    assert res2 == [Interval(4, 6), Interval(8, 9)], f"Test 2 failed: {res2}"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    sched3 = [[Interval(1, 3)], [Interval(2, 4)], [Interval(3, 5), Interval(7, 9)]]
    res3 = find_employee_free_time(sched3)
    assert res3 == [Interval(5, 7)], "Edge 1: Overlapping chain"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N log N) — Where N is the total number of intervals across all employees. Sorting takes O(N log N). 💾 Space: O(N) — To store the flattened list and the resulting gaps.
Medium Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine there are several long balloons taped to a wall. You have a bow and arrow. When you shoot an arrow straight up, it pops EVERY balloon it touches on its way up!

You want to pop all the balloons using the FEWEST arrows possible.

To pop the most balloons with a single arrow, you want to wait as long as possible before shooting. Specifically, you should shoot at the exact moment the FIRST balloon in your line of sight is about to end.

If you shoot there, you pop that balloon, AND you pop any other balloons that have already started!

To do this easily, we DON'T sort the balloons by when they start. We sort the balloons by when they END. Then we just shoot an arrow at the end of the first balloon, and skip over all other balloons that get popped by that arrow!

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses a Greedy Strategy by sorting intervals by their END time.

  1. Sort the balloons based on their end time, not start time.
  2. Initialize arrows = 1. (Assuming there is at least one balloon, we always need at least one arrow).
  3. Set current_arrow_pos = balloons[0].end. This is where we aggressively shoot our first arrow.
  4. Loop through the remaining balloons:
  5. Missed!: If the next balloon starts strictly AFTER our current_arrow_pos (balloon.start > current_arrow_pos):
  6. Our current arrow completely missed this balloon! We need to shoot a new one.
  7. Increment arrows += 1.
  8. Update our new shooting spot to the end of this new balloon: current_arrow_pos = balloon.end.
  9. Popped!: If the next balloon starts BEFORE or EXACTLY ON the current_arrow_pos (balloon.start <= current_arrow_pos), it gets popped by our current arrow! We do absolutely nothing and move to the next balloon.
  10. Return the total number of arrows.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: balloons = [[10, 16], [2, 8], [1, 6], [7, 12]]

  1. Sort by End Time: [[1, 6], [2, 8], [7, 12], [10, 16]]
  2. Initialize: arrows = 1, current_arrow_pos = 6 (End of the first balloon).

2[7, 12]67 > 6? YES!Missed! New arrow.122

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N \log N)$. Sorting the balloons by their end times takes $O(N \log N)$. The subsequent greedy pass only loops through the array once, taking $O(N)$ time. The total complexity is dominated by the sort.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$ or $O(\log N)$ depending on the underlying sorting algorithm used by the language (Python's Timsort uses $O(N)$ space).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Balloons exactly touch boundaries: e.g., [1, 2] and [2, 3]. Arrow shoots at x=2. For the second balloon, start (2) > arrow (2) is False. The code perfectly recognizes that a single arrow shot exactly at the boundary pops both!
  • Empty List: Fast-path if not balloons: return 0 handles it safely.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
class Interval:
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

def find_min_arrows(balloons: list[Interval]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the minimum number of arrows required to burst all balloons.
    """
    if not balloons:
        return 0

    # 1. Sort the balloons by END time (Greedy strategy)
    balloons.sort(key=lambda x: x.end)

    arrows: int = 1
    # 2. Shoot the first arrow at the end of the first balloon
    current_arrow_pos: int = balloons[0].end

    for i in range(1, len(balloons)):
        current_balloon = balloons[i]

        # 3. If the next balloon starts AFTER our arrow, it is completely missed.
        if current_balloon.start > current_arrow_pos:
            # We need a new arrow
            arrows += 1
            # Shoot this new arrow at the end of the current balloon
            current_arrow_pos = current_balloon.end

    return arrows

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    b1 = [Interval(10, 16), Interval(2, 8), Interval(1, 6), Interval(7, 12)]
    # Sorted by end: [1,6], [2,8], [7,12], [10,16]
    # Arrow 1 at 6 pops [1,6], [2,8]
    # Arrow 2 at 12 pops [7,12], [10,16]
    assert find_min_arrows(b1) == 2, "Test 1 failed"

    b2 = [Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4), Interval(5, 6), Interval(7, 8)]
    assert find_min_arrows(b2) == 4, "Test 2 failed: 4 distinct balloons"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    b3 = [Interval(1, 2), Interval(2, 3)]
    assert find_min_arrows(b3) == 1, "Edge 1: Touching boundaries pop with 1 arrow"
    
    assert find_min_arrows([]) == 0, "Edge 2: Empty list"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N log N) — Sorting by end time takes O(N log N). The greedy pass takes O(N). 💾 Space: O(N) or O(log N) — Depending on Python's sort overhead.
Medium Non-overlapping Intervals
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Non-overlapping Intervals

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a bunch of meetings scheduled, but you realize that a lot of them overlap! You are exhausted, so you want to cancel the FEWEST number of meetings possible so that none of the remaining meetings overlap.

Here is the trick: to cancel the fewest meetings, we want to KEEP the most meetings.

How do we fit the most meetings into a day? We always choose the meeting that FINISHES the earliest! By finishing early, it leaves the rest of the day wide open for more meetings.

So, we sort the meetings by their END time.

We attend the first meeting. If the next meeting overlaps with the one we are attending, we just skip it (cancel it). If it doesn't overlap, we attend it!

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses a Greedy Strategy by sorting intervals by their END time, exactly like the "Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons" problem.

  1. Sort the intervals by their end time. This is the crucial greedy step: always favor the interval that ends first to leave room for future intervals.
  2. Initialize removed_count = 0.
  3. Set current_end = intervals[0].end. This tracks the end time of the meeting we have chosen to attend.
  4. Loop through the remaining intervals. For each interval:
  5. Conflict: If the next interval starts BEFORE our current meeting ends (interval.start < current_end):
  6. We have an overlap! Because we sorted by end time, the current_end meeting we already chose finishes earlier (or at the same time) as this conflicting one. Keeping the earlier-ending one is mathematically always the better choice.
  7. So, we KEEP the current one and CANCEL the new conflicting one: removed_count += 1.
  8. No Conflict: If the next interval starts exactly when or after our current meeting ends:
  9. We can safely attend this new meeting!
  10. Update current_end = interval.end.
  11. Return removed_count.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: intervals = [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4], [1, 3]]

  1. Sort by End Time: [[1, 2], [2, 3], [1, 3], [3, 4]]
  2. Initialize: removed_count = 0, current_end = 2 (from the first meeting [1, 2]).
StepCurrent Meetingcurrent_endConflict? (start < current_end)Actionremoved_count
1[2, 3]22 < 2? No.Attend! Update current_end to 3.0
2[1, 3]31 < 3? YES!Conflict! Cancel this meeting.1
3[3, 4]33 < 3? No.Attend! Update current_end to 4.1

Result: 1 meeting removed.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N \log N)$. Sorting the intervals by their end times takes $O(N \log N)$. The subsequent greedy pass loops through the array exactly once, taking $O(N)$ time. The total complexity is dominated by the sorting step.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$ or $O(\log N)$ depending on the underlying sorting algorithm used by the language (Python's Timsort uses $O(N)$ space).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Touching boundaries: e.g., [1, 2] and [2, 3]. The condition checks if 2 < 2. This evaluates to False. The algorithm correctly recognizes that these do NOT overlap and attends both.
  • Empty List: Fast-path if not intervals: return 0 handles an empty schedule instantly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
class Interval:
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

def erase_overlap_intervals(intervals: list[Interval]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the minimum number of intervals to remove to make the rest non-overlapping.
    """
    if not intervals:
        return 0

    # 1. Sort the intervals by END time (Greedy strategy)
    intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x.end)

    removed_count: int = 0
    current_end: int = intervals[0].end

    for i in range(1, len(intervals)):
        interval = intervals[i]

        # 2. Check for overlap
        if interval.start < current_end:
            # Overlap! We remove this interval.
            removed_count += 1
        else:
            # No overlap! We keep it and update our current end time.
            current_end = interval.end

    return removed_count

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [Interval(1, 2), Interval(2, 3), Interval(3, 4), Interval(1, 3)]
    assert erase_overlap_intervals(arr1) == 1, "Test 1 failed: Remove [1,3]"

    arr2 = [Interval(1, 2), Interval(1, 2), Interval(1, 2)]
    assert erase_overlap_intervals(arr2) == 2, "Test 2 failed: Keep one [1,2], remove others"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [Interval(1, 2), Interval(2, 3)]
    assert erase_overlap_intervals(arr3) == 0, "Edge 1: Touching boundaries don't overlap"
    
    assert erase_overlap_intervals([]) == 0, "Edge 2: Empty list"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N log N) — Sorting by end time takes O(N log N). The loop takes O(N). 💾 Space: O(N) or O(log N) — Depending on Python's sort overhead.
Hard Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Data Stream as Disjoint Intervals

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you are building a jigsaw puzzle, but someone is handing you pieces one by one. Each piece has a number.

If someone hands you piece 1, you put it down. If someone hands you piece 3, you put it down. Right now you have two separate blocks: [1, 1] and [3, 3].

If someone then hands you piece 2, suddenly all three pieces connect! You can merge them all together to say you have a single solid block from [1, 3].

Because pieces are handed to you one by one, you need a fast way to slot a piece into the correct place in your sorted list, and then just check if it connects to its immediate left or right neighbors.

🎯 Core Strategy

Since the integers arrive as a stream, we can't afford to re-sort the entire list every single time using $O(N \log N)$. Instead, we use Binary Search and Dynamic Insertion.

  1. Maintain a intervals list that is always sorted and merged.
  2. When a new value arrives, use Binary Search to find its exact insertion position.
  3. If the value is already completely inside one of the existing intervals, it's a duplicate! Ignore it entirely.
  4. If it's not a duplicate, insert a tiny single-point interval [value, value] at the found index.
  5. Merge Left: Check the newly inserted interval against its immediate LEFT neighbor.
  6. If left_neighbor.end + 1 == new_interval.start, they connect perfectly!
  7. Expand the left neighbor's end, and delete the new_interval. The left neighbor is now the "active" merged interval.
  8. Merge Right: Check the active interval against its immediate RIGHT neighbor.
  9. If active_interval.end + 1 == right_neighbor.start, they connect perfectly!
  10. Expand the active interval's end, and delete the right neighbor.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Stream: add(1), add(3), add(7), add(2)

ActionStreamBinary Search IndexInsertion & Merge LogicResulting intervals
add(1)10Insert [1, 1]. No neighbors to merge.[[1, 1]]
add(3)31Insert [3, 3]. Left 1+1 != 3. No merge.[[1, 1], [3, 3]]
add(7)72Insert [7, 7]. Left 3+1 != 7. No merge.[[1, 1], [3, 3], [7, 7]]
add(2)21Insert [2, 2] at idx 1. <br> Merge Left: 1+1 == 2. Merge into [1, 2]. <br> Merge Right: 2+1 == 3. Merge into [1, 3].[[1, 3], [7, 7]]

Result after all additions: [[1, 3], [7, 7]]

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity:
  • addNum(value): $O(N)$. Binary search takes $O(\log N)$, but inserting an element into the middle of a Python list takes $O(N)$ because elements must be shifted. Merging takes $O(1)$.
  • getIntervals(): $O(1)$. We just return the already-maintained list.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. We store up to $N$ disjoint intervals in the worst case where no numbers connect.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Duplicate numbers: Handled gracefully by the Binary Search phase. if interval.start <= value <= interval.end: return. This guarantees $O(\log N)$ time for duplicates, instantly rejecting them.
  • Cascading Merges: This algorithm relies on the fact that inserting ONE number can at most merge ONE interval on the left and ONE interval on the right. It cannot trigger a massive chain reaction, so the double if check is perfectly sufficient without needing a while loop.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
class Interval:
    def __init__(self, start, end):
        self.start = start
        self.end = end

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.start == other.start and self.end == other.end
        
    def __repr__(self):
        return f"[{self.start}, {self.end}]"

class SummaryRanges:
    def __init__(self):
        self.intervals: list[Interval] = []

    def addNum(self, value: int) -> None:
        # Binary search to find the correct insertion index
        left, right = 0, len(self.intervals) - 1
        
        while left <= right:
            mid = (left + right) // 2
            interval = self.intervals[mid]
            
            # If the value is already completely inside an existing interval, do nothing
            if interval.start <= value <= interval.end:
                return
            elif interval.start > value:
                right = mid - 1
            else:
                left = mid + 1
                
        # Insert the new interval at the found position
        idx = left
        self.intervals.insert(idx, Interval(value, value))
        
        # Merge with the left neighbor if they connect
        if idx > 0 and self.intervals[idx - 1].end + 1 == self.intervals[idx].start:
            self.intervals[idx - 1].end = self.intervals[idx].end
            self.intervals.pop(idx)
            idx -= 1  # The active interval shifted one spot left
            
        # Merge with the right neighbor if they connect
        if idx < len(self.intervals) - 1 and self.intervals[idx].end + 1 == self.intervals[idx + 1].start:
            self.intervals[idx].end = self.intervals[idx + 1].end
            self.intervals.pop(idx + 1)

    def getIntervals(self) -> list[Interval]:
        return self.intervals

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    sr = SummaryRanges()
    
    sr.addNum(1)
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 1)]
    
    sr.addNum(3)
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 1), Interval(3, 3)]
    
    sr.addNum(7)
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 1), Interval(3, 3), Interval(7, 7)]
    
    sr.addNum(2) # Connects 1 and 3!
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 3), Interval(7, 7)]
    
    sr.addNum(6) # Connects to 7
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 3), Interval(6, 7)]
    
    sr.addNum(6) # Duplicate, should do nothing
    assert sr.getIntervals() == [Interval(1, 3), Interval(6, 7)]

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) per `addNum` — Binary search is O(log N), but list insertion is O(N). 💾 Space: O(N) — To store the disjoint intervals.

06 - Cyclic Sort

Sorters 8 Problems
📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 06: Cyclic Sort

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you are a teacher and you have 5 students. Their ID numbers are exactly

1, 2, 3, 4, and 5.

They are sitting in 5 chairs, but they are all jumbled up!

Student #4 is sitting in Chair #1, Student #2 is in Chair #5, etc.

You want them sorted. You COULD make them all stand up, compare heights or IDs

(which takes a long time, like regular sorting).

OR, you can use a magic trick:

You walk up to Chair #1 and see Student #4 sitting there. You say, "Hey! You

belong in Chair #4!"

You make Student #4 swap seats with whoever is currently in Chair #4.

You keep doing this until the person in Chair #1 is actually Student #1. Then

you move to Chair #2 and do the same thing!

Because every single swap puts at least ONE student in their forever-correct seat,

you only ever have to do exactly 5 swaps! It's incredibly fast.

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

The Cyclic Sort pattern is the absolute best way to solve problems involving arrays containing numbers in a given range (e.g., 1 to N or 0 to N).

When to use it:

  • The problem explicitly mentions an array of numbers in the range 1 to N (or 0 to N).
  • You are asked to find missing, duplicate, or smallest numbers in an array.
  • You are required to solve the problem in O(N) time and O(1) space. (This is the biggest giveaway!)

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Standard Cyclic Sort

  1. Iterate through the array with a while loop and an index pointer i = 0.
  2. Determine the "correct" index for the current number.
  3. If numbers are 1 to N, the correct index is j = nums[i] - 1.
  4. If numbers are 0 to N, the correct index is j = nums[i].
  5. If nums[i] is within the valid bounds AND nums[i] != nums[j]:
  6. Swap nums[i] and nums[j].
  7. Do NOT increment i. We need to re-evaluate the new number that just landed at index i!
  8. If it IS at the correct index (or it's an out-of-bounds number we don't care about):
  9. Increment i += 1.
  10. After the array is sorted, do a second pass (a simple for loop). Any index i where nums[i] != i + 1 points to the missing/duplicate number!

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Base PatternDO use a while i < len(nums) loop. You only increment i when the current index holds the correct number.DON'T use a for loop to sort. A for loop forces i to increment on every step, even if the newly swapped number is in the wrong spot!
Out-of-bounds numbersDO add a check if 0 < nums[i] <= len(nums) before swapping. Ignore numbers that don't belong in the range.DON'T let Python throw an IndexError. Always validate j.
DuplicatesDO realize that if you try to swap nums[i] to j, but nums[j] ALREADY equals nums[i], you've found a duplicate!DON'T get stuck in an infinite swapping loop of identical numbers. The swap condition must be nums[i] != nums[j].

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)Although there is a while loop that doesn't always increment i, every single swap places at least one number in its correct, final position. Thus, at most N-1 swaps occur across the entire traversal.
SpaceO(1)All sorting and swapping is done completely in-place.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Infinite Swapping Loop: If your swap condition is just nums[i] != i + 1, and the array contains duplicates (e.g., [1, 1]), you will try to swap the 1 at index 0 with the 1 at index 0 forever. The condition MUST compare values: nums[i] != nums[nums[i] - 1].
  2. 0-indexed vs 1-indexed: Be extremely careful about whether the problem guarantees numbers from 0 to N or 1 to N.
  3. If 1 to N: j = nums[i] - 1. The second pass checks nums[i] != i + 1.
  4. If 0 to N: j = nums[i]. The second pass checks nums[i] != i.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Cyclic Sort

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a bunch of numbered boxes mixed up in a row. The numbers on the boxes are exactly 1, 2, 3, up to $N$.

You want to put Box 1 in the 1st spot, Box 2 in the 2nd spot, and so on.

Instead of looking at all the boxes at once and getting confused, you just look at the box in the 1st spot.

If it's Box 4, you say, "Hey! You belong in the 4th spot!" So you take Box 4 and swap it with whatever box is currently sitting in the 4th spot.

Now you look at the 1st spot again (it has a new box in it now). Is it Box 1 yet? If not, keep swapping it with the spot where it belongs!

Once Box 1 is finally in the 1st spot, you move on to the 2nd spot and repeat.

Eventually, every box gets swapped exactly once into its perfect home.

🎯 Core Strategy

When you are given an array of numbers in a known range (like $1$ to $N$), the Cyclic Sort pattern is the most powerful $O(N)$ sorting algorithm because it uses the numbers themselves as indices.

  1. Initialize a pointer i = 0.
  2. Loop through the array using a while loop (because we only want to move i forward when a condition is met).
  3. The correct index for the number nums[i] is nums[i] - 1 (because numbers start at 1, but array indices start at 0). Let's call this correct index j.
  4. Not Happy: If nums[i] is NOT currently sitting at its correct index j (nums[i] != nums[j]):
  5. Swap nums[i] and nums[j].
  6. Do NOT increment i yet! The new number we just swapped into index i might still be wrong, so we have to check it again on the next loop.
  7. Happy: If nums[i] IS at its correct index:
  8. Everything is perfect here. Increment i += 1.
  9. Return the sorted array.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Even though there is a while loop containing an if/else, every single time a swap happens, at least one number is permanently placed in its correct, final position. Since there are $N$ numbers, there can be at most $N-1$ swaps. The outer while loop iterates $N$ times. Total operations bounded by $2N \rightarrow O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All sorting is done in-place by swapping elements. No extra memory is used.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Already Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The if nums[i] != nums[j] condition will always be false. i will increment $N$ times with 0 swaps.
  • Reverse Order: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Performs exactly $O(N)$ swaps, constantly tossing the numbers into their proper buckets.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def cyclic_sort(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Sorts an array containing numbers from 1 to N in O(N) time and O(1) space.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    while i < n:
        # The correct index for the number at nums[i]
        j: int = nums[i] - 1
        
        # If the number is not at its correct index, swap them
        if nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            # Only increment if the current number is happy
            i += 1

    return nums

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [3, 1, 5, 4, 2]
    assert cyclic_sort(arr1) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], f"Test 1 failed: {arr1}"

    arr2 = [2, 6, 4, 3, 1, 5]
    assert cyclic_sort(arr2) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], f"Test 2 failed: {arr2}"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    assert cyclic_sort(arr3) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "Edge 1: Already sorted"
    
    arr4 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    assert cyclic_sort(arr4) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "Edge 2: Reverse order"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Even though there's a while loop, every swap places at least one number in its correct position. The maximum number of swaps is N-1. Total time is O(N) + O(N-1) = O(N). 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find the Missing Number

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a set of puzzle pieces numbered from 0 to $N$. But there is one problem: your box only holds $N$ pieces, so exactly ONE piece is missing!

Because the pieces are numbered starting at 0, their numbers match their spots perfectly! (Piece 0 belongs at index 0, Piece 3 belongs at index 3).

Wait, what if we find Piece $N$? There is no index $N$ since the box only holds $N$ pieces (indices 0 to $N-1$). That's totally fine! If we find Piece $N$, we just ignore it and leave it where it is. We just keep swapping all the OTHER pieces into their correct spots.

Once we are done swapping, we just walk down the line. If we look at index 2 and don't see Piece 2, we know that Piece 2 is the missing one!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a standard Cyclic Sort with two minor twists: numbers start at $0$, and one number ($N$) is out of bounds.

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  4. The correct index for the number nums[i] is exactly nums[i]. Let j = nums[i].
  5. Check Bounds & Swap: If the number is a valid index (j < n) AND it is not already at its correct index (nums[i] != nums[j]):
  6. Swap nums[i] and nums[j].
  7. Do NOT increment i.
  8. Ignore / Happy: Else (the number is $N$, or it's already in the correct spot):
  9. Increment i += 1.
  10. Find (Second pass):
  11. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  12. The first index where the number doesn't match the index (nums[i] != i) is the missing number! Return i.
  13. If all indices match their numbers perfectly, the missing number must be $N$ itself. Return n.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. The first pass places elements in their correct indices using at most $N-1$ swaps. The second pass iterates through the array once. $O(N) + O(N) = O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All operations are done in-place.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Missing number is $N$: e.g., [0, 1, 2]. The sort phase finishes doing absolutely nothing. The second pass verifies 0==0, 1==1, 2==2. The loop finishes without returning, so the function hits the final line return n, which correctly returns 3.
  • Missing number is 0: e.g., [1, 2, 3]. The sort phase results in [3, 1, 2]. The second pass immediately checks index 0, sees 3 != 0, and returns 0.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_missing_number(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the missing number from an array containing numbers in the range 0 to N.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i]
        
        # If the number is within bounds and not at its correct index, swap
        if j < n and nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            # We either found the correct number, OR we found 'n' which is out of bounds
            i += 1

    # 2. Second pass to find the missing number
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i:
            return i

    # 3. If all numbers are correct, then 'n' itself is the missing number
    return n

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [4, 0, 3, 1]
    assert find_missing_number(arr1) == 2, "Test 1 failed: Missing 2"

    arr2 = [8, 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 0, 1]
    assert find_missing_number(arr2) == 7, "Test 2 failed: Missing 7"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [0, 1, 2, 3]
    assert find_missing_number(arr3) == 4, "Edge 1: Missing N"
    
    arr4 = [1, 2, 3]
    assert find_missing_number(arr4) == 0, "Edge 2: Missing 0"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to sort (with at most N swaps), one pass to find the missing number. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find all Missing Numbers

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a box of 8 puzzle pieces, but someone mixed them up, and even worse, they accidentally put some duplicate pieces in the box and lost some of the original pieces! The pieces are supposed to be numbered 1 through 8.

We use our Cyclic Sort magic trick to put every piece in its correct spot. If we pick up Piece 3, we put it in the 3rd spot.

But what if we pick up another Piece 3 later? We look at the 3rd spot, see that a Piece 3 is already sitting there perfectly happy, and we say, "Oh well, you're a duplicate." We just leave the duplicate exactly where we found it and move on!

After we try to sort the whole box, we just walk down the line. If the 5th spot doesn't have a Piece 5 in it (maybe it has a duplicate Piece 3 stuck there instead), we know Piece 5 is missing! We write down '5' and keep checking the rest of the spots.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a standard Cyclic Sort designed to naturally handle duplicates by ignoring them.

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  4. The correct index for the number nums[i] is nums[i] - 1. Let j = nums[i] - 1.
  5. Check & Swap: If the number is NOT already sitting at its correct index (nums[i] != nums[j]):
  6. Crucially, this check also means "if the number currently sitting at the target index j is not an identical duplicate". If they are identical, nums[i] == nums[j] would evaluate to True!
  7. Swap nums[i] and nums[j]. Do NOT increment i.
  8. Ignore / Happy: If nums[i] == nums[j], the number is either happily in its perfect home, OR it is a duplicate trapped in the wrong spot because its home is already occupied by its twin. Either way, just i += 1.
  9. Find (Second pass):
  10. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  11. If nums[i] != i + 1, then the number i + 1 is missing. Add it to a missing_numbers list.
  12. Return missing_numbers.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. The cyclic sort takes at most $N-1$ swaps, and the array iteration takes exactly $N$ steps. The second pass takes another $N$ steps. Total is strictly $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All operations are done in-place, ignoring the space required for the output array.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • No missing numbers: e.g., [1, 2, 3]. The array perfectly sorts. The second pass verifies 1==1, 2==2, 3==3 and returns an empty list [].
  • Many missing numbers: The logic flawlessly scales to multiple gaps. Every index that doesn't match i+1 is appended to the result.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_all_missing_numbers(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds all missing numbers in an array containing numbers from 1 to N with duplicates.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i] - 1
        
        # Only swap if the number is not already at the correct index
        # This implicitly handles duplicates (it won't swap identical numbers infinitely)
        if nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            i += 1

    missing_numbers: list[int] = []

    # 2. Second pass to find all missing numbers
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            missing_numbers.append(i + 1)

    return missing_numbers

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [2, 3, 1, 8, 2, 3, 5, 1]
    assert find_all_missing_numbers(arr1) == [4, 6, 7], "Test 1 failed"

    arr2 = [2, 4, 1, 2]
    assert find_all_missing_numbers(arr2) == [3], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [2, 3, 2, 1]
    assert find_all_missing_numbers(arr3) == [4], "Edge 1: Missing N"
    
    arr4 = [1, 2, 3]
    assert find_all_missing_numbers(arr4) == [], "Edge 2: No missing numbers"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to sort (with at most N swaps), one pass to find missing numbers. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place. (Excluding the space for the output list).
Easy Find the Duplicate Number
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find the Duplicate Number

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have N+1 boxes, and exactly N unique toys to put in them.

Because you have more boxes than unique toys, ONE of the toys must be a duplicate!

We can use our Cyclic Sort trick to put every toy into its correct box. Toy 3 goes into Box 3. Toy 5 goes into Box 5.

If we pick up a Toy 4, we walk over to Box 4 to put it away. But wait! There is ALREADY a Toy 4 sitting right there in Box 4!

Since we found two of the exact same toy trying to claim the exact same spot, we caught the duplicate red-handed! We don't even need to finish sorting; we can just shout out the answer immediately.

Note: We solved this same problem in the "Fast & Slow Pointers" chapter using a magical trick that didn't modify the array at all. Cyclic Sort WILL modify the array by swapping elements around, but it is much easier to understand!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a standard Cyclic Sort where we proactively look for a clash.

  1. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  2. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  3. Check if the current number is happy: if nums[i] != i + 1:
  4. If it's NOT at its correct index, we look at where it belongs: j = nums[i] - 1.
  5. Now we check the number currently sitting at index j. Is it the EXACT SAME number?
  6. Clash (nums[i] == nums[j]): Yes! We found two identical numbers fighting for the same spot. It's the duplicate! Return nums[i].
  7. No Clash (nums[i] != nums[j]): They are different numbers. Swap them, and do not increment i so we can process the newly swapped number.
  8. If it IS at the correct index (nums[i] == i + 1):
  9. The number is perfectly happy where it is. Increment i += 1.
  10. Return -1 if no duplicate is found (though the problem guarantees one).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Every swap places a number permanently in its correct position. The maximum number of swaps is $N$. The function will return as soon as it hits the duplicate, making it highly efficient.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All sorting is done in-place.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Multiple copies of the duplicate: e.g., [2, 4, 1, 4, 4]. The algorithm will still just catch the very first clash between any two 4s and return 4 immediately. It does not matter how many extra copies exist.
  • Minimum possible array: [1, 1]. nums[0] = 1, i+1 = 1. Happy, i increments. nums[1] = 1, i+1 = 2. Unhappy. j = 1-1 = 0. nums[0] is 1. Clash! Returns 1. Works perfectly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_duplicate(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the duplicate number in an array using Cyclic Sort.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    while i < n:
        # If the number is not at its correct index
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            j = nums[i] - 1
            
            # If the spot it wants to go to is occupied by a DIFFERENT number, swap
            if nums[i] != nums[j]:
                nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
            else:
                # The spot is occupied by the EXACT SAME number! It's a duplicate.
                return nums[i]
        else:
            # The number is perfectly happy where it is
            i += 1

    return -1

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [1, 4, 4, 3, 2]
    assert find_duplicate(arr1) == 4, "Test 1 failed"

    arr2 = [2, 1, 3, 3, 5, 4]
    assert find_duplicate(arr2) == 3, "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [2, 4, 1, 4, 4]
    assert find_duplicate(arr3) == 4, "Edge 1: Multiple duplicates"
    
    arr4 = [1, 1]
    assert find_duplicate(arr4) == 1, "Edge 2: Minimum possible array"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every swap puts at least one number in its correct spot. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find all Duplicate Numbers

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

This is just like the "Find all Missing Numbers" problem!

You have a box of $N$ puzzle pieces. You try to sort them into their $N$ spots.

If you pick up a Piece 3, and you look at the 3rd spot and see a Piece 3 is already sitting there, you just say, "You're a duplicate!" and leave the extra Piece 3 sitting right where it is.

After you've done this for the whole box, every "correct" piece will be perfectly in its home.

Any piece that is sitting in the WRONG spot MUST be a duplicate!

For example, if you look at the 5th spot, and instead of a Piece 5, you see another Piece 3 sitting there, you just write down "3" on your list of duplicates!

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses the exact same Cyclic Sort algorithm as "Find all Missing Numbers", but we change what we extract during the second pass.

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  4. The correct index for the number nums[i] is nums[i] - 1. Let j = nums[i] - 1.
  5. Check & Swap: If nums[i] != nums[j], swap them! This implicitly ignores duplicates because identical twins will evaluate to nums[i] == nums[j].
  6. Ignore / Happy: If nums[i] == nums[j], just increment i += 1.
  7. Find (Second pass):
  8. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  9. Check if the number matches the spot: if nums[i] != i + 1.
  10. In the Missing Numbers problem, we added i + 1 (the missing index) to our list.
  11. In this Duplicate Numbers problem, we add nums[i] (the number illegally occupying the spot) to our list!
  12. Return the duplicates list.

Complexity

Edge Cases Handled Safely

def find_all_duplicates(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds all duplicate numbers in an array containing numbers from 1 to N.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i] - 1
        
        if nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            i += 1

    duplicates: list[int] = []

    # 2. Second pass to find all numbers sitting in the wrong spots
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            # The number AT this wrong spot is the duplicate
            duplicates.append(nums[i])

    return duplicates

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [3, 4, 4, 5, 5]
    assert find_all_duplicates(arr1) == [5, 4], "Test 1 failed"

    arr2 = [5, 4, 7, 2, 3, 5, 3]
    assert find_all_duplicates(arr2) == [3, 5], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [1, 2, 3]
    assert find_all_duplicates(arr3) == [], "Edge 1: No duplicates"
    
    arr4 = [2, 2]
    assert find_all_duplicates(arr4) == [2], "Edge 2: Only duplicates"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to sort (with at most N swaps), one pass to find duplicates. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place. (Excluding the output list).

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find the Corrupt Pair

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a box of $N$ puzzle pieces that should be numbered 1 to $N$.

But the factory made a mistake (a corruption!). They accidentally put two copies of one piece into the box, and entirely forgot to put another piece in!

Since the box still has exactly $N$ pieces, this means exactly ONE number is duplicated, and exactly ONE number is missing.

We use our Cyclic Sort trick to put every piece into its correct spot.

After we finish swapping, exactly ONE spot will have the wrong piece in it.

If the 4th spot has a Piece 2 sitting in it, what does that tell us?

  1. Piece 2 is the DUPLICATE (because the real Piece 2 is already sitting happily in the 2nd spot).
  2. Piece 4 is MISSING (because its spot was stolen by the duplicate, and it's nowhere to be found in the box!)

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses the standard Cyclic Sort algorithm to sort the array, followed by a single pass to find the one mismatch. This is effectively combining "Find Missing Number" and "Find Duplicate Number" into a single result!

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  4. The correct index for the number nums[i] is nums[i] - 1. Let j = nums[i] - 1.
  5. Check & Swap: If nums[i] != nums[j], swap them! This implicitly ignores the duplicate because identical twins evaluate to nums[i] == nums[j].
  6. Ignore / Happy: If nums[i] == nums[j], just increment i += 1.
  7. Find (Second pass):
  8. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  9. Find the single index where the number doesn't match the spot: if nums[i] != i + 1.
  10. When we find this mismatch:
  11. nums[i] is the number illegally sitting in the spot. It is the duplicate.
  12. i + 1 is the spot that was stolen. It is the missing number.
  13. Return [nums[i], i + 1].

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

  • We return [2, 4] immediately.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. The cyclic sort takes at most $N-1$ swaps, and the array iteration takes at most $N$ steps. Total is strictly $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All operations are done in-place, and we return a tiny array of exactly two elements.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Minimum possible array: e.g., [2, 2]. Array is already sorted. Second pass checks index 0 (Spot 1). It sees 2. 2 != 1. Returns [2, 1] instantly.
  • Missing number is at the end: e.g., [1, 2, 2]. Sort finishes. Array is [1, 2, 2]. Index 2 (Spot 3) has 2. Returns [2, 3]. Works perfectly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_corrupt_pair(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds the duplicate and missing numbers in a corrupted array.
    Returns: [duplicate, missing]
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i] - 1
        
        if nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            i += 1

    # 2. Second pass to find the corrupt pair
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            # nums[i] is the duplicate, i + 1 is the missing number
            return [nums[i], i + 1]

    return [-1, -1]

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [3, 1, 2, 5, 2]
    assert find_corrupt_pair(arr1) == [2, 4], "Test 1 failed: Duplicate 2, Missing 4"

    arr2 = [3, 1, 2, 3, 6, 4]
    assert find_corrupt_pair(arr2) == [3, 5], "Test 2 failed: Duplicate 3, Missing 5"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [2, 2]
    assert find_corrupt_pair(arr3) == [2, 1], "Edge 1: Minimum possible array"
    
    arr4 = [1, 2, 2, 4]
    assert find_corrupt_pair(arr4) == [2, 3], "Edge 2: Already sorted except for corruption"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to sort (with at most N swaps), one pass to find the corrupt pair. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place.
Medium Find the Smallest Missing Positive Number

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find the Smallest Missing Positive Number

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a really messy room full of toys. Some toys have negative numbers (like -5), some have zero (0), and some have huge numbers (like 1,000,000).

Your parents tell you to find the SMALLEST positive toy number that is missing from your room. Positive numbers start at 1, 2, 3...

Here is a big secret: Because your room can only hold $N$ toys total, the smallest missing positive number MUST be somewhere between 1 and $N+1$.

Why? If your room holds 5 toys, the absolutely best you could possibly do is have toys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. In that perfect case, the missing one is 6 (which is $N+1$). In literally any other case (like having a -5 or a 1,000,000), one of the spots for 1 through 5 is wasted, meaning the missing number is 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5!

So, we use Cyclic Sort to try and put Toy 1 in Spot 1, Toy 2 in Spot 2, and so on...

If we find a toy like -5 or 1,000,000, we just IGNORE IT! It doesn't belong in Spots 1 to $N$, so we just let it sit wherever it lands.

After sorting, we walk through the spots. The first spot that doesn't have the right toy is our answer!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a brilliant application of Cyclic Sort that uses the array itself as a hash map, while safely ignoring out-of-bounds values.

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop through the array using a while i < n loop.
  4. The correct index for a number nums[i] is j = nums[i] - 1.
  5. Bounds Check: We ONLY care about nums[i] if it's a valid positive number that fits perfectly inside our array's capacity: 0 < nums[i] <= n.
  6. Check & Swap: If it is valid AND not already at its correct spot (nums[i] != nums[j]), swap them!
  7. Ignore / Happy: Else (it's negative, zero, too big, or already perfectly placed), increment i += 1. This naturally filters out the "junk".
  8. Find (Second pass):
  9. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  10. Find the first index where nums[i] != i + 1. This means the number i + 1 was nowhere to be found in the array! Return i + 1.
  11. If all spots are perfectly filled with 1 to $N$, then the array was [1, 2, ..., N]. The missing one is the very next number: N + 1. Return n + 1.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. The cyclic sort takes at most $N-1$ swaps, ignoring out-of-bounds elements in $O(1)$ time per check. The second pass takes at most $N$ steps. Total is strictly $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All operations are done in-place, achieving the strict $O(1)$ space requirement of the problem.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • All negatives: e.g., [-1, -2, -3]. The while loop ignores everything. Array remains unchanged. Second pass checks index 0 (Spot 1), sees -1 != 1. Returns 1 instantly. Correct!
  • Perfect array: e.g., [1, 2, 3]. The while loop verifies everyone is happy. Second pass verifies everyone matches. Loop finishes. Code reaches return n + 1, which returns 4. Correct!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_first_smallest_missing_positive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the smallest missing positive integer in O(N) time and O(1) space.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort, ignoring out-of-bounds numbers
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i] - 1
        
        # Only swap if the number is a valid positive integer that fits in our array
        # AND it is not already in the correct position
        if 0 < nums[i] <= n and nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            i += 1

    # 2. Second pass to find the first missing positive
    for i in range(n):
        if nums[i] != i + 1:
            return i + 1

    # 3. If the array has all numbers from 1 to N, the missing one is N + 1
    return n + 1

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [-3, 1, 5, 4, 2]
    assert find_first_smallest_missing_positive(arr1) == 3, "Test 1 failed"

    arr2 = [3, -2, 0, 1, 2]
    assert find_first_smallest_missing_positive(arr2) == 4, "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [3, 2, 5, 1]
    assert find_first_smallest_missing_positive(arr3) == 4, "Edge 1: Missing number in the middle"
    
    arr4 = [1, 2, 3]
    assert find_first_smallest_missing_positive(arr4) == 4, "Edge 2: Perfect array, missing is N+1"

    arr5 = [-1, -2, -3]
    assert find_first_smallest_missing_positive(arr5) == 1, "Edge 3: All negatives"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to sort (ignoring out-of-bounds numbers), one pass to check. 💾 Space: O(1) — Sorting is done completely in-place.
Hard Find the First K Missing Positive Numbers
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find the First K Missing Positive Numbers

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have your messy room full of toys, just like the last problem. But this time, your parents want you to find the first $K$ missing positive toy numbers. (Like, find the first 3 missing toys starting from 1).

First, we do the exact same trick: Cyclic Sort. We try to put Toy 1 in Spot 1, Toy 2 in Spot 2... ignoring negatives and toys with huge numbers.

When we are done sorting, we walk through the spots.

If Spot 1 doesn't have Toy 1, then Toy 1 is missing! We write down "1".

But wait! What if the toy sitting in Spot 1 is Toy 100?

Toy 100 is an "extra" toy that we don't care about right now, but we absolutely need to remember we have it. Why? Because if we still need to find more missing numbers after checking all $N$ spots, we have to start counting up: $N+1$, $N+2$, $N+3$...

If we accidentally say "Oh, Toy 100 is missing," we'd be wrong, because it was sitting right there in Spot 1!

So we keep a little notepad (extra_numbers set) to write down any out-of-bounds toys we see sitting in wrong spots. Then we can safely count up past $N$ without making a mistake.

🎯 Core Strategy

This builds on the "Smallest Missing Positive" logic but requires us to keep track of the junk we ignored, because that junk might actually be one of the numbers we are searching for beyond $N$.

  1. Sort (Cyclic Sort pass):
  2. Initialize pointer i = 0.
  3. Loop while i < n and Cyclic Sort. Ignore out-of-bounds numbers (nums[i] <= 0 or nums[i] > n).
  4. Find inside $N$ (Second pass):
  5. Initialize missing_numbers = [] and extra_numbers = set().
  6. Iterate through the array for i in range(n).
  7. If we have found $K$ missing numbers, stop entirely! (break).
  8. If nums[i] != i + 1:
  9. The number i + 1 is missing. Add it to missing_numbers.
  10. The number currently sitting here (nums[i]) is an extra out-of-bounds number. Add it to extra_numbers.
  11. Find outside $N$ (Third pass):
  12. If we STILL need more numbers (len(missing_numbers) < k), we start checking numbers greater than $N$: candidate = n + 1.
  13. while len(missing_numbers) < k:
  14. If candidate is NOT in extra_numbers, it's truly missing! Add it.
  15. candidate += 1.
  16. Return missing_numbers.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: nums = [3, -1, 4, 5, 5], K = 3. Length $N = 5$.

Initialization: i = 0.

Phase 1: Cyclic Sort

Ignoring negatives and duplicates.

Array becomes: [-1, 5, 3, 4, 5] (Spot 1 is -1, Spot 2 is 5, Spot 3 is 3, Spot 4 is 4, Spot 5 is 5).

Phase 2: Find Inside $N$

Walk through [-1, 5, 3, 4, 5]:

  • Spot 1 (Index 0): -1. Mismatch!
  • Add 1 to missing_numbers.
  • Add -1 to extra_numbers.
  • Spot 2 (Index 1): 5. Mismatch!
  • Add 2 to missing_numbers.
  • Add 5 to extra_numbers.
  • Spot 3 (Index 2): 3. (Match)
  • Spot 4 (Index 3): 4. (Match)
  • Spot 5 (Index 4): 5. (Match)

missing_numbers = [1, 2]. We still need 1 more! (Because $K=3$).

extra_numbers = {-1, 5}.

Phase 3: Find Outside $N$

Start candidate = 6 ($N+1$).

  • Is 6 in extra_numbers? No.
  • Add 6 to missing_numbers.
  • Now len(missing_numbers) == 3. Stop!

Result: [1, 2, 6].

📊 Visual Diagram

Here is why tracking extra_numbers is critical for numbers beyond $N$:

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N + K)$. The cyclic sort takes at most $N-1$ swaps. The second pass takes exactly $N$ steps. The third pass takes at most $K$ steps. Total time is $O(N + K)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(K)$. The extra_numbers set will store at most $K$ out-of-bounds numbers (because we stop looking after finding $K$ missing numbers). The missing_numbers list takes $O(K)$ space.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • $K$ is much larger than missing numbers inside array: The third pass while loop cleanly generates N+1, N+2, N+3... checking against the extra_numbers set until it fulfills the quota.
  • Perfectly sorted array: e.g., [1, 2, 3], $K=2$. Sort does nothing. Second pass does nothing. extra_numbers is empty. Third pass generates 4 and 5. Result: [4, 5]. Perfectly logical.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def find_first_k_missing_positive(nums: list[int], k: int) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds the first K missing positive numbers in an unsorted array.
    """
    i: int = 0
    n: int = len(nums)

    # 1. Sort the array using Cyclic Sort
    while i < n:
        j = nums[i] - 1
        if 0 < nums[i] <= n and nums[i] != nums[j]:
            nums[i], nums[j] = nums[j], nums[i]
        else:
            i += 1

    missing_numbers: list[int] = []
    extra_numbers: set[int] = set()

    # 2. Find missing numbers within the bounds of the array
    for i in range(n):
        if len(missing_numbers) < k:
            if nums[i] != i + 1:
                missing_numbers.append(i + 1)
                # Keep track of the out-of-bounds number that stole this spot
                extra_numbers.add(nums[i])
        else:
            break

    # 3. If we still need more missing numbers, look beyond N
    candidate: int = n + 1
    while len(missing_numbers) < k:
        if candidate not in extra_numbers:
            missing_numbers.append(candidate)
        candidate += 1

    return missing_numbers

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [3, -1, 4, 5, 5]
    assert find_first_k_missing_positive(arr1, 3) == [1, 2, 6], "Test 1 failed"

    arr2 = [2, 3, 4]
    assert find_first_k_missing_positive(arr2, 3) == [1, 5, 6], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [-2, -3, 4]
    assert find_first_k_missing_positive(arr3, 2) == [1, 2], "Edge 1: Missing before and inside"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N + K) — O(N) to sort and scan, O(K) to find the remaining numbers if they are beyond N. 💾 Space: O(K) — To store the `extra_numbers` set and the `missing_numbers` list.

07 - In-place Reversal of a LinkedList

Connectors 6 Problems
📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 07: In-place Reversal of a LinkedList

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a line of friends holding hands, all facing the same direction.

Friend 1 is holding Friend 2's hand, Friend 2 is holding Friend 3's hand, etc.

You want them to turn around so Friend 3 holds Friend 2's hand, and Friend 2 holds

Friend 1's hand!

But here's the catch: You can't ask them to let go of everyone all at once, or

they will get lost and wander away. You can only tell ONE friend to change hands

at a time.

To do this safely, you need three pieces of information at any given moment:

  1. Who did I just finish talking to? (previous)
  2. Who am I talking to right now? (current)
  3. Who is next in line? (next)

You tell current: "Let go of next and grab previous instead!"

Then you step sideways. The person you just talked to becomes the new previous,

and the next person in line becomes your new current. You do this until

everyone is facing backward!

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

The In-place Reversal pattern describes an efficient way to reverse the links between nodes of a LinkedList without using any extra memory (like putting them in an array and building a new list).

When to use it:

  • You need to reverse a LinkedList, or a sub-portion of it.
  • You need to rotate a LinkedList.
  • You need to reverse segments of a LinkedList (like reversing every K elements).
  • The problem explicitly asks for O(1) extra space.
Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    START["Initialize pointers: prev = None, current = head"] --> LOOP["While current is not None"]
    LOOP --> SAVE["1. Save next: next_node = current.next"]
    SAVE --> REVERSE["2. Reverse link: current.next = prev"]
    REVERSE --> MOVE_PREV["3. Move prev: prev = current"]

    MOVE_CURR --> LOOP
    LOOP -- "current is None" --> END["prev is now the new head"]
State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Standard Reversal

The standard reversal uses exactly three pointers inside a loop.

  1. prev = None (The new tail will point to None)
  2. current = head (The starting node)
  3. while current is not None:
  4. next_node = current.next (Temporarily save the rest of the list so we don't lose it)
  5. current.next = prev (Flip the arrow to point backward)
  6. prev = current (Move the prev pointer one step forward)
  7. current = next_node (Move the current pointer one step forward)
  8. Return prev (Because current is None, prev is sitting on the very last node, which is now the new head!)

100%

    participant C as Current (1)
    participant N as NextNode (2)

    C->>N: 4. Move Current (Current = 2)

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Standard ReversalDO memorize the 4-step variable swapping block exactly. It is the foundation of all other variants.DON'T try to do it with only two variables. If you don't save next_node before breaking the link, you lose the rest of the list forever!
Sub-list ReversalDO save pointers to the nodes immediately before and immediately after the reversed sub-list, so you can reconnect them when finished.DON'T forget that the head of the reversed portion becomes the tail, and the tail becomes the head!
K-Group ReversalDO write a helper function for reversing a specific portion to keep your main logic clean.DON'T reverse a chunk if there are less than K nodes left, UNLESS the problem explicitly asks you to (pay close attention to the instructions!).

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)We traverse the list exactly once (or twice in sub-list problems to find the starting node).
SpaceO(1)We only ever use a handful of pointer variables (prev, current, next_node), regardless of how massive the LinkedList is.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Losing the Head: When reconnecting a reversed sub-list, what if the sub-list started at the very first node? You won't have a node_before_sublist to reconnect to! You must update the global head instead.
  2. Infinite Loops (Cycles): If you don't correctly set the tail's .next to None (or to the rest of the list), you can accidentally create a cycle where nodes point to each other in a circle.
  3. Off-by-One Errors: Counting steps to reach the p-th node is tricky. If you start at 1, you do a for loop p-1 times to reach the p-th node. Test this manually!

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse a LinkedList

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine a line of people holding hands, all facing forward. Person A is holding Person B's hand, Person B is holding Person C's hand.

You want everyone to turn around, so Person C holds Person B's hand, and Person B holds Person A's hand.

You can't just tell everyone to turn around at once! If Person A lets go of Person B, Person A might forget who Person B was.

So you walk down the line. You ask Person A to let go of Person B, and instead reach out their hand behind them (to nothing, None). But before they let go, you memorized that Person B was next!

Then you step over to Person B. You tell them to let go of Person C (after memorizing Person C), and reach back to grab Person A.

You repeat this until you reach the end of the line!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the fundamental In-place Reversal pattern that is the building block for all other LinkedList problems in this chapter.

  1. We need 3 variables to keep track of state:
  2. prev: The node we just processed (starts as None).
  3. current: The node we are currently looking at (starts as head).
  4. next_node: The node coming up next (we temporarily save this).
  5. Loop while current is not None (until we fall off the end of the list):
  6. Save: next_node = current.next (Memorize the next node so we don't sever the list and lose it).
  7. Reverse: current.next = prev (Turn around! Point to the previous node).
  8. Advance prev: prev = current (Step forward. You are now the 'previous' node for the next step).
  9. Advance current: current = next_node (Step forward. Move to the node we saved).
  10. When the loop ends, current has fallen off the edge and is None. prev is standing on the very last node. That last node is now the new head of our reversed list! Return prev.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 2 -> 4 -> 6 -> 8 -> null

Initialization: prev = null, current = 2.

StepcurrentSave next_nodeReverse (current.next = prev)Advance prevAdvance current
1242.next = null (2 points backwards)prev = 2current = 4
2464.next = 2 (4 points to 2)prev = 4current = 6
3686.next = 4 (6 points to 4)prev = 6current = 8
48null8.next = 6 (8 points to 6)prev = 8current = null

Loop ends because current is null.

Result: prev is 8. The list is now 8 -> 6 -> 4 -> 2 -> null.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We iterate exactly once over the linked list of $N$ nodes.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. We only use three temporary pointers (prev, current, next_node), regardless of how massive the linked list is.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty list: If head is None, the while current is not None: loop never runs. The function instantly returns prev, which is initialized to None. This is perfectly correct.
  • Single node: head = 2 -> null. Loop runs exactly once. 2 points to null. prev becomes 2. Loop terminates and returns 2. Correct!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def reverse(head: Optional[Node]) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Reverses a Singly LinkedList in-place and returns the new head.
    """
    prev: Optional[Node] = None
    current: Optional[Node] = head

    while current is not None:
        # 1. Save the next node so we don't lose the rest of the list
        next_node = current.next
        
        # 2. Reverse the pointer
        current.next = prev
        
        # 3. Advance both pointers forward
        prev = current
        current = next_node

    # After the loop, current is None, and prev is the new head!
    return prev

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def get_list_values(node):
        res = []
        while node:
            res.append(node.value)
            node = node.next
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    head1 = Node(2, Node(4, Node(6, Node(8, Node(10)))))
    res1 = reverse(head1)
    assert get_list_values(res1) == [10, 8, 6, 4, 2], f"Test 1 failed: {get_list_values(res1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert reverse(None) is None, "Edge 1: Empty list"
    
    head2 = Node(1)
    res2 = reverse(head2)
    assert get_list_values(res2) == [1], "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We walk down the list exactly once. 💾 Space: O(1) — We only use three variables, regardless of how long the line is.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse a Sub-list

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a line of friends holding hands. This time, you don't want everyone to turn around. You only want the friends from position $P$ to position $Q$ to turn around!

If the line is: Alice $\rightarrow$ Bob $\rightarrow$ Charlie $\rightarrow$ Dave $\rightarrow$ Eve

And you want to reverse from position 2 (Bob) to position 4 (Dave):

First, you walk up to Alice. Alice is the "friend right before the flip".

You ask Alice to wait for a second and let go of Bob.

Then, you take the group (Bob, Charlie, Dave) and use the standard reversal trick we learned to flip them around: Dave $\rightarrow$ Charlie $\rightarrow$ Bob.

Now, you have a flipped group, but they are detached from the main line!

You just need to reconnect them:

  1. Alice needs to hold the hand of the new front of the group (Dave).
  2. The new back of the group (Bob) needs to reach out and hold Eve's hand.

Boom! The line is back together, with just the middle part reversed!

🎯 Core Strategy

This builds perfectly upon the standard In-place Reversal pattern. We just need to carefully keep track of the boundaries so we can stitch the list back together.

  1. Skip: Fast-forward your current and prev pointers by skipping exactly p - 1 nodes.
  2. After skipping, prev will sit right before the sublist (node_before_sublist).
  3. current will sit on the very first node of the sublist. Once reversed, this specific node will end up at the very back of the group! So we also memorize it as last_node_of_sublist.
  4. Reverse: We want to reverse exactly from $P$ to $Q$, which means we perform exactly q - p + 1 reversals. We run our standard 4-step reversal loop exactly that many times.
  5. Reconnect:
  6. Front Edge: If node_before_sublist exists (which means $P > 1$), we point its .next to prev (because prev is now the new head of the reversed group). If it does NOT exist (because $P = 1$), the reversal happened at the very beginning of the list, so prev becomes the new global head!
  7. Back Edge: The last_node_of_sublist reaches out and sets its .next to current (who is patiently waiting as the first un-reversed node after $Q$).
  8. Return the global head.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, $P = 2$, $Q = 4$.

Phase 1: Skip

We loop p - 1 (1) times.

  • prev = 1, current = 2.
  • node_before_sublist = 1.
  • last_node_of_sublist = 2.

Phase 2: Reverse Sublist

We loop q - p + 1 (3) times.

LoopcurrentSave next_nodeReverse (current.next = prev)Advance prevAdvance current
1232.next = 1prev = 2current = 3
2343.next = 2prev = 3current = 4
3454.next = 3prev = 4current = 5

After loop: prev = 4 (new front of group). current = 5 (waiting after group).

Phase 3: Reconnect

  • Front Edge: node_before_sublist (1).next = prev (4). (1 now points to 4).
  • Back Edge: last_node_of_sublist (2).next = current (5). (2 now points to 5).

Result: 1 -> 4 -> 3 -> 2 -> 5.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We skip nodes until we reach $P$, then reverse nodes until we reach $Q$. We visit nodes at most once, running strictly in $O(N)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All sorting is done in-place using just a few pointers.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • $P = 1$: node_before_sublist will be None. The if node_before_sublist is not None: check will fail, and it will execute the else: head = prev branch, correctly updating the global head of the linked list.
  • $P = Q$: The initial check if p == q: instantly returns head, doing 0 work.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def reverse_sub_list(head: Optional[Node], p: int, q: int) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Reverses a sub-list of a Singly LinkedList from position p to q in-place.
    """
    if p == q or not head:
        return head

    # 1. Skip the first p-1 nodes
    current: Optional[Node] = head
    prev: Optional[Node] = None
    
    # Example: if p=2, we loop 1 time.
    for _ in range(p - 1):
        prev = current
        current = current.next
        
    # 'prev' is now sitting on the node right before the sublist
    # 'current' is sitting on the first node of the sublist
    node_before_sublist = prev
    last_node_of_sublist = current
    
    # 2. Reverse the nodes between p and q
    # We do exactly q - p + 1 reversals
    for _ in range(q - p + 1):
        next_node = current.next
        current.next = prev
        prev = current
        current = next_node
        
    # 3. Reconnect the severed edges
    if node_before_sublist is not None:
        # The node before the sublist now points to the reversed head
        node_before_sublist.next = prev
    else:
        # We reversed from the very beginning! The head of the list changes.
        head = prev
        
    # The last node of the reversed sublist points to whatever comes next
    last_node_of_sublist.next = current
    
    return head

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def get_list_values(node):
        res = []
        while node:
            res.append(node.value)
            node = node.next
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, reverse 2 to 4
    head1 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res1 = reverse_sub_list(head1, 2, 4)
    assert get_list_values(res1) == [1, 4, 3, 2, 5], f"Test 1 failed: {get_list_values(res1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # Start at 1 (head changes)
    head2 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res2 = reverse_sub_list(head2, 1, 3)
    assert get_list_values(res2) == [3, 2, 1, 4, 5], "Edge 1 failed (p=1)"
    
    # p == q
    head3 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
    res3 = reverse_sub_list(head3, 2, 2)
    assert get_list_values(res3) == [1, 2, 3], "Edge 2 failed (p=q)"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We only walk down the list once to reach the node and perform the reversal. 💾 Space: O(1) — Only a few pointer variables are used.
Medium Reverse every K-element Sub-list
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse every K-element Sub-list

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You still have a line of friends holding hands. This time, you want them to turn around in groups of $K$.

If $K=3$, you count 1, 2, 3 friends, and ask those 3 to flip around.

Then you step over to the next group, count 1, 2, 3 friends, and ask them to flip around.

You keep doing this until you reach the end of the line.

If you get to the very end of the line and there are only 2 friends left (which is less than $K$), you just flip those last 2 friends anyway.

We can solve this by taking our "Reverse a Sub-list" magic trick and simply putting it inside a giant loop that keeps running until everyone in the line is done!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an iterative application of the "Reverse a Sub-list" logic. Instead of jumping to position $P$ and stopping after position $Q$, we just start at the head and run the reversal block $K$ times, repeatedly, until current is None.

  1. Initialize current = head, prev = None.
  2. Loop while current is not None:
  3. Memorize Borders:
  4. node_before_sublist = prev (The node sitting right before this current $K$-group).
  5. last_node_of_sublist = current (The node we are currently on, which will end up at the back of this group after it gets reversed).
  6. Reverse: Run the standard 4-step reversal logic inside an inner while loop that stops when it hits $K$ iterations, or when current runs out early.
  7. Reconnect Borders:
  8. Front edge: node_before_sublist.next = prev (or update the global head to prev if this was the very first group).
  9. Back edge: last_node_of_sublist.next = current.
  10. Prepare for Next Group:
  11. Set prev = last_node_of_sublist. This is the most crucial step! The tail of the group we just reversed will act exactly as the "node before" for the next group!
  12. Return head.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, $K = 3$.

Initialization: current = 1, prev = null.

Group 1 (Nodes 1, 2, 3)

  • Memorize: node_before = null, last_node = 1.
  • Reverse 3 nodes. current moves to 4, prev moves to 3.
  • Reconnect:
  • node_before is null, so head = prev (head = 3).
  • last_node (1).next = current (4).
  • List is now 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5.
  • Prepare next: prev = last_node (prev = 1).

Group 2 (Nodes 4, 5)

  • Memorize: node_before = 1, last_node = 4.
  • Reverse remaining 2 nodes. current runs out (null), prev moves to 5.
  • Reconnect:
  • node_before (1).next = prev (5). (1 now points to 5).
  • last_node (4).next = current (null). (4 points to null).
  • List is now 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 5 -> 4 -> null.
  • Prepare next: prev = 4.

Outer loop terminates because current is null.

Result: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 5 -> 4 -> null.
