🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit and reverse every node exactly once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All reversal and stitching is done in-place with a few pointers.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Leftover elements < $K$: Handled perfectly. The inner loop while current is not None and i < k: will gracefully stop early when current hits None. It reverses what it can and reconnects it normally.
  • $K = 1$: Handled as a fast-path at the very beginning: if k <= 1 or not head: return head. Reversing groups of 1 means doing nothing at all.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def reverse_every_k_elements(head: Optional[Node], k: int) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Reverses every K-element sub-list in a Singly LinkedList in-place.
    """
    if k <= 1 or not head:
        return head

    current: Optional[Node] = head
    prev: Optional[Node] = None

    while current is not None:
        # Save pointers to reconnect later
        node_before_sublist = prev
        last_node_of_sublist = current
        
        # Reverse 'k' nodes
        i = 0
        while current is not None and i < k:
            next_node = current.next
            current.next = prev
            prev = current
            current = next_node
            i += 1
            
        # Reconnect the reversed sub-list
        if node_before_sublist is not None:
            node_before_sublist.next = prev
        else:
            # We are reversing the very first group, so the head changes
            head = prev
            
        last_node_of_sublist.next = current
        
        # Prepare for the next group
        # The tail of our newly reversed group becomes the 'prev' for the next group
        prev = last_node_of_sublist

    return head

        res = []
        while node:
            res.append(node.value)
            node = node.next
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> 7 -> 8
    # k = 3
    # Expected: 3->2->1 -> 6->5->4 -> 8->7
    head1 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5, Node(6, Node(7, Node(8))))))))
    res1 = reverse_every_k_elements(head1, 3)
    assert get_list_values(res1) == [3, 2, 1, 6, 5, 4, 8, 7], f"Test 1 failed: {get_list_values(res1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases

    head2 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5, Node(6, Node(7, Node(8))))))))
    res2 = reverse_every_k_elements(head2, 2)
    assert get_list_values(res2) == [2, 1, 4, 3, 6, 5, 8, 7], "Edge 1 failed (k=2)"

    # k = 1 (No reversal needed)
    head3 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
    res3 = reverse_every_k_elements(head3, 1)

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse Alternating K-element Sub-list

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a line of friends holding hands, and you want them to turn around in groups of $K$, but skipping every other group!

If $K=2$:

  1. The first 2 friends flip.
  2. The next 2 friends stay EXACTLY the same (just walk past them).
  3. The next 2 friends flip.
  4. The next 2 friends stay the same.

You keep doing this alternating pattern until you run out of friends.

This is exactly like our last problem ("Reverse every K-element Sub-list"), except after we reconnect the reversed group, we literally just tell our pointers to walk forward by $K$ steps before we repeat the giant loop!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an iterative application of the "Reverse a Sub-list" logic, interleaved with a simple "Skip" logic.

  1. Initialize current = head, prev = None.
  2. Loop while current is not None:
  3. PHASE 1: REVERSE
  4. Memorize node_before_sublist = prev.
  5. Memorize last_node_of_sublist = current.
  6. Run standard 4-step reversal logic for exactly $K$ steps (or until current is None).
  7. Reconnect edges (node_before_sublist.next = prev, last_node_of_sublist.next = current).
  8. Set prev = last_node_of_sublist. (This prepares the prev anchor for the skipped group).
  9. PHASE 2: SKIP
  10. We just reversed a group of $K$. Now we must skip a group of $K$!
  11. Loop while current is not None and i < k:
  12. prev = current
  13. current = current.next
  14. Increment i.
  15. After this skip loop finishes, prev is resting on the final node of the skipped group. This perfectly sets it up to act as node_before_sublist for the NEXT reversal group!
  16. Return head.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, $K = 2$.

Initialization: current = 1, prev = null.

Phase 1: Reverse Group (Nodes 1, 2)

  • Memorize: node_before = null, last_node = 1.
  • Reverse 2 nodes. current moves to 3, prev moves to 2.
  • Reconnect:
  • head = prev (head = 2).
  • last_node (1).next = current (3).
  • List is now 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5.
  • Set prev = last_node (prev = 1).

Phase 2: Skip Group (Nodes 3, 4)

  • Loop 2 times:
  • Iteration 1: prev = 3, current = 4.
  • Iteration 2: prev = 4, current = 5.

Phase 1 Again: Reverse Group (Node 5)

  • Memorize: node_before = 4, last_node = 5.
  • Reverse 2 nodes (but only 1 exists). current hits null, prev moves to 5.
  • Reconnect:
  • node_before (4).next = prev (5). (4 points to 5).
  • last_node (5).next = current (null).
  • List is now 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null.
  • Outer loop terminates.

Result: 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> null.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once—either during the inner reversal loop or the inner skip loop. The outer while loop guarantees we process the entire array without going backwards.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. All reversal and skipping is done using in-place pointer manipulation.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Leftover elements < $K$ (in skip phase): Handled perfectly. The inner skip loop while current is not None and i < k: gracefully stops early when current hits None.
  • Leftover elements < $K$ (in reverse phase): Handled perfectly. Reverses whatever is left and reconnects it exactly like normal.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def reverse_alternate_k_elements(head: Optional[Node], k: int) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Reverses alternating K-element sub-lists in a Singly LinkedList in-place.
    """
    if k <= 1 or not head:
        return head

    current: Optional[Node] = head
    prev: Optional[Node] = None

    while current is not None:
        # Save pointers to reconnect later
        node_before_sublist = prev
        last_node_of_sublist = current
        
        # 1. Reverse 'k' nodes
        i = 0
        while current is not None and i < k:
            next_node = current.next
            current.next = prev
            prev = current
            current = next_node
            i += 1
            
        # 2. Reconnect the reversed sub-list
        if node_before_sublist is not None:
            node_before_sublist.next = prev
        else:
            head = prev
            
        last_node_of_sublist.next = current
        prev = last_node_of_sublist

        # 3. Skip the next 'k' nodes (leave them in their original order)
        i = 0
        while current is not None and i < k:
            prev = current
            current = current.next
            i += 1

    return head

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Rotate a LinkedList

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a line of friends holding hands again: 1 $\rightarrow$ 2 $\rightarrow$ 3 $\rightarrow$ 4 $\rightarrow$ 5.

You want to "rotate" the line to the right by 2.

This means the last 2 friends in the line (4 and 5) get detached from the back and moved to the very front of the line!

Result: 4 $\rightarrow$ 5 $\rightarrow$ 1 $\rightarrow$ 2 $\rightarrow$ 3.

How do we do this easily?

Imagine taking the last friend (5) and having them reach out to hold the first friend's hand (1).

Now they are standing in a perfect circle! (1 $\rightarrow$ 2 $\rightarrow$ 3 $\rightarrow$ 4 $\rightarrow$ 5 $\rightarrow$ 1...)

To make the line straight again, we just need to break the circle at the right spot.

Since 2 friends moved to the front, that means the remaining 3 friends (5 - 2 = 3) stayed at the back.

So we walk exactly 3 steps from the start, break the hand-hold there, and whatever is next becomes the new front of the line!

🎯 Core Strategy

This doesn't actually require the standard node-by-node reversal! Instead, we can elegantly solve this by temporarily converting the Singly LinkedList into a Circular LinkedList.

  1. Find Length & Tail: Traverse the entire list to find its length and the last node (tail).
  2. Normalize $K$: If someone asks to rotate a line of 5 people by 12 steps, it's the exact same as rotating it by 2 steps ($12 \pmod 5 = 2$). So, k = k % length. If $K = 0$, we just return the head because the list doesn't change!
  3. Form a Circle: Connect the end to the beginning: tail.next = head.
  4. Find the Break Point:
  5. The new tail of the list will be at position length - k.
  6. We walk from head for (length - k) - 1 steps to land exactly on this new_tail.
  7. Break the Circle:
  8. The node directly after our new_tail is the new_head!
  9. We break the circle by setting new_tail.next = None.
  10. Return the new_head.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, $K = 2$.

Phase 1: Setup

  • Traverse to find length: 5. tail is pointing at 5.
  • Normalize $K$: 2 % 5 = 2.
  • Form Circle: tail.next = head. (Node 5 now points to Node 1).

Phase 2: Break the Circle

  • Calculate steps to new tail: length - k = 5 - 2 = 3.
  • Walk 3 - 1 = 2 steps from the head:
  • Start at head (1).
  • Step 1: new_tail = 2.
  • Step 2: new_tail = 3.
  • The new head is new_tail.next, which is 4.
  • Break the circle: new_tail (3).next = None.

Result: new_head is 4. The list is 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> null.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We do one full pass to find the length and the tail, and then a partial pass (at most $N$ steps) to find the new tail. Total time is $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. We are only manipulating existing pointers in place.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • $K$ is much larger than length: e.g., $K = 7$, Length = 5. k % length gracefully turns $K$ into 2.
  • $K$ is exactly a multiple of length: e.g., $K = 5$, Length = 5. k % length turns $K$ into 0. The check if k == 0: return head instantly catches this and does zero work!
  • Empty list or single node: Handled immediately at the top if not head or not head.next: return head.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def rotate_linked_list(head: Optional[Node], k: int) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Rotates a Singly LinkedList to the right by k nodes.
    """
    if not head or not head.next or k <= 0:
        return head

    # 1. Find the length and the tail of the list
    length = 1
    tail = head
    while tail.next is not None:
        tail = tail.next
        length += 1

    # 2. Normalize k (if k is a multiple of length, the list doesn't change)
    k %= length
    if k == 0:
        return head

    # 3. Connect tail to head to form a circle
    tail.next = head

    # 4. Find the new tail, which is at position (length - k)
    # We walk (length - k - 1) steps from the head to land exactly on the new tail
    steps_to_new_tail = length - k
    new_tail = head
    for _ in range(steps_to_new_tail - 1):
        new_tail = new_tail.next

    # 5. The new head is right after the new tail
    new_head = new_tail.next
    
    # 6. Break the circle
    new_tail.next = None

    return new_head

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def get_list_values(node):
        res = []
        while node:
            res.append(node.value)
            node = node.next
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2
    # Expected: 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3
    head1 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res1 = rotate_linked_list(head1, 2)
    assert get_list_values(res1) == [4, 5, 1, 2, 3], f"Test 1 failed: {get_list_values(res1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # k = 7, length = 5 (effective k = 2)
    head2 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res2 = rotate_linked_list(head2, 7)
    assert get_list_values(res2) == [4, 5, 1, 2, 3], "Edge 1 failed (k > length)"

    # k = 5, length = 5 (effective k = 0)
    head3 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res3 = rotate_linked_list(head3, 5)
    assert get_list_values(res3) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "Edge 2 failed (k == length)"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to find the length and tail. Another partial pass to find the new tail. Total O(N). 💾 Space: O(1) — Only modifying pointers.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse Nodes in k-Group

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

This is a very strict version of the "Reverse every K-element Sub-list" problem.

Imagine you have a line of friends and $K=3$.

You walk up to the first 3 friends, and flip them around.

You walk up to the next 3 friends, and flip them around.

Finally, you reach the end of the line, and there are only 2 friends left.

In the old problem, we flipped them anyway!

But in THIS problem, the rule is: "If there are less than 3 friends, DO NOT touch them!"

So you just leave the last 2 friends exactly as they are and go home.

To do this safely, before we even start flipping a group, we just do a quick count:

"1, 2, 3... okay, we have enough, let's flip!"

If the count stops at 2 because the line ended, we just stop entirely.

🎯 Core Strategy

We use the exact same logic from "Reverse every K-element Sub-list", but we add a "Look-Ahead" helper function to count the remaining nodes.

  1. Look-Ahead (has_k_nodes): Write a small helper function that takes a node and walks forward $K$ steps. If it hits None before reaching $K$, it returns False. Otherwise True.
  2. Initialize current = head, prev = None.
  3. Loop while current is not None:
  4. NEW STEP: Run has_k_nodes(current, k). If it returns False, we simply break out of the entire while loop! The leftover nodes stay exactly where they are.
  5. Memorize Borders: node_before_sublist = prev and last_node_of_sublist = current.
  6. Reverse: Run the standard 4-step reversal logic for exactly $K$ steps.
  7. Reconnect Borders:
  8. node_before_sublist.next = prev (or update head = prev).
  9. last_node_of_sublist.next = current.
  10. Prepare for Next Group: Set prev = last_node_of_sublist.
  11. Return head.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, $K = 3$.

Initialization: current = 1, prev = null.

Group 1 (Nodes 1, 2, 3)

  • has_k_nodes(1, 3): Counts 1, 2, 3. Returns True!
  • Memorize: node_before = null, last_node = 1.
  • Reverse 3 nodes. current moves to 4, prev moves to 3.
  • Reconnect:
  • head = prev (head = 3).
  • last_node (1).next = current (4).
  • List is now 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5.
  • Set prev = last_node (prev = 1).

Group 2 (Nodes 4, 5)

  • current is 4.
  • has_k_nodes(4, 3): Counts 4, 5... hits null. Count is 2. Returns False!
  • The outer while loop breaks instantly!

Result: 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 4 -> 5. The 4 -> 5 part was completely untouched!

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Every node is visited twice. Once by the has_k_nodes helper function to verify it's part of a valid group, and once by the main pointer to actually reverse it. $O(2N)$ simplifies strictly to $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. It's completely in-place.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Length of list is not a multiple of $K$: Handled perfectly by the break condition. The leftover nodes remain untouched.
  • $K = 1$: The fast-path if k <= 1: return head handles this instantly.
  • Empty list: Handled instantly by the fast-path check.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.next = next

def has_k_nodes(node: Optional[Node], k: int) -> bool:
    count = 0
    while node and count < k:
        node = node.next
        count += 1
    return count == k

def reverse_k_group(head: Optional[Node], k: int) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Reverses nodes in k-group. If the final group has < k nodes, it is left unchanged.
    """
    if k <= 1 or not head:
        return head

    current: Optional[Node] = head
    prev: Optional[Node] = None

    while current is not None:
        # Check if we have at least k nodes remaining
        if not has_k_nodes(current, k):
            break

        # Save pointers to reconnect later
        node_before_sublist = prev
        last_node_of_sublist = current
        
        # Reverse EXACTLY 'k' nodes
        i = 0
        while current is not None and i < k:
            next_node = current.next
            current.next = prev
            prev = current
            current = next_node
            i += 1
            
        # Reconnect the reversed sub-list
        if node_before_sublist is not None:
            node_before_sublist.next = prev
        else:
            head = prev
            
        last_node_of_sublist.next = current
        
        # Prepare for the next group
        prev = last_node_of_sublist

    return head

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def get_list_values(node):
        res = []
        while node:
            res.append(node.value)
            node = node.next
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 2
    # Expected: 2->1 -> 4->3 -> 5 (leftover)
    head1 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res1 = reverse_k_group(head1, 2)
    assert get_list_values(res1) == [2, 1, 4, 3, 5], f"Test 1 failed: {get_list_values(res1)}"

    # 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, k = 3
    # Expected: 3->2->1 -> 4->5 (leftover)
    head2 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3, Node(4, Node(5)))))
    res2 = reverse_k_group(head2, 3)
    assert get_list_values(res2) == [3, 2, 1, 4, 5], "Test 2 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # k = 1 (No reversal needed)
    head3 = Node(1, Node(2, Node(3)))
    res3 = reverse_k_group(head3, 1)
    assert get_list_values(res3) == [1, 2, 3], "Edge 1 failed (k=1)"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited twice (once by `has_k_nodes` to count, once to reverse/skip). 💾 Space: O(1) — Completely in-place.

Pattern 08: Stacks

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a spring-loaded plate dispenser at a buffet.

When you wash a clean plate, you push it down onto the top of the stack.

When a customer comes along, they always grab the plate that is on the VERY TOP.

They can't easily grab the plate at the bottom without taking all the other plates

off first!

This is called LIFO (Last-In, First-Out). The LAST plate you put on the stack

is the FIRST plate that gets taken off.

In coding, a Stack helps us remember things in the exact reverse order that they

happened. If we are walking through a maze and keep pushing every turn we make onto

a Stack, when we hit a dead-end, we can just "pop" the Stack to take back our

most recent step!

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

The Stack is a fundamental data structure perfectly suited for problems involving matching, reversing, or remembering a strict history of events where you only care about the most recent event.

When to use it:

  • You need to reverse the order of items.
  • You need to track matching pairs (like parentheses, HTML tags, or brackets).
  • You are parsing strings, evaluating mathematical expressions, or simplifying directory paths.
  • The problem involves backtracking or undoing recent actions.

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Standard Stack Operations

In Python, we use a standard list to represent a Stack because it is highly optimized for adding and removing from the end (the "top").

  1. Initialization: stack = []
  2. Push: stack.append(item) — Adds an item to the top. O(1) time.
  3. Pop: item = stack.pop() — Removes and returns the top item. O(1) time.
  4. Peek: item = stack[-1] — Looks at the top item without removing it. O(1) time.
  5. IsEmpty: len(stack) == 0 (or just if not stack:).

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Parentheses/MatchingDO push opening brackets ( { [ onto the stack, and when you see a closing bracket, pop() to ensure it matches the correct type.DON'T just count +1 for opening and -1 for closing if there are MULTIPLE types of brackets. ([)] is invalid, but counting would say it's valid!
String ReversalDO realize that append all then pop all naturally reverses data.DON'T use a Stack for string reversal in real Python production code (just use s[::-1]), but use it to demonstrate understanding in an interview!
Path SimplificationDO split the path by /, ignore . and empty strings, and pop() when you see ...DON'T pop() without checking if the stack is empty first. You can't go up from the root directory!

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)We typically iterate over the input exactly once, doing O(1) pushes or pops.
SpaceO(N)The Stack can grow to store every single element in the worst case (e.g., all opening brackets, or a string).

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Popping an Empty Stack: Calling .pop() or [-1] on an empty list in Python throws an IndexError. Always check if stack: before popping or peeking.
  2. Forgetting to check if Stack is empty at the end: In parentheses matching, if the string is "((()", you will finish the loop without errors, but the stack won't be empty! You must check len(stack) == 0 at the very end.

Easy Balanced Parentheses
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Balanced Parentheses

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a bunch of nested boxes.

A square box [ can go inside a round box (, which gives you ([ ]).

But you can't close a round box if the square box inside it is still open! ([ )] is wrong.

Every time you open a box (an opening bracket), you write it down on a notepad (Push it to a Stack).

Every time you want to close a box, you look at the last box you opened (Pop from the Stack).

If it's the exact same shape, great! You close it.

If it's a different shape, or if your notepad is empty (you didn't open any boxes!), then it's an error.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the textbook problem for learning how Stacks operate with a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) pattern.

  1. Create a stack (in Python, just a standard list).
  2. Create a mapping (dictionary) to match closing brackets to opening brackets: mapping = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}.
  3. Loop through every character in the string:
  4. If the character is an opening bracket ({[, push it to the stack.
  5. If the character is a closing bracket )}]:
  6. If the stack is empty, return False (trying to close something that isn't open).
  7. Pop the top character from the stack.
  8. Check if the popped character matches mapping[char]. If not, return False.
  9. After the loop finishes, check the stack. If the stack is NOT empty, it means we opened boxes we never closed! Return False. Otherwise, return True.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We iterate through the string of length $N$ exactly once. Pushing to and popping from the end of a Python list is $O(1)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst case (e.g., "((((((((("), the stack stores every single character.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • String is completely empty: The for loop skips entirely. len(stack) == 0 evaluates to True. Correct!
  • String only has closing brackets: e.g. "))) ". The very first character ) triggers a pop(). The code handles this via stack.pop() if stack else '#', which safely returns #. Since # != (, it immediately returns False.
  • String only has opening brackets: e.g. "(((". The loop pushes three ( characters and finishes. The stack length is 3. len(stack) == 0 evaluates to False. Correct!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def is_balanced(s: str) -> bool:
    """
    Checks if a string of brackets is validly balanced using a Stack.
    """
    stack: list[str] = []
    mapping = {')': '(', '}': '{', ']': '['}

    for char in s:
        # If it's a closing bracket
        if char in mapping:
            # Pop from stack if not empty, else assign a dummy character
            top_element = stack.pop() if stack else '#'
            
            # If the popped opening bracket doesn't match the required opening bracket
            if mapping[char] != top_element:
                return False
        else:
            # It's an opening bracket, push it to the stack
            stack.append(char)

    # If the stack is empty, all brackets were matched perfectly!
    return len(stack) == 0

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert is_balanced("()") == True, "Test 1 failed"
    assert is_balanced("()[]{}") == True, "Test 2 failed"
    assert is_balanced("(]") == False, "Test 3 failed"
    assert is_balanced("([)]") == False, "Test 4 failed"
    assert is_balanced("{[]}") == True, "Test 5 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert is_balanced("") == True, "Edge 1: Empty string"
    assert is_balanced("(((") == False, "Edge 2: Only opening brackets"
    assert is_balanced("]]]") == False, "Edge 3: Only closing brackets"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Iterate through the string once. Push and pop are O(1). 💾 Space: O(N) — Worst case (e.g., `((((((`), the stack stores every character.
Easy Reverse a String using a Stack
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse a String using a Stack

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a stack of blocks with letters on them.

You have the word "CAT".

First, you put 'C' on the table.

Then, you put 'A' on top of 'C'.

Then, you put 'T' on top of 'A'.

Now you have a tower of blocks: 'T' is on top, 'A' is in the middle, 'C' is at the bottom.

To take them down, you have to take the top block first.

You take off 'T' and write it down.

You take off 'A' and write it down.

You take off 'C' and write it down.

What did you write? "TAC"!

You just reversed the word just by using the natural rules of a Stack.

🎯 Core Strategy

A Stack naturally follows the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle. By pushing all elements into a stack and then immediately popping them out, the elements naturally come out in the exact reverse order.

  1. Initialize an empty stack (Python list).
  2. Loop through every character in the string, pushing it onto the stack.
  3. Initialize an empty list for the result (building strings via lists is faster in Python).
  4. While the stack is not empty, pop the top character and append it to the result list.
  5. Return the joined result string.

(Note: In real-world Python code, you would simply use string slicing s[::-1] which is highly optimized in C. However, this problem tests fundamental understanding of the Stack data structure, which is widely applicable across languages).

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: "CAT"

Phase 1: Push

  • Char 'C' $\rightarrow$ Stack: ['C']
  • Char 'A' $\rightarrow$ Stack: ['C', 'A']
  • Char 'T' $\rightarrow$ Stack: ['C', 'A', 'T']

Phase 2: Pop

  • Pop! Returns 'T'. Result = ['T']
  • Pop! Returns 'A'. Result = ['T', 'A']
  • Pop! Returns 'C'. Result = ['T', 'A', 'C']

Final Result: "TAC"

Here is how LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) naturally flips data:

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Pushing $N$ characters onto a stack takes $O(N)$ time. Popping $N$ characters off the stack takes $O(N)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The stack stores exactly $N$ characters.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty string: "". The first for loop skips. Stack is empty. The while loop skips. Returns "".join([]) which is "". Perfectly handled.
  • Single character: "a". Pushes "a". Pops "a". Returns "a". Perfectly handled.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def reverse_string(s: str) -> str:
    """
    Reverses a string using a Stack data structure.
    """
    stack: list[str] = []

    # 1. Push all characters onto the stack
    for char in s:
        stack.append(char)

    # 2. Pop all characters off the stack
    reversed_chars: list[str] = []
    while stack:
        reversed_chars.append(stack.pop())

    # 3. Join them back into a single string
    return "".join(reversed_chars)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert reverse_string("Hello, World!") == "!dlroW ,olleH", "Test 1 failed"
    assert reverse_string("Python") == "nohtyP", "Test 2 failed"
    assert reverse_string("racecar") == "racecar", "Test 3 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert reverse_string("") == "", "Edge 1: Empty string"
    assert reverse_string("a") == "a", "Edge 2: Single character"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Pushing N characters takes O(N), popping N characters takes O(N). 💾 Space: O(N) — We store all N characters in the stack.
Easy Decimal to Binary Conversion
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Decimal to Binary Conversion

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

How do you turn a normal number (like 13) into binary (0s and 1s)?

You just keep dividing by 2!

13 divided by 2 is 6, with a remainder of 1.

6 divided by 2 is 3, with a remainder of 0.

3 divided by 2 is 1, with a remainder of 1.

1 divided by 2 is 0, with a remainder of 1.

If you read the remainders exactly as they came out, you get "1, 0, 1, 1".

But wait! Binary is written backwards. The FIRST remainder you got should actually be the very LAST digit of your binary number!

The correct binary for 13 is "1101".

This sounds like a perfect job for a Stack!

We push every remainder onto a Stack as we get it. Since the first remainder is pushed to the very bottom of the stack, it will be the very LAST thing to be popped off!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a standard base-conversion algorithm, naturally solved by a Stack due to the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) requirement.

  1. Initialize an empty stack (Python list).
  2. Handle Zero: If the input n is 0 to begin with, just return "0".
  3. Push Phase (Modulo & Divide):
  4. Loop while n > 0:
  5. Calculate the binary digit: remainder = n % 2.
  6. Push str(remainder) to the stack.
  7. Shrink the number: n = n // 2 (integer division).
  8. Pop Phase:
  9. Pop elements from the stack one by one and append them to a result list. (In Python, it's faster to build lists and .join() them rather than doing string concatenation).
  10. Return the joined result string.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: n = 13

Phase 1: Push Remainders

nn % 2 (Remainder)n // 2 (New n)ActionStack State
1316Push "1"['1']
603Push "0"['1', '0']
311Push "1"['1', '0', '1']
110Push "1"['1', '0', '1', '1']

Loop ends because $N = 0$.

Phase 2: Pop to Read Backwards

  • Pop! Returns "1".
  • Pop! Returns "1".
  • Pop! Returns "0".
  • Pop! Returns "1".

Result list: ["1", "1", "0", "1"].

Joined: "1101".

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(\log N)$. We divide $N$ by 2 at every step. This means the loop runs exactly $\approx \log_2(N)$ times. Pushing and popping take $O(1)$ per operation. Total time is $O(\log N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(\log N)$. The stack stores exactly $\approx \log_2(N)$ string characters.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Input is 0: The while n > 0: loop would never run, returning an empty string. We specifically handle this with a fast-path at the very top: if n == 0: return "0".
  • Input is 1: The loop runs exactly once. Stack becomes ['1']. Returns "1". Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def decimal_to_binary(n: int) -> str:
    """
    Converts a positive decimal integer into its binary representation string using a Stack.
    """
    if n == 0:
        return "0"

    stack: list[str] = []

    # 1. Push remainders to the stack
    while n > 0:
        remainder = n % 2
        stack.append(str(remainder))
        n = n // 2

    # 2. Pop to read them in reverse order
    binary_chars: list[str] = []
    while stack:
        binary_chars.append(stack.pop())

    return "".join(binary_chars)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert decimal_to_binary(2) == "10", "Test 1 failed"
    assert decimal_to_binary(7) == "111", "Test 2 failed"
    assert decimal_to_binary(13) == "1101", "Test 3 failed"
    assert decimal_to_binary(18) == "10010", "Test 4 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert decimal_to_binary(0) == "0", "Edge 1: Input is zero"
    assert decimal_to_binary(1) == "1", "Edge 2: Input is one"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(log N) — We divide `n` by 2 every step, which takes log(N) steps. 💾 Space: O(log N) — The stack stores log(N) remainders.
Medium Sort a Stack
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Sort a Stack

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a stack of heavy boxes with numbers on them, and they are all out of order.

You want to sort them so the smallest number is at the top, and the biggest number is at the bottom.

But you only have ONE empty space next to you (a temporary stack) to help you sort.

Here is the trick:

  1. You take the top box off the main stack and hold it in your hands.
  2. You look at the temporary stack. Is the top box there BIGGER than the one in your hands?

If it is, you can't put your box down! You have to move the bigger box back to the main stack for a second, to make room.

  1. You keep moving boxes back until you find the perfect spot in the temporary stack.
  2. Then you put your box down on the temporary stack.
  3. You repeat this until the main stack is empty.

Now the temporary stack has all the boxes sorted (with the biggest at the top).

Wait, if we want the smallest at the top, we just pour the temporary stack back into the main stack!

🎯 Core Strategy

This algorithm is a variation of Insertion Sort, adapted perfectly for Stack constraints.

  1. Initialize temp_stack = [].
  2. Loop while stack is not empty:
  3. Pop the top element from stack and store it in temp (this is the box in your hands).
  4. Make Room: While temp_stack is not empty AND temp_stack[-1] > temp:
  5. Pop from temp_stack and push it back to stack.
  6. Place: Now it's safe to push temp onto temp_stack.
  7. After the loop, temp_stack is completely sorted, but the largest element is at the top.
  8. To return a stack with the smallest element at the top, we simply pop everything from temp_stack and push it back into stack.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: stack = [34, 3, 31] (Top is 31)

Phase 1: Sort into Temp Stack

stacktemp (In Hand)temp_stackAction
[34, 3]31[]temp_stack is empty. Push 31.
[34]3[31]31 > 3. Move 31 back to stack. Push 3 to temp_stack.
[34, 31]-[3](Intermediate state after moving 31)
[34]31[3]3 < 31. Push 31.
[]34[3, 31]31 < 34. Push 34.

temp_stack is now [3, 31, 34] (Top is 34).

Phase 2: Pour Back

  • Pop 34 from temp_stack, push to stack. stack = [34].
  • Pop 31 from temp_stack, push to stack. stack = [34, 31].
  • Pop 3 from temp_stack, push to stack. stack = [34, 31, 3].

Result: [34, 31, 3] (Top is 3, which is the smallest element!).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N^2)$. In the worst case (where the input stack is sorted in reverse), every single element has to move back and forth between the two stacks. This acts identically to the $O(N^2)$ time of Insertion Sort.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. We use one additional temporary stack that eventually holds all $N$ elements.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Already Sorted: [34, 31, 3] (Top is 3). The inner while temp_stack[-1] > temp: loop will never trigger! It just pops from stack and immediately pushes to temp_stack. Runs in $O(N)$ time.
  • Empty Stack: Handled flawlessly. The outer while stack: loop never triggers. Returns [].
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def sort_stack(stack: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Sorts a stack such that the smallest elements are on top, 
    using only one additional stack.
    """
    temp_stack: list[int] = []

    while stack:
        # 1. Take the top element
        temp = stack.pop()
        
        # 2. While the temporary stack has larger elements on top, 
        # move them back to the main stack to make room for 'temp'.
        while temp_stack and temp_stack[-1] > temp:
            stack.append(temp_stack.pop())
            
        # 3. Now the top of temp_stack is smaller than or equal to temp, so it's safe to place it.
        temp_stack.append(temp)

    # 4. temp_stack now has the largest elements at the top. 
    # Pour them back into the original stack so the smallest end up on top!
    while temp_stack:
        stack.append(temp_stack.pop())

    return stack

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    stack1 = [34, 3, 31, 98, 92, 23]
    # Expected output (smallest on top): [98, 92, 34, 31, 23, 3] 
    # Wait! Python lists have the 'top' at the END (index -1). 
    # So if smallest is on top, the list should look like [biggest, ..., smallest].
    # So [98, 92, 34, 31, 23, 3] is correct.
    res1 = sort_stack(stack1)
    assert res1 == [98, 92, 34, 31, 23, 3], f"Test 1 failed: {res1}"

    stack2 = [3, 5, 1, 4, 2, 8]
    res2 = sort_stack(stack2)
    assert res2 == [8, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1], f"Test 2 failed: {res2}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert sort_stack([]) == [], "Edge 1: Empty stack"
    assert sort_stack([1]) == [1], "Edge 2: Single element"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N^2) — In the worst case (reverse sorted), we have to move elements back and forth many times. 💾 Space: O(N) — We use one additional stack of size N.
Medium Simplify Path
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Simplify Path

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you are exploring folders on a computer. You start at the very beginning (the root /).

The path you are given is like a map with some weird, messy instructions:

  • /a/ means "go into folder 'a'".
  • . means "stay in the current folder".
  • .. means "go BACK out of this folder to the previous one".
  • // means nothing special, it's just a typo, treat it like a single /.

You want to read this messy map and draw a clean, simple map that gets you to the exact same final folder without any backtracking or typos.

Since .. literally means "undo my last move", this is the perfect job for a Stack!

Every time you go into a folder, you push it onto the stack.

Every time you see .., you pop the top folder off the stack (undoing your last move).

If you see . or empty spaces from typos, you just ignore them!

🎯 Core Strategy

Because of the "undo" operation (..), this problem is perfectly suited for a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) Stack.

  1. Initialize an empty stack.
  2. Tokenize: Split the input path by /. This automatically breaks the string into distinct parts, and turns multiple slashes like // into empty string tokens "".

(e.g., "/a//b/./../c/" becomes ['', 'a', '', 'b', '.', '..', 'c', '']).

  1. Loop through each part in the parts:
  2. Undo: If part == '..': We need to go back! pop() from the stack IF the stack is not empty.
  3. Ignore: If part == '.' or part == '': Just continue and ignore it.
  4. Enter Folder: Else: It's a real folder name! push() it to the stack.
  5. After the loop, the stack contains exactly the sequence of folders you need to enter.
  6. Reconstruct the final string by joining the stack with /, and prepend a leading / because it's an absolute path.

Return "/" + "/".join(stack).

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: "/a/./b/../../c/"

Split into parts: ['', 'a', '.', 'b', '..', '..', 'c', '']

"a"Push "a"["a"]
"."Ignore["a"]
"b"Push "b"["a", "b"]
".."Pop! (Undoes "b")["a"]
".."Pop! (Undoes "a")[]
"c"Push "c"["c"]
""Ignore["c"]

Loop ends.

Join stack elements with /: "c".

Prepend /: "/c".

Final Result: "/c".

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Splitting the string takes $O(N)$. Iterating through the parts takes $O(N)$ because pushing and popping are $O(1)$. Total time is $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The stack can store up to $O(N)$ parts if the path is very deep and contains no .. commands.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Trying to go above root ("/../"): The split yields ['', '..', '']. When it processes '..', it sees the stack is empty. The if stack: stack.pop() logic prevents an error and safely ignores it. The final result is "/". Perfect.
  • Multiple slashes ("/a//b"): The split yields ['', 'a', '', 'b']. The empty strings '' are safely ignored by the elif part == '': check.
  • Dots as valid names ("/..."): Only . and .. are special. ... is technically a valid folder name in Unix. The else: block catches it and pushes it to the stack perfectly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def simplify_path(path: str) -> str:
    """
    Simplifies an absolute Unix-style file path.
    """
    stack: list[str] = []
    
    # 1. Split the path by the directory separator
    parts = path.split('/')

    for part in parts:
        if part == '..':
            # Go back one directory if possible
            if stack:
                stack.pop()
        elif part == '.' or part == '':
            # Stay in current directory / ignore multiple slashes
            continue
        else:
            # Go into the directory
            stack.append(part)

    # Reconstruct the absolute path
    return '/' + '/'.join(stack)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert simplify_path("/a/./b/../../c/") == "/c", "Test 1 failed"
    assert simplify_path("/home/") == "/home", "Test 2 failed"
    assert simplify_path("/a//b/c") == "/a/b/c", "Test 3 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert simplify_path("/../") == "/", "Edge 1: Trying to go above root"
    assert simplify_path("/...") == "/...", "Edge 2: '...' is a valid directory name, not '..'"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We split the string once and iterate through the parts. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can store up to N parts if the path is very deep.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a sentence that has some parentheses in it, like a)b(c)d.

But oh no! The parentheses are messed up. There is a closing parenthesis ) right after a that never had an opening parenthesis before it.

We want to fix the sentence by erasing the MINIMUM number of parentheses possible. We never erase the letters.

If we use our Stack trick, it's really easy to find the bad parentheses!

Every time we see an opening (, we put its index (its location in the word) onto our Stack.

When we see a closing ), we try to pop from the Stack.

If the Stack is empty, it means this ) is an extra, invalid parenthesis! We write down its index on our "erase list".

If we finish reading the whole sentence, and there are still numbers left in our Stack, that means we had some ( that we never closed! Those are invalid too, so we add them to our "erase list".

Finally, we just rewrite the sentence, skipping any index that is on our erase list!

🎯 Core Strategy

This takes the standard "Balanced Parentheses" logic and modifies it to track indices instead of just validating correctness.

  1. Initialize an empty stack to keep track of unmatched ( indices.
  2. Initialize an invalid_indices set to hold the indices of brackets we need to erase.
  3. First Pass (Identify Invalid Indices):
  4. Loop through the string s using enumerate to get the index and char.
  5. If char == '(': Push index to the stack.
  6. If char == ')':
  7. If stack is empty, this ) is unmatched. Add index to invalid_indices.
  8. Else, pop from stack (we successfully matched the ) with a ().
  9. Clean up Stack: After the loop, any indices left in the stack belong to ( characters that were never closed. Add all of them to invalid_indices.
  10. Second Pass (Build Result):
  11. Create a result list.
  12. Loop through s again with enumerate.
  13. If the current index is NOT in invalid_indices, append the char to the result list.
  14. Join and return the result string.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

5')'Pop index 3. Matched![]{1}
6'd'Ignore[]{1}

Stack is empty. No left-over opening brackets.

invalid_indices = {1}.

Phase 2: Build String

Walk through the string "a)b(c)d" again.

Skip any character at index 1.

  • Index 0: "a"
  • Index 1: Skip!
  • Index 2: "b"
  • Index 3: "("
  • Index 4: "c"
  • Index 5: ")"
  • Index 6: "d"

Result list: ["a", "b", "(", "c", ")", "d"].

Joined: "ab(c)d".

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We iterate through the string of length $N$ exactly twice. Set lookups in Python are $O(1)$. Total time is $O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The stack can store up to $N$ indices. The set can store up to $N$ indices. The result array stores up to $N$ characters. Total space is $O(N)$.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • No Parentheses: e.g., "hello". Stack is empty, set is empty. Second pass copies the string exactly. Returns "hello".
  • Nested valid with extra closing: e.g., "(a(b)c)d)". Finds the final ) at the very end is invalid. Returns "(a(b)c)d". Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def min_remove_to_make_valid(s: str) -> str:
    """
    Removes the minimum number of invalid parentheses to make a string valid.
    """
    stack: list[int] = []
    invalid_indices: set[int] = set()

    # 1. Identify all invalid parentheses
    for i, char in enumerate(s):
        if char == '(':
            stack.append(i)
        elif char == ')':
            if stack:
                stack.pop()
            else:
                invalid_indices.add(i)

    # 2. Any unmatched opening parentheses left in the stack are also invalid
    for index in stack:
        invalid_indices.add(index)

    # 3. Build the final string without the invalid characters
    result: list[str] = []
    for i, char in enumerate(s):
        if i not in invalid_indices:
            result.append(char)

    return "".join(result)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert min_remove_to_make_valid("lee(t(c)o)de)") == "lee(t(c)o)de", "Test 1 failed"
    assert min_remove_to_make_valid("a)b(c)d") == "ab(c)d", "Test 2 failed"
    assert min_remove_to_make_valid("))((") == "", "Test 3 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert min_remove_to_make_valid("hello") == "hello", "Edge 1: No parentheses"
    assert min_remove_to_make_valid("(a(b)c)d)") == "(a(b)c)d", "Edge 2: Nested valid with extra closing"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass to find invalid indices, one pass to build the string. 💾 Space: O(N) — Stack, set, and result list can all store up to N elements.

09 - Monotonic Stack

Connectors 6 Problems
📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 09: Monotonic Stack

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a line of people standing in front of a giant movie screen.

You are walking down the line, trying to figure out who can see the screen and who

is blocked.

If you (height 5) stand behind a very tall person (height 10), you can't see anything

past them! That tall person basically "blocks" you forever from seeing anything

further down the line.

A Monotonic Stack is like keeping a list of people who are still useful.

If a new, super-tall person walks into the line, they instantly block everyone shorter

than them who was standing behind them. So, we tell all those shorter people to

leave the line (we pop them off the stack!).

By doing this, the stack only ever contains people standing in perfectly increasing

(or perfectly decreasing) height order. "Monotonic" is just a fancy math word for

"always going in one direction without turning back."

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

A Monotonic Stack is a regular stack with one strict rule: Elements inside the stack must always remain sorted (either strictly increasing or strictly decreasing).

Whenever we try to push a new element that breaks the rule, we fiercely pop elements off the top until the rule is satisfied again.

When to use it:

  • The problem asks you to find the "Next Greater" or "Next Smaller" element for every item in an array.
  • The problem asks you to find how many days you have to wait until it gets warmer (Daily Temperatures).
  • The problem asks you to maximize a rectangle area in a histogram.
  • A brute force solution takes O(N²) because of nested loops looking ahead, but you need an O(N) solution.
Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100% 
flowchart TD
    START["Initialize Monotonic Stack []"] --> LOOP["For each item in array:"]
    LOOP --> CHECK{"Does 'item' break the sorted rule?"}
    CHECK -- "Yes (e.g. item is bigger than stack top)" --> POP["Pop the top of the stack"]
    POP --> PROCESS["The 'item' is the Next Greater element for the popped value!"]
    PROCESS --> CHECK
CHECK -- "No (or stack is empty)" --> PUSH["Push 'item' to stack"]
    PUSH --> LOOP
State convergence & algorithmic execution graph

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Next Greater Element (Monotonic Decreasing Stack)

If we want to find the NEXT GREATER element, we want our stack to be strictly decreasing. That way, if a BIG number comes along, it breaks the rule, and we pop the small numbers.

  1. stack = []
  2. result = [-1] * len(arr)
  3. for i, num in enumerate(arr):
  4. while stack and num > stack[-1].value: (The rule is broken!)
  5. popped_node = stack.pop()
  6. result[popped_node.index] = num (We just found the next greater element for the popped node!)
  7. stack.append(Node(i, num))
  8. Any elements left in the stack at the end never found a greater element, so they remain -1.
Algorithm State Machine · Flow Execution
100%

    Array->>Stack: Push 1 (Index 1) -> Valid, 1 < 2
    Array->>Stack: Try to Push 5 (Index 2)
    
    Note over Stack: 5 > 1! Rule broken!
    Stack-->>Result: Pop 1. Next Greater for '1' is 5!

    Stack-->>Result: Pop 2. Next Greater for '2' is 5!

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Next Greater ElementDO use a Monotonic DECREASING stack. Big numbers trigger the pops.DON'T forget to store the original index of the elements in the stack, so you know exactly where to put the answer in the result array!
Next Smaller ElementDO use a Monotonic INCREASING stack. Small numbers trigger the pops.DON'T just store the values. Indices are almost always required to calculate distances (like in Daily Temperatures).
Circular ArraysDO loop through the array twice list * 2 (or use i % n) so elements at the end can wrap around and find greater elements at the start.DON'T let the loop run infinitely. Exactly 2*N steps are enough.

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)Even though there is a while loop inside a for loop, every element is pushed exactly ONCE and popped exactly ONCE. 2N operations total = O(N).
SpaceO(N)The stack can grow to size N if the array is already perfectly sorted and no pops occur.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Storing Values vs Indices: In almost all Monotonic Stack problems, it is infinitely better to push the INDEX to the stack, not just the value. You can always look up arr[index] to get the value, but you can't easily find the index if you only stored the value.
  2. Strictly vs Non-Strictly Monotonic: Does >= break the rule, or only >?
  3. If you want the Next Strictly Greater element, pop when num > arr[stack[-1]].
  4. If duplicates matter, read the prompt carefully.

Easy Next Greater Element
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Next Greater Element

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are walking down a line of people of different heights.

For every single person, you want to tell them: "Hey, the very next person who is TALLER than you is standing right over there!"

If no one taller is standing behind them, you tell them "-1".

Instead of each person individually looking all the way down the line (which takes a long time), we can just have everyone who hasn't found a taller person yet wait in a special "Waiting Room" (our Stack).

When a super tall person walks into the room, EVERYONE in the waiting room who is shorter than the tall person says "Aha! That's my Next Greater Element!"

They write down the tall person's height and happily leave the waiting room.

Then the tall person enters the waiting room themselves to see if anyone even taller comes along later!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the foundational Monotonic Stack pattern. A "monotonic" stack is just a stack whose elements are always completely sorted (either always increasing or always decreasing). In this case, we maintain a monotonically decreasing stack.

  1. Initialize a result array of the same length as the input, filled with -1.
  2. Initialize an empty stack. The stack will store the indices of the elements waiting to find a greater element.
  3. Loop for i, num in enumerate(arr):
  4. Pop & Resolve: While the stack is not empty AND num is GREATER than the element currently at the top of the stack (arr[stack[-1]]):
  5. The rule of our monotonically decreasing stack is broken by num!
  6. Pop the index from the stack: popped_index = stack.pop().
  7. Update the result for that person: result[popped_index] = num.
  8. Push: Push the current person's index into the waiting room: stack.append(i).
  9. Any indices left in the stack at the end never found a greater element, so they correctly remain -1 in the result array. Return result.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the array of length $N$ exactly once. Even though there is a while loop inside, every single index is pushed onto the stack exactly once, and popped off at most once. So the inner loop only executes $N$ times total across the entire program.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst-case scenario (an array sorted in descending order like [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]), nobody ever finds a greater element, and the stack grows to hold all $N$ indices.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Descending Array: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. The while stack and num > arr[stack[-1]] loop literally never executes. The stack just fills up. Result remains identically [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1]. Perfect!
  • Ascending Array: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Every single number pops the previous one immediately. Result is [2, 3, 4, 5, -1]. Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def next_greater_element(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds the Next Greater Element for every element in an array.
    """
    if not arr:
        return []

    result: list[int] = [-1] * len(arr)
    stack: list[int] = []  # Stores *indices*, not values!

    for i, num in enumerate(arr):
        # The 'rule' of our Monotonic Stack is perfectly decreasing.
        # If 'num' is greater, the rule is broken! Pop the smaller elements.
        while stack and num > arr[stack[-1]]:
            popped_index = stack.pop()
            result[popped_index] = num
            
        # Push the current index to the waiting room
        stack.append(i)

    return result

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [4, 6, 3, 2, 8, 1]
    assert next_greater_element(arr1) == [6, 8, 8, 8, -1, -1], f"Test 1 failed: {next_greater_element(arr1)}"

    arr2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    assert next_greater_element(arr2) == [2, 3, 4, 5, -1], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
    assert next_greater_element(arr3) == [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1], "Edge 1: Descending array"
    
    assert next_greater_element([]) == [], "Edge 2: Empty array"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every element is pushed to the stack once and popped at most once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can store all elements in the worst case (e.g., sorted descending).

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Next Smaller Element

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

This is exactly the same as the "Next Greater Element" problem, but reversed!

Instead of a very TALL person walking in and telling all the shorter people they can leave the waiting room...

A very SHORT person walks in!

If you are height 10, and a person of height 3 stands behind you, you can't see anyone shorter than 3 ever again. That short person blocks the view of anything shorter down the line.

So, when a SHORT person enters the waiting room, EVERYONE in the room who is TALLER than them says "Aha! That's my Next Smaller Element!"

They write down the short person's height and leave the room.

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses a monotonically increasing stack. We only allow the stack to contain values that are strictly getting larger. If a small number arrives, the rule is broken, and we pop the large numbers!

  1. Initialize an array result of the same length as the input, filled with -1.
  2. Initialize an empty stack. The stack will store the indices of the elements waiting to find a smaller element.
  3. Loop for i, num in enumerate(arr):
  4. Pop & Resolve: While the stack is not empty AND num is SMALLER than the element currently at the top of the stack (arr[stack[-1]]):
  5. The rule of our monotonically increasing stack is broken by num!
  6. Pop the index from the stack: popped_index = stack.pop().
  7. Update the result for that person: result[popped_index] = num.
  8. Push: Push the current person's index into the waiting room: stack.append(i).
  9. Return result.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the array of length $N$ exactly once. Every index is pushed and popped at most once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst-case scenario (an array sorted in ascending order), nobody ever finds a smaller element, and the stack grows to hold all $N$ indices.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Ascending Array: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The while stack and num < arr[stack[-1]] loop literally never executes. The stack just fills up completely. Result remains identically [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1]. Perfect!
  • Descending Array: [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]. Every single number pops the previous one immediately. Result is [4, 3, 2, 1, -1]. Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def next_smaller_element(arr: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds the Next Smaller Element for every element in an array.
    """
    if not arr:
        return []

    result: list[int] = [-1] * len(arr)
    stack: list[int] = []  # Stores *indices*, not values!

    for i, num in enumerate(arr):
        # The 'rule' of our Monotonic Stack is perfectly increasing.
        # If 'num' is smaller, the rule is broken! Pop the larger elements.
        while stack and num < arr[stack[-1]]:
            popped_index = stack.pop()
            result[popped_index] = num
            
        # Push the current index to the waiting room
        stack.append(i)

    return result

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    arr1 = [4, 8, 5, 2, 25]
    assert next_smaller_element(arr1) == [2, 5, 2, -1, -1], f"Test 1 failed: {next_smaller_element(arr1)}"

    arr2 = [13, 7, 6, 12]
    assert next_smaller_element(arr2) == [7, 6, -1, -1], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    arr3 = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
    assert next_smaller_element(arr3) == [-1, -1, -1, -1, -1], "Edge 1: Ascending array"
    
    assert next_smaller_element([]) == [], "Edge 2: Empty array"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every element is pushed to the stack once and popped at most once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can store all elements in the worst case (e.g., sorted ascending).

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Daily Temperatures

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a list of temperatures for the next few days.

For every single day, you want to know: "How many days do I have to wait until it is WARMER than today?"

If it never gets warmer, you just say "0 days".

This is exactly the "Next Greater Element" problem, but instead of writing down the temperature of the warmer day, you want to write down the distance (number of days) between today and the warmer day.

Because we store the index of the day in our Monotonic Stack, calculating the distance is super easy! It's just warmer_day_index - today_index.

🎯 Core Strategy

We use a monotonically decreasing stack. The stack will store the indices of days that are waiting for a warmer day. Because it's monotonically decreasing, the temperatures corresponding to the indices in the stack will strictly decrease from bottom to top.

  1. Initialize a result array of the same length as temperatures, filled with 0 (default if no warmer day is found).
  2. Initialize an empty stack to store indices.
  3. Loop for i, temp in enumerate(temperatures):
  4. Pop & Resolve: While the stack is not empty AND temp is GREATER than the temperature of the day currently at the top of the stack (temperatures[stack[-1]]):
  5. A warmer day has arrived!
  6. Pop the index from the stack: popped_day = stack.pop().
  7. Calculate how long that day waited: wait_time = i - popped_day.
  8. Update the result for that day: result[popped_day] = wait_time.
  9. Push: Push the current day's index into the waiting room: stack.append(i).
  10. Return result.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the array of length $N$ exactly once. Every index is pushed and popped at most once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst-case scenario (an array sorted in descending order), nobody ever finds a warmer day, and the stack grows to hold all $N$ indices.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Decreasing Temperatures: [90, 80, 70, 60]. The while stack and temp > temperatures[stack[-1]] loop literally never executes. The stack just fills up completely. Result remains identically [0, 0, 0, 0]. Perfect!
  • Single temperature: [30]. Loop runs once, pushes index 0. Returns [0]. Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def daily_temperatures(temperatures: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """
    Given an array of daily temperatures, returns an array of wait days for a warmer temperature.
    """
    if not temperatures:
        return []

    result: list[int] = [0] * len(temperatures)
    stack: list[int] = []  # Stores indices of the days

    for i, temp in enumerate(temperatures):
        # The 'rule' of our Monotonic Stack is perfectly decreasing temperatures.
        # If today is warmer, the rule is broken! Pop the colder days.
        while stack and temp > temperatures[stack[-1]]:
            popped_day = stack.pop()
            # Calculate how many days they had to wait
            result[popped_day] = i - popped_day
            
        # Push today into the waiting room
        stack.append(i)

    return result

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    temps1 = [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]
    # Expected: [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]
    assert daily_temperatures(temps1) == [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0], f"Test 1 failed: {daily_temperatures(temps1)}"

    temps2 = [30, 40, 50, 60]
    assert daily_temperatures(temps2) == [1, 1, 1, 0], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    temps3 = [90, 80, 70, 60]
    assert daily_temperatures(temps3) == [0, 0, 0, 0], "Edge 1: Decreasing temperatures"
    
    temps4 = [30]
    assert daily_temperatures(temps4) == [0], "Edge 2: Single temperature"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every day is pushed to the stack once and popped at most once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can store all days if the temperature is constantly dropping.
Medium Online Stock Spanner
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Online Stock Spanner

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are tracking the stock price of your favorite toy company every day.

When you check the price today, you want to know: "How many days in a row (looking backward from today) was the price lower than or equal to today's price?"

If the prices were: [10, 20, 30]

  • On day 1 (price 10), it's the first day, so the streak is 1.
  • On day 2 (price 20), 20 is bigger than 10. So the streak is today (1) + yesterday's streak (1) = 2.
  • On day 3 (price 30), 30 is bigger than 20. So the streak is today (1) + yesterday's streak (2) = 3.

We can use a Stack to remember previous days! But instead of just remembering the price, we remember a combo meal: (price, streak).

When a big price comes in, it "eats" all the smaller prices in the stack and absorbs their streaks!

🎯 Core Strategy

We use a monotonically decreasing stack to store tuples of (price, span).

Because it's a decreasing stack, every element below the top element is guaranteed to be strictly larger than the top element.

  1. Initialize self.stack = [].
  2. When next(price) is called:
  3. Initialize the span for today as 1 (because today always counts).
  4. Pop & Absorb: While the stack is not empty AND the price at the top of the stack is <= price:
  5. This older price is smaller or equal, so it gets absorbed!
  6. popped_price, popped_span = self.stack.pop()
  7. Add its span to our current span: span += popped_span.
  8. Push: Push our new combo (price, span) onto the stack.
  9. Return the span.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: Amortized $O(1)$ per call to next. Each element is pushed onto the stack exactly once and popped off at most once. Over $N$ calls, the total time spent in the while loop is $O(N)$, meaning the average time per call is $O(1)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The stack can grow to size $N$ if the prices strictly decrease every day (e.g., 100, 90, 80...), as nothing ever gets popped.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Prices strictly decrease: [50, 40, 30]. The while loop never triggers. Span is always 1. Stack grows smoothly.
  • Prices are identical: [50, 50, 50]. The condition self.stack[-1][0] <= price properly catches the equal prices and absorbs them, yielding spans of 1, 2, 3. Perfect!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
class StockSpanner:
    def __init__(self):
        # Stack stores tuples of (price, span)
        self.stack: list[tuple[int, int]] = []

    def next(self, price: int) -> int:
        span = 1
        
        # While the stack has elements and the top price is less than or equal to today's price
        while self.stack and self.stack[-1][0] <= price:
            # Pop it and absorb its span!
            popped_price, popped_span = self.stack.pop()
            span += popped_span
            
        # Push the new price and its total accumulated span
        self.stack.append((price, span))
        
        return span

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    spanner = StockSpanner()
    
    # ✅ Normal cases (Prices: 100, 80, 60, 70, 60, 75, 85)
    assert spanner.next(100) == 1, "Test 1 failed"  # [ (100, 1) ]
    assert spanner.next(80) == 1, "Test 2 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (80, 1) ]
    assert spanner.next(60) == 1, "Test 3 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (80, 1), (60, 1) ]
    
    # 70 is greater than 60, so it absorbs 60.
    assert spanner.next(70) == 2, "Test 4 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2) ]
    
    assert spanner.next(60) == 1, "Test 5 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (80, 1), (70, 2), (60, 1) ]
    
    # 75 is greater than 60 (span 1) and 70 (span 2), so it absorbs both! (1 + 1 + 2 = 4)
    assert spanner.next(75) == 4, "Test 6 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (80, 1), (75, 4) ]
    
    # 85 is greater than 75 (span 4) and 80 (span 1), so it absorbs both! (1 + 4 + 1 = 6)
    assert spanner.next(85) == 6, "Test 7 failed"   # [ (100, 1), (85, 6) ]

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: Amortized O(1) per call to `next`. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can grow to size N if prices are strictly decreasing.
Medium Remove K Digits
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Remove K Digits

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are given a huge number like "1432219" and you are allowed to erase exactly $K$ digits to make the number as small as possible.

If $K = 3$, which digits do you erase?

You always want smaller numbers at the front! (e.g., 100 is smaller than 900).

So we read the numbers one by one and put them in a stack.

If we see a '4' at the top of our stack, and the next number coming along is a '3', we think:

"Wait! If I erase this '4' right now, the '3' will slide over and take its place, making the whole number smaller!"

So as long as we have "erasers" left ($K > 0$), any time a smaller number comes along, we POP the bigger numbers off the stack to make room for the small guy!

This naturally builds a small increasing sequence (1, 2, 3...) which guarantees the smallest possible number.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a Greedy algorithm executed via a monotonically increasing stack. At every step, we try to keep the stack strictly increasing by throwing away (popping) larger digits when a smaller digit is encountered, limited only by $K$.

  1. Initialize an empty stack.
  2. Greedy Deletion: Loop through every digit in the string num:
  3. While the stack is not empty, AND we still have removals left (k > 0), AND the digit is SMALLER than the top of the stack (stack[-1] > digit):
  4. We found a better (smaller) digit to take this place!
  5. Pop the top of the stack.
  6. Decrement k (we just used an eraser).
  7. Push the current digit onto the stack.
  8. Handle Leftovers: What if we still have erasers left? (e.g., the number was already sorted like "1234"). Then we just erase the biggest numbers, which are naturally sitting at the very end of our stack! stack = stack[:-k].
  9. Clean up: Join the stack into a string. We might have leading zeros (like "0200"). We must strip them using .lstrip('0').
  10. If the final string is completely empty (we erased everything), return "0". Otherwise, return the string.

"4"34 > 1. Push 4["1", "4"]

"2"12 == 2. Push 2.["1", "2", "2"]
"1"11 < 2. Pop 2! k = 0. (Erasers gone!).<br>Push 1.["1", "2", "1"]
"9"0k=0, just push 9.["1", "2", "1", "9"]

Loop finishes. k = 0.

Result string: "1219". No leading zeros to strip.

Final Result: "1219".

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We iterate through the $N$ digits of the string exactly once. Each digit is pushed to the stack once and popped at most once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$ to store the characters in the stack and to build the final string.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Already Sorted: num = "12345", k = 2. The inner while loop never triggers because stack[-1] < digit. At the end, k is still 2. The code handles this via if k > 0: stack = stack[:-k], cleanly slicing off the last two characters to return "123".
  • Leading Zeros Formed: num = "10200", k = 1. 0 pops 1 (because 0 < 1). Stack becomes ["0", "2", "0", "0"]. The .lstrip('0') cleans it to "200".
  • Everything is Erased / All Zeros: num = "10", k = 2 or num = "9", k = 1. Stack ends up empty. .lstrip('0') leaves an empty string "". The return statement result if result else "0" safely turns this into "0".
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def remove_k_digits(num: str, k: int) -> str:
    """
    Returns the smallest possible integer after removing k digits from num.
    """
    if k == len(num):
        return "0"
        
    stack: list[str] = []

    for digit in num:
        # If we still have removals left, and the current digit is smaller 
        # than the last digit we kept, it's better to replace the last digit!
        while stack and k > 0 and stack[-1] > digit:
            stack.pop()
            k -= 1
            
        stack.append(digit)

    # If we still have removals left (e.g., all digits were ascending like "12345")
    # we just chop off the largest ones at the end.
    if k > 0:
        stack = stack[:-k]

    # Join the stack and strip any leading zeros
    result = "".join(stack).lstrip('0')

    # If the result is completely empty, it means we erased everything or all zeros
    return result if result else "0"

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    # 1432219 -> 1 32219 (erase 4) -> 1 2219 (erase 3) -> 12 19 (erase 2) = 1219
    assert remove_k_digits("1432219", 3) == "1219", "Test 1 failed"
    
    # 10200 -> 0200 (erase 1) -> strip leading 0 -> 200
    assert remove_k_digits("10200", 1) == "200", "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert remove_k_digits("10", 2) == "0", "Edge 1: Erase everything"
    assert remove_k_digits("9", 1) == "0", "Edge 2: Erase single digit"
    assert remove_k_digits("1111", 2) == "11", "Edge 3: Identical digits"
    assert remove_k_digits("12345", 2) == "123", "Edge 4: Already sorted"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Each digit is pushed and popped at most once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can store up to N characters.
Hard Largest Rectangle in Histogram
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Largest Rectangle in Histogram

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you built a city skyline using LEGO blocks, all lined up in a row.

You want to paint the absolute largest solid rectangle possible across these buildings.

If you pick a short building, you can paint a very wide rectangle across all the taller buildings next to it! But it will be short.

If you pick a very tall building, the rectangle will be tall, but probably very skinny, because the next building might be shorter and block it.

How do we find the biggest one?

We use a Monotonic INCREASING Stack!

We push buildings onto our stack as long as they keep getting taller.

But the moment a SHORT building appears, it ruins the streak!

It tells the tall buildings on the stack: "You can't stretch any further to the right!"

So, we pop the tall buildings one by one, and for each one, we calculate:

"Okay, how tall are you? And how far to the LEFT did you stretch before you hit another short building?" (The answer is whatever is underneath it on the stack!).

We multiply Height $\times$ Width, and keep track of the biggest rectangle we find.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the classic, hard-level application of the Monotonic Stack. We maintain a strictly increasing stack of indices.

  1. Initialize max_area = 0.
  2. Initialize an empty stack to store indices of the buildings.
  3. The Janitor Trick: Append a 0 height building to the very end of the array. This acts as a tiny "janitor" building that forces the stack to pop and calculate the area for ALL remaining buildings at the very end of the loop, saving us from writing duplicate code outside the loop.
  4. Loop through for i, h in enumerate(heights):
  5. Calculate Trapped Areas: While the stack is not empty AND the current building h is SHORTER than the building at the top of the stack (heights[stack[-1]]):
  6. The top building is trapped! It cannot expand to the right anymore.
  7. Pop it: height = heights[stack.pop()].
  8. Calculate width:
  9. If the stack is empty after popping, this building was the shortest so far, so it stretches all the way to the left: width = i.
  10. If the stack is not empty, it stretches to the left down to the new top of the stack (exclusive): width = i - stack[-1] - 1.
  11. Update area: max_area = max(max_area, height * width).
  12. Push: Push the current index i onto the stack.
  13. (Optional but good practice) Remove the dummy 0 from the end of the array.
  14. Return max_area.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the array of length $N+1$ exactly once. Every building index is pushed onto the stack exactly once, and popped off exactly once. The total number of operations inside the while loop across the entire execution is strictly bounded by $N$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The stack can store up to $N$ indices if the histogram is strictly increasing (e.g., [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Flat Histogram: [2, 2, 2, 2]. Stack holds [0, 1, 2, 3]. The 0 at the end pops them one by one. The final pop (Index 0, height 2) sees an empty stack and calculates width = 4. Area = $2 \times 4 = 8$. Perfect!
  • Ascending Histogram: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Nothing gets popped until the dummy 0 at the very end forces everything to pop. The max area (3x3 = 9) is correctly found during the flush.
  • Empty Array: Handled by the if not heights: return 0 check.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def largest_rectangle_area(heights: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the largest rectangular area possible in a histogram.
    """
    if not heights:
        return 0

    max_area = 0
    stack: list[int] = []
    
    # Append a 0 to act as a trigger to flush the stack at the end
    heights.append(0)

    for i, h in enumerate(heights):
        # A shorter building forces us to calculate the area for taller buildings
        while stack and h < heights[stack[-1]]:
            # 1. Get the height of the trapped building
            height = heights[stack.pop()]
            
            # 2. Calculate the width
            # If stack is empty, it means this building was the shortest so far, 
            # so it stretches all the way from index 0 to i.
            if not stack:
                width = i
            else:
                # It stretches from the building just to its left (the new stack top) up to i.
                width = i - stack[-1] - 1
                
            # 3. Update max area
            max_area = max(max_area, height * width)
            
        stack.append(i)

    # Clean up the array by removing the dummy 0
    heights.pop()

    return max_area

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert largest_rectangle_area([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]) == 10, "Test 1 failed"  # 5 and 6 give 5*2 = 10
    assert largest_rectangle_area([2, 4]) == 4, "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert largest_rectangle_area([2, 2, 2, 2]) == 8, "Edge 1: Flat histogram"
    assert largest_rectangle_area([5]) == 5, "Edge 2: Single bar"
    assert largest_rectangle_area([]) == 0, "Edge 3: Empty"
    
    # Ascending array (flushed by the 0 at the end)
    assert largest_rectangle_area([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == 9, "Edge 4: Ascending (3*3)"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every building is pushed and popped exactly once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The stack can grow up to size N.
