📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 10: Hash Maps

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a giant library with a million books.

If someone asks you, "Do you have the book 'Harry Potter'?", it would take you

hours to check every single bookshelf one by one.

But what if you had a magical notebook? In this notebook, every time you buy a

book, you write down its name and exactly which shelf it's on.

Now, when someone asks for 'Harry Potter', you just flip the notebook exactly to

the 'H' page, look for 'Harry Potter', and instantly know the answer!

A Hash Map (or a Dictionary in Python) is exactly this magical notebook.

It lets you store a Key (the book's name) and a Value (the shelf number),

and it lets you look them up instantly, in O(1) time!

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

Hash Maps are the most commonly used data structure in coding interviews. They trade a little bit of Space (to store the dictionary) for a massive amount of Time savings (turning O(N) or O(N²) lookups into O(1)).

When to use it:

  • The problem requires you to count the frequency of items.
  • You need to check if something exists very quickly without looping.
  • You are trying to find pairs or sums (like Two Sum).
  • You want to group items by a common property (like Anagrams).
  • You are repeatedly looking backward to see if you've seen a specific value before.

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe 1: Frequency Counters

If you want to count how many times characters or words appear:

  1. freq_map = {}
  2. for item in array:
  3. freq_map[item] = freq_map.get(item, 0) + 1

Recipe 2: The "Look-Back" Pattern (Two Sum)

Instead of looking forward in nested loops, look backward at what you've already seen:

  1. seen_map = {}
  2. for i, num in enumerate(nums):
  3. needed = target - num
  4. if needed in seen_map: return [seen_map[needed], i]
  5. seen_map[num] = i

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Two Sum / Look-BackDO store values in the map AS you iterate. This prevents using the same element twice.DON'T put everything in the map first and then loop again, unless the problem strictly allows re-using elements or has edge cases.
Anagram GroupingDO use a sorted string (or a tuple of character counts) as the Key.DON'T use a list or a set as a Key! Dictionary keys must be immutable (hashable).
Prefix SumsDO use a Hash Map to store (prefix_sum -> count). Initialize the map with {0: 1} to catch sub-arrays starting from index 0.DON'T forget that negative numbers exist. Sliding Window won't work for arrays with negatives; you MUST use Prefix Sum + Hash Map.

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(1) averageLooking up a key in a Hash Map is generally instant. Overall time complexity for a loop drops from O(N²) to O(N).
SpaceO(N)We have to store up to N items in our Hash Map.

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Mutable Keys: You cannot use a list [1, 2, 3] as a key in a Python dictionary. You must convert it to a tuple (1, 2, 3).
  2. KeyError: Trying to read my_dict["apple"] if "apple" doesn't exist will crash your program. Use my_dict.get("apple", default_value) or check if "apple" in my_dict: first.
  3. Hash Collisions: In theoretical computer science, if many keys hash to the same spot, O(1) can degrade to O(N). Python handles this automatically, but it's good to know for interviews!

Easy Two Sum
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Two Sum

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a bunch of numbers: [2, 7, 11, 15] and a target number: 9.

You need to find exactly two numbers that add up to 9, and give their indices.

You COULD look at 2, and then ask every single other number: "Hey, are you 7?"

But if the list is a million numbers long, that takes forever!

Instead, as you walk down the line, you use a magical notebook (Hash Map).

When you look at 2, you write down: "I saw a 2 at index 0."

When you get to 7, you think: "I need a 2 to make 9. Let me check my notebook!"

You look in the notebook, see that you found a 2 earlier at index 0, and boom!

You instantly know the answer is index 0 and index 1.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the foundational Hash Map problem. It teaches you how to trade space for time, bringing an $O(N^2)$ brute-force approach down to an elegant $O(N)$ solution.

  1. Initialize an empty dictionary seen_map = {}. This will store number -> index mappings.
  2. Loop through the array using enumerate to get both i (index) and num.
  3. For the current num, calculate what number you would NEED to reach the target: needed = target - num.
  4. O(1) Lookup: Check if needed is already a key in your seen_map.
  5. If it is, you found your pair! Return [seen_map[needed], i].
  6. If it's not, store the current number and its index in the map for future numbers to look up: seen_map[num] = i.
  7. (Optional) Return an empty list if the loop finishes without finding a pair.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the array of length $N$ exactly once. Hash Map lookups (needed in seen_map) take amortized $O(1)$ time in Python.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst-case scenario (the pair is at the very end of the array, or doesn't exist), we will store $N$ elements in the dictionary.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Same numbers forming the target: nums = [3, 3], target = 6. When processing the first 3, we put {3: 0} in the map. When processing the second 3 at index 1, needed = 6 - 3 = 3. We check the map, see that 3 exists at index 0, and return [0, 1]. By adding to the map after checking, we prevent a number from matching with itself!
  • Negative numbers: nums = [-1, -2, -3], target = -5. The math target - num perfectly handles negatives: -5 - (-2) = -3. It correctly searches for -3.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def two_sum(nums: list[int], target: int) -> list[int]:
    """
    Finds two numbers such that they add up to a specific target number.
    Returns their indices.
    """
    seen_map: dict[int, int] = {}

    for i, num in enumerate(nums):
        needed = target - num
        
        # O(1) instant lookup in our magical notebook!
        if needed in seen_map:
            return [seen_map[needed], i]
            
        # Store the current number and its index for future reference
        seen_map[num] = i

    return []

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1], "Test 1 failed"
    assert two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) == [1, 2], "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1], "Edge 1: Same numbers"
    
    # Negative numbers
    assert two_sum([-1, -2, -3, -4, -5], -8) == [2, 4], "Edge 2: Negative numbers"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We loop through the array exactly once. Looking up things in a Hash Map takes O(1) time. 💾 Space: O(N) — The Hash Map can store up to N numbers in the worst case.
Easy First Non-repeating Character
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: First Non-repeating Character

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a word like "apple".

You want to find the first letter that appears exactly ONE time in the whole word.

If you look at 'a', it appears 1 time. It's the very first letter! So the answer is 'a'.

What about "aabbc"?

'a' appears 2 times. 'b' appears 2 times. 'c' appears 1 time. So the answer is 'c'.

To solve this quickly, we just read the word twice:

  • First time: We write down in our magical notebook how many times we see every single letter.
  • Second time: We look at the letters in order from left to right, check the notebook, and as soon as we find a letter with a count of exactly 1, we stop and return its index!

🎯 Core Strategy

This uses a Hash Map for Frequency Counting, which is one of the most common applications of a Hash Map. By counting the frequencies first, we can answer questions about uniqueness in $O(1)$ time on the second pass.

  1. Initialize an empty dictionary freq_map = {} to store character counts (char -> int).
  2. First Pass (Build): Loop through the string.
  3. For every character, increment its count in freq_map.
  4. Python idiom: freq_map[char] = freq_map.get(char, 0) + 1
  5. Second Pass (Find): Loop through the string again using enumerate to get the index i and char.
  6. Check the frequency: if freq_map[char] == 1.
  7. If true, instantly return the index i.
  8. If the loop finishes and we didn't return anything, it means every character was repeated! Return -1.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: "loveleetcode"

Phase 1: Build the Frequency Map

We scan the entire string and count occurrences.

freq_map = {'l': 2, 'o': 2, 'v': 1, 'e': 4, 't': 1, 'c': 1, 'd': 1}

Phase 2: Find the First Unique

Now we walk through the string from left to right and check the map.

icharfreq_map[char]Action
0'l'2Continue
1'o'2Continue
2'v'1Return 2!

Final Result: 2.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We loop through the string of length $N$ exactly twice. $O(2N)$ simplifies to $O(N)$. Dictionary lookups and insertions are $O(1)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$ strictly speaking. Even though we create a Hash Map, the string only consists of English letters. There are at most 26 unique lowercase English letters. The dictionary will never grow beyond size 26, which is an $O(1)$ constant space bound.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • All characters repeat: e.g., "aabb". The second loop checks a (count 2) and b (count 2), finds nothing with count 1, finishes the loop, and safely returns -1.
  • Empty string: "". Both loops skip entirely. Returns -1.
  • Single character: "z". Map built as {'z': 1}. Second pass immediately finds z at index 0 and returns 0.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def first_uniq_char(s: str) -> int:
    """
    Finds the index of the first non-repeating character in a string.
    Returns -1 if it doesn't exist.
    """
    freq_map: dict[str, int] = {}

    # 1. First Pass: Build the frequency map
    for char in s:
        freq_map[char] = freq_map.get(char, 0) + 1

    # 2. Second Pass: Find the first character with a frequency of 1
    for i, char in enumerate(s):
        if freq_map[char] == 1:
            return i

    # No unique character found
    return -1

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert first_uniq_char("leetcode") == 0, "Test 1 failed"       # 'l' is at 0
    assert first_uniq_char("loveleetcode") == 2, "Test 2 failed"   # 'v' is at 2
    assert first_uniq_char("aabbc") == 4, "Test 3 failed"          # 'c' is at 4
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert first_uniq_char("aabb") == -1, "Edge 1: All repeat"
    assert first_uniq_char("") == -1, "Edge 2: Empty string"
    assert first_uniq_char("z") == 0, "Edge 3: Single character"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We loop through the string twice. 2N is still O(N). 💾 Space: O(1) — The Hash Map will at most store 26 characters (if only lowercase English letters).
Easy Ransom Note
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Ransom Note

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you want to write a secret message (a ransom note) by cutting out letters from a magazine.

If your note needs the letter 'A' two times, but the magazine only has one 'A', you can't write your note!

You can only use each letter from the magazine exactly as many times as it appears.

So, what's the plan?

First, you read the whole magazine and write down exactly how many of each letter you have. (e.g., A: 5, B: 2, C: 0...)

Then, you look at your ransom note letter by letter.

For every letter, you check your list. Do I have this letter?

If yes, cross one out (subtract 1 from the count).

If no (or if the count is 0), then it's impossible to write the note!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is another application of the Hash Map Frequency Counter. It tracks available "inventory" (the magazine) and then deducts from it to fulfill a "demand" (the ransom note).

  1. Quick Optimization: If the ransom_note is longer than the magazine, it is physically impossible to construct it. Return False immediately.
  2. Initialize an empty dictionary magazine_freq = {}.
  3. Build Inventory: Loop through every character in the magazine.
  4. Add 1 to its count in magazine_freq.
  5. Fulfill Demand: Loop through every character in the ransom_note.
  6. Check if the character exists in magazine_freq AND its count is $> 0$.
  7. If yes: We have the letter! Subtract 1 from its count in the dictionary (we "used" it).
  8. If no: We don't have the letter, or we ran out of it. Return False.
  9. If we made it through the whole ransom note loop without returning False, it means we successfully found all the letters we needed. Return True.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: ransom_note = "aa", magazine = "aab"

Phase 1: Build Inventory (Magazine)

We scan "aab":

  • 'a': count becomes 1
  • 'a': count becomes 2
  • 'b': count becomes 1

magazine_freq = {'a': 2, 'b': 1}

Phase 2: Fulfill Demand (Ransom Note)

We scan "aa":

  • Char 'a': Is it in our map? Yes, count is 2. 2 > 0. Subtract 1. magazine_freq is now {'a': 1, 'b': 1}.
  • Char 'a': Is it in our map? Yes, count is 1. 1 > 0. Subtract 1. magazine_freq is now {'a': 0, 'b': 1}.

Loop finishes! Return True.

Example Input 2: ransom_note = "aa", magazine = "ab"

Inventory: {'a': 1, 'b': 1}

Demand:

  • Char 'a': Count is 1. Use it. Inventory becomes {'a': 0, 'b': 1}.
  • Char 'a': Count is 0. 0 > 0 is False! Return False!

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N + M)$ where $N$ is the length of the ransom note and $M$ is the length of the magazine. We iterate through both strings exactly once. Dictionary operations are $O(1)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(1)$. Since the problem specifies lowercase English letters, the Hash Map will never store more than 26 key-value pairs, which is a constant $O(1)$ space bound, regardless of how huge the magazine string is.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Note longer than magazine: Instantly caught by if len(ransom_note) > len(magazine): return False. Avoids all processing!
  • Empty note: " ". Handled gracefully. Note loop skips, returns True.
  • Empty magazine: Catch by the length optimization check. Returns False.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def can_construct(ransom_note: str, magazine: str) -> bool:
    """
    Returns True if ransom_note can be constructed from magazine, False otherwise.
    """
    # Quick optimization: If the note is longer, it's impossible
    if len(ransom_note) > len(magazine):
        return False

    magazine_freq: dict[str, int] = {}

    # 1. Count all letters available in the magazine
    for char in magazine:
        magazine_freq[char] = magazine_freq.get(char, 0) + 1

    # 2. Try to construct the ransom note
    for char in ransom_note:
        if magazine_freq.get(char, 0) > 0:
            # Use one letter
            magazine_freq[char] -= 1
        else:
            # We don't have this letter (or we ran out of it)
            return False

    return True

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert can_construct("a", "b") == False, "Test 1 failed"
    assert can_construct("aa", "ab") == False, "Test 2 failed"
    assert can_construct("aa", "aab") == True, "Test 3 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert can_construct("", "abc") == True, "Edge 1: Empty note"
    assert can_construct("abc", "") == False, "Edge 2: Empty magazine"
    assert can_construct("longer", "short") == False, "Edge 3: Note longer than magazine"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N + M) — Where N is length of the note, M is length of the magazine. 💾 Space: O(1) — The Hash Map stores at most 26 lowercase English letters.
Medium Group Anagrams
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Group Anagrams

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a bucket of words: ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"].

An anagram is a word made by mixing up the letters of another word. "eat", "tea", and "ate" all have exactly one 'e', one 'a', and one 't'.

You want to group all the mixed-up words together!

How do you know if two words are anagrams of each other?

If you put their letters in alphabetical order, they will look EXACTLY the same!

  • "eat" sorted is "aet".
  • "tea" sorted is "aet".
  • "ate" sorted is "aet".

We can use a Hash Map where the "Key" is the sorted word ("aet"), and the "Value" is a list of all the original words that sort to that key: ["eat", "tea", "ate"].

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a grouping problem, which perfectly fits a Hash Map mapping to Lists (dict[str, list[str]]). The main trick is finding a "canonical" key that all anagrams share. Sorting the string provides this canonical key.

  1. Initialize an empty dictionary groups = {}.
  2. Loop through every word in the input list.
  3. Generate Key: Sort the characters in the word and join them back into a single string to form the key.
  4. sorted_word = "".join(sorted(word))
  5. Group: Check if sorted_word is already a key in groups.
  6. If not, initialize it with an empty list.
  7. Append the original word to the list at groups[sorted_word].
  8. Finally, return all the values from the dictionary as a list of lists.
  9. return list(groups.values())

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]

wordSorted KeyActiongroups Dictionary

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N \cdot K \log K)$. Where $N$ is the number of words, and $K$ is the maximum length of a word. We iterate through $N$ strings, and for each string, we sort it, which takes $K \log K$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N \cdot K)$. The Hash Map stores all $N$ strings of length $K$.

(Note: An alternative $O(N \cdot K)$ time approach involves using a frequency array of size 26 as a tuple key instead of sorting. This is faster for very long strings but more verbose to code).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty string: [""]. Sorting "" yields "". It is placed in the dictionary at key "". Returns [[""]]. Correct!
  • Single character: ["a"]. Returns [["a"]]. Correct!
  • Words with identical characters but different frequencies: ["aab", "abb"].
  • "aab" sorts to "aab".
  • "abb" sorts to "abb".
  • They correctly map to different keys. Returns [["aab"], ["abb"]]. Correct!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def group_anagrams(strs: list[str]) -> list[list[str]]:
    """
    Groups an array of strings into anagrams.
    """
    groups: dict[str, list[str]] = {}

    for word in strs:
        # Sort the word to use as the dictionary key
        sorted_word = "".join(sorted(word))
        
        # If we haven't seen this sorted word before, create a new list
        if sorted_word not in groups:
            groups[sorted_word] = []
            
        # Add the original word to the correct group
        groups[sorted_word].append(word)

    # Return just the grouped lists
    return list(groups.values())

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def compare_groups(g1, g2):
        # Helper to compare lists of lists irrespective of order
        return sorted([sorted(g) for g in g1]) == sorted([sorted(g) for g in g2])

    # ✅ Normal cases
    strs1 = ["eat", "tea", "tan", "ate", "nat", "bat"]
    expected1 = [["bat"], ["nat", "tan"], ["ate", "eat", "tea"]]
    res1 = group_anagrams(strs1)
    assert compare_groups(res1, expected1), f"Test 1 failed: {res1}"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert group_anagrams([""]) == [[""]], "Edge 1: Empty string"
    assert group_anagrams(["a"]) == [["a"]], "Edge 2: Single character"
    
    # Words with identical characters but different frequencies
    strs2 = ["aab", "aba", "baa", "abb", "bab", "bba"]
    expected2 = [["aab", "aba", "baa"], ["abb", "bab", "bba"]]
    res2 = group_anagrams(strs2)
    assert compare_groups(res2, expected2), "Edge 3: Similar but different counts"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N * K log K) — Where N is the number of words, and K is the maximum length of a word. Sorting each word takes K log K time. 💾 Space: O(N * K) — The Hash Map stores all the words.
Medium Subarray Sum Equals K
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Subarray Sum Equals K

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a line of numbers, some positive and some negative: [1, -1, 1, 1, 1, 1].

You want to find how many continuous blocks (subarrays) add up exactly to $K$ (e.g., $K=3$).

Normally, we could use the "Sliding Window" pattern for subarrays.

BUT WAIT! Sliding Window ONLY works if all numbers are positive (because adding makes the sum bigger, and shrinking makes the sum smaller).

Here, we have negative numbers! Adding a '-1' actually makes the sum smaller, so the Sliding Window breaks.

Instead, we keep a "Running Total" (Prefix Sum) from the very beginning.

If our Running Total right now is 10, and we are looking for $K = 3$...

We just need to look in our magical notebook to see: "Did my Running Total ever equal 7 in the past?"

If it was 7 in the past, and it's 10 now, that means the numbers in between must add up exactly to 3!

We use a Hash Map to keep track of how many times we've seen every Running Total.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the quintessential Prefix Sum + Hash Map pattern. It reduces an $O(N^2)$ brute-force subarray search into an elegant $O(N)$ solution.

  1. Initialize count = 0 (our answer) and current_sum = 0.
  2. Initialize a dictionary prefix_sums = {0: 1}.
  3. Crucial step: Why {0: 1}? Because before we look at any numbers, our running total is $0$. If we find a number that exactly equals $K$ on its own, current_sum - K will be $0$. If $0$ isn't in the map, we'd miss it!
  4. Loop through every num in the array:
  5. Update Running Total: current_sum += num.
  6. Check for Complement: Calculate what prefix we would need to chop off to leave exactly $K$: needed = current_sum - k.
  7. If needed is in our prefix_sums map, add that frequency to count.
  8. Update Map: Finally, add the new current_sum to our prefix_sums map (or increment its count if we've seen it before).
  9. Return count.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input: nums = [1, 2, 3], $k = 3$

Initialization: count = 0, current_sum = 0, prefix_sums = {0: 1}.

23$3 - 3 = 0$Yes (freq 1)1{0: 1, 1: 1, 3: 1}
36$6 - 3 = 3$Yes (freq 1)2{0: 1, 1: 1, 3: 1, 6: 1}

Result: 2. (The subarrays are [1, 2] and [3]).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We iterate through the array exactly once. Dictionary lookups and updates in Python are $O(1)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. In the worst case, every single prefix sum is unique, meaning we store $N$ distinct values in the Hash Map.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Array with negative numbers and zeros: [1, -1, 0], target $K=0$.
  • Init: map={0:1}, sum=0, count=0
  • num=1: sum=1, needed=1-0=1. Not in map. map={0:1, 1:1}.
  • num=-1: sum=0, needed=0-0=0. In map! count += 1 (now 1). map={0:2, 1:1}.
  • num=0: sum=0, needed=0-0=0. In map! count += 2 (now 3). map={0:3, 1:1}.
  • Returns 3. Correct! (The subarrays are [1, -1], [-1, 0], and [1, -1, 0]). The frequency counter handled overlapping zero-sums flawlessly.
  • Empty Array: Loop skips. Returns 0. Correct!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def subarray_sum(nums: list[int], k: int) -> int:
    """
    Finds the total number of continuous subarrays whose sum equals to k.
    """
    count = 0
    current_sum = 0
    
    # Base case: A prefix sum of 0 has been seen exactly 1 time (before we start)
    prefix_sums: dict[int, int] = {0: 1}

    for num in nums:
        # 1. Update our running total
        current_sum += num
        
        # 2. Check if we can chop off a previous prefix to leave exactly 'k'
        needed = current_sum - k
        if needed in prefix_sums:
            count += prefix_sums[needed]
            
        # 3. Add the current running total to our magical notebook
        prefix_sums[current_sum] = prefix_sums.get(current_sum, 0) + 1

    return count

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert subarray_sum([1, 1, 1], 2) == 2, "Test 1 failed"  # [1, 1] at start, and [1, 1] at end
    assert subarray_sum([1, 2, 3], 3) == 2, "Test 2 failed"  # [1, 2] and [3]
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # Array with negative numbers and zeros
    assert subarray_sum([1, -1, 0], 0) == 3, "Edge 1 failed" 
    # The 3 subarrays are: [1, -1], [-1, 0] wait, no. 
    # [1, -1] = 0
    # [1, -1, 0] = 0
    # [0] = 0. Yes, 3 subarrays!
    
    assert subarray_sum([], 0) == 0, "Edge 2 failed"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — One pass through the array. Map lookups are O(1). 💾 Space: O(N) — The Hash Map can store up to N distinct prefix sums.
Medium Longest Consecutive Sequence
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Longest Consecutive Sequence

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a bucket of completely random numbers: [100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2].

You want to find the longest sequence of numbers that count up by 1.

In this bucket, the longest sequence is 1, 2, 3, 4 (length 4).

How do we do this without sorting the bucket? (Sorting takes too long, $O(N \log N)$).

First, we pour the bucket into a magical Hash Set. A Set is just a Hash Map that only stores Keys (no Values). It lets us ask "Do you have this number?" instantly.

Then, we pick up a number, like 4. We ask: "Is 3 in the Set?"

If 3 IS in the set, that means 4 is NOT the beginning of a sequence! It's just the middle or end. So we ignore 4 for now.

But if we pick up 1 and ask "Is 0 in the set?" The answer is NO!

That means 1 is the glorious START of a new sequence!

Since we found a starting line, we just start counting up: "Do you have 2? 3? 4? 5?" until the set says NO.

We keep track of the longest streak we find.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the premier Hash Set problem. A Hash Set gives us $O(1)$ constant time lookups. We use this to identify the start of a sequence, and then build the sequence from there.

  1. Build Hash Set: Convert the input array into a nums_set (a Hash Set). This removes duplicates and allows $O(1)$ lookups.
  2. Initialize longest_streak = 0.
  3. Loop through every num in the nums_set:
  4. Identify the Start: Check if num is the START of a sequence. It is the start ONLY if num - 1 is NOT in the set.
  5. If it is the start:
  6. Initialize current_num = num and current_streak = 1.
  7. Count Up: While current_num + 1 IS in the set:
  8. Increment current_num and current_streak.
  9. Update our record: longest_streak = max(longest_streak, current_streak).
  10. Return longest_streak.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We build the set in $O(N)$. Then we loop through the set. We ONLY enter the while loop if we are at the start of a sequence. Thus, the while loop only runs for the exact length of that sequence. Every number is visited at most twice (once in the outer loop, and once in the inner while loop). $O(N + N) = O(N)$.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$ because we pour all the numbers into a Hash Set.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Array: Handled by if not nums: return 0 at the very top.
  • Array with Duplicates: [1, 2, 0, 1]. The set(nums) automatically removes the duplicates! It becomes {0, 1, 2}. Then it correctly identifies 0 as the start, and counts up to 2, returning length 3. Perfectly handled.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
def longest_consecutive(nums: list[int]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence in O(N) time.
    """
    if not nums:
        return 0

    # 1. Pour everything into a Hash Set for O(1) lookups and to remove duplicates
    nums_set = set(nums)
    longest_streak = 0

    # 2. Iterate through the set
    for num in nums_set:
        # 3. Only start counting if this number is the START of a sequence
        if num - 1 not in nums_set:
            current_num = num
            current_streak = 1
            
            # 4. Count upwards as long as the next number exists in the set
            while current_num + 1 in nums_set:
                current_num += 1
                current_streak += 1
                
            # 5. Update our record
            longest_streak = max(longest_streak, current_streak)

    return longest_streak

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    assert longest_consecutive([100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2]) == 4, "Test 1 failed"  # 1, 2, 3, 4
    assert longest_consecutive([0, 3, 7, 2, 5, 8, 4, 6, 0, 1]) == 9, "Test 2 failed"  # 0 to 8
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert longest_consecutive([]) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty array"
    assert longest_consecutive([5, 5, 5, 5]) == 1, "Edge 2: All duplicates"
    assert longest_consecutive([1]) == 1, "Edge 3: Single element"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We only start counting if we are at the beginning of a sequence. The inner `while` loop only runs for the exact length of that sequence. Every number is visited at most twice. 💾 Space: O(N) — The Hash Set stores all N numbers.

Explorers 14 Problems
📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 11: Tree Breadth First Search (BFS)

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine a giant family tree hanging on the wall.

At the very top is the Great-Grandparent (the Root).

Below them are the Grandparents (Level 1).

Below them are the Parents (Level 2).

Below them are the Kids (Level 3).

If you want to introduce yourself to the whole family, you could start at the top,

and then just randomly run up and down the branches. That would be chaotic!

Instead, you use Breadth First Search (BFS).

You shake hands with the Great-Grandparent first.

Then, you shake hands with ALL the Grandparents from left to right.

Then, you shake hands with ALL the Parents from left to right.

Finally, you shake hands with ALL the Kids from left to right.

You visit the tree Level by Level, never going down to the next level until you

have met everyone on the current level.

To do this, we use a special line at a theme park called a Queue.

The first person who gets in line is the first person who gets on the ride

(FIFO - First In, First Out).

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

The BFS pattern works by using a Queue to keep track of all the nodes on the current level before moving on to the next level. We process nodes level-by-level, from top to bottom, left to right.

When to use it:

  • The problem asks you to traverse a tree level-by-level.
  • You need to find the shortest path or minimum depth in an unweighted tree/graph.
  • You need to connect nodes that are on the same level (siblings).
  • The problem mentions "Zigzag" or "Level averages".

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Standard BFS Level Traversal

In Python, we use collections.deque (double-ended queue) for our Queue because popping from the front of a standard list takes O(N) time, but deque.popleft() takes O(1) time!

  1. Initialization: queue = deque([root])
  2. Main Loop: while queue:
  3. Level Size: level_size = len(queue) (Crucial! Takes a snapshot of the current level).
  4. Level Loop: for _ in range(level_size):
  5. current_node = queue.popleft()
  6. Process current_node.
  7. if current_node.left: queue.append(current_node.left)
  8. if current_node.right: queue.append(current_node.right)

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Standard Level OrderDO take level_size = len(queue) at the START of the while loop.DON'T use for _ in range(len(queue)): because len(queue) changes dynamically as you append children!
Zigzag TraversalDO use a regular deque, but when adding values to the current_level list, insert them at the beginning (collections.deque.appendleft()) if the direction is reversed.DON'T try to append children to the queue in reverse order. It messes up the next level completely. Just reverse the output!
Minimum DepthDO return the depth immediately as soon as you find the first leaf node (a node with no left or right child).DON'T traverse the entire tree to find the minimum depth. BFS guarantees the first leaf found is the shallowest!

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)We visit every node in the tree exactly once. popleft() and append() are O(1).
SpaceO(N)The Queue can store at most N/2 nodes (the maximum number of leaf nodes at the bottom level of a perfectly balanced tree). O(N/2) simplifies to O(N).

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Using a standard List for the Queue: queue.pop(0) is strictly O(N) because every element behind it has to shift forward. This makes the whole algorithm O(N²). Always from collections import deque and use .popleft().
  2. Forgetting to check if Root is None: If the input tree is empty, queue = deque([None]) will crash your code inside the loop. Always start with if not root: return [].
  3. Dynamic length in the for loop: Do not write for i in range(len(queue)):. As you append children, the length grows, and the loop runs forever! Always save it to a variable first: level_size = len(queue).

✅ Problems in This Pattern

#ProblemDifficultyKey Twist
1Binary Tree Level OrderEasyThe foundational BFS Level loop.
2Reverse Level OrderEasyInsert the level lists at the beginning of the result list.
3Zigzag TraversalMediumUse a boolean flag left_to_right to reverse the current level list before appending to result.
4Level AveragesEasyAccumulate sum for the level, divide by level_size.
5Minimum DepthEasyReturn depth immediately upon finding the first leaf node.
6Level Order SuccessorEasyDon't need level_size! Just standard BFS, return the next node popped after the target.
7Connect SiblingsMediumAdvanced: Link current_node.next = queue[0] during the level traversal.
Easy Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You have a family tree. You want to take a picture of every generation separately.

  • First, a picture of the Great-Grandparents.
  • Then, a picture of the Grandparents.
  • Then, a picture of the Parents.

We can do this easily using a Queue (like a line for a rollercoaster).

First, the Great-Grandparents get in line.

You look at the line and say, "Okay, there is 1 person in line right now. Let's take a picture of just them."

While they are getting their picture taken, they tell all their kids (the Grandparents) to get in the back of the line!

Once the first picture is done, you look at the line again. Now there are 2 people in line (the Grandparents). You say, "Okay, I will take a picture of the next 2 people!"

They get their picture taken, and tell THEIR kids to get in line.

By strictly counting how many people are in line before you start taking pictures for that round, you perfectly separate every generation!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the foundational Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. We use a Queue data structure (FIFO - First In, First Out) to process nodes level by level.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return an empty list []. Otherwise, initialize a queue using collections.deque and add the root to it. Initialize an empty result list.
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. Snapshot the Level: Get the number of nodes currently in the queue: level_size = len(queue). This is the most crucial step! It tells us exactly how many nodes belong to the current level.
  4. Initialize current_level = [] to hold the values for this level.
  5. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  6. Pop the front node: node = queue.popleft().
  7. Add its value to current_level.
  8. If node.left exists, add it to the back of the queue.
  9. If node.right exists, add it to the back of the queue.
  10. After the inner loop finishes, append the populated current_level list to result.
  11. Return result.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
12
     /  \
    7    1
   / \  / \
  9  2 10  5

Initialization: queue = [12], result = [].

Level 1

  • level_size = 1.
  • current_level = []
  • Node 12: Pop. Add 12. Add children 7 and 1 to queue.
  • current_level is [12]. Append to result.
  • Queue is now [7, 1].

Level 2

  • level_size = 2.
  • current_level = []
  • Node 7: Pop. Add 7. Add children 9 and 2. Queue: [1, 9, 2].
  • Node 1: Pop. Add 1. Add children 10 and 5. Queue: [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • current_level is [7, 1]. Append to result.

Level 3

  • level_size = 4.
  • current_level = []
  • Node 9: Pop. Add 9. No children.
  • Node 2: Pop. Add 2. No children.
  • Node 10: Pop. Add 10. No children.
  • Node 5: Pop. Add 5. No children.
  • current_level is [9, 2, 10, 5]. Append to result.
  • Queue is empty!

Final result: [[12], [7, 1], [9, 2, 10, 5]].

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We traverse each node in the tree exactly once. The operations inside the loop (queue push/pop) take $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. We need to store nodes in the queue. In the worst case (a perfectly balanced tree), the bottom level contains roughly $N/2$ nodes, meaning the queue will hold $O(N)$ elements at once. We also need $O(N)$ space to store the final result array.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: return [] catches a None input immediately and safely returns an empty list.
  • Single Node Tree: Works perfectly. Queue has size 1, processes the root, finds no children, and returns [[root.value]].
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def level_order(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Returns the level order traversal of a binary tree's nodes' values.
    """
    if not root:
        return []

    result: List[List[int]] = []
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        # Take a snapshot of how many nodes are on the current level
        level_size = len(queue)
        current_level: List[int] = []

        # Process exactly that many nodes
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            current_level.append(node.value)

            # Enqueue the children for the NEXT level
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        # Store the current level's results
        result.append(current_level)

    return result

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    / \  / \
    #   9  2 10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    expected1 = [[12], [7, 1], [9, 2, 10, 5]]
    assert level_order(root1) == expected1, f"Test 1 failed: {level_order(root1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert level_order(None) == [], "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert level_order(TreeNode(42)) == [[42]], "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is added to the queue once and removed once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The queue can hold up to N/2 nodes at the bottom level of the tree.
Easy Reverse Level Order Traversal
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Reverse Level Order Traversal

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Remember taking pictures of every generation in the family tree?

What if the photo album company wants the pictures in the book backwards?

They want the youngest kids on Page 1, the parents on Page 2, the grandparents on Page 3, and the Great-Grandparent on the very last page!

We STILL take the pictures in the exact same order (top to bottom).

But when we put a picture into the photo album, instead of putting it at the END of the album, we shove it into the very FRONT of the album!

By always putting the newest picture at the front, the very first picture we took (the top of the tree) ends up at the very back of the album.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is almost identical to the standard Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. The only modification is how we store the results. Instead of appending levels to the end of an array, we prepend them to the beginning. To do this efficiently, we use a deque (Double-Ended Queue) for our results array as well as for our BFS queue.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize a queue using collections.deque with the root.
  2. Result Deque: Initialize result = deque(). We use a deque for the result because inserting at the front of a standard Python list takes $O(N)$ time, but inserting at the front of a deque (appendleft) takes $O(1)$ time.
  3. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  4. level_size = len(queue)
  5. current_level = []
  6. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  7. Pop node from queue.
  8. Add node.value to current_level.
  9. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  10. Prepend: INSTEAD of result.append, do result.appendleft(current_level). This pushes the current level to the front of the result list.
  11. Finalize: Return list(result).

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

    7    1
   / \  / \
  9  2 10  5

  • Nodes processed: 12.
  • current_level = [12].
  • result.appendleft([12]).
  • result is now [[12]].
  • Queue is now [7, 1].

Level 2 (Middle Level)

  • Nodes processed: 7, 1.
  • current_level = [7, 1].
  • result.appendleft([7, 1]).
  • result is now [[7, 1], [12]].
  • Queue is now [9, 2, 10, 5].

Level 3 (Bottom Level)

  • Nodes processed: 9, 2, 10, 5.
  • current_level = [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • result.appendleft([9, 2, 10, 5]).
  • result is now [[9, 2, 10, 5], [7, 1], [12]].
  • Queue is empty!

Convert result to list and return.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Every node is visited exactly once. The appendleft() operation on a deque is $O(1)$, so inserting levels at the front is extremely fast. Converting the deque to a list at the very end takes $O(N)$ time, keeping the overall time complexity linear.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes. The result deque also holds $O(N)$ elements.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: return [] catches it instantly.
  • Unbalanced Tree / Single Sided: Because BFS strictly processes nodes by depth, an unbalanced tree is handled perfectly. The levels are collected left-to-right exactly as they appear at that depth, regardless of how skewed the tree is.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def reverse_level_order(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Returns the reverse level order traversal of a binary tree's nodes' values.
    (i.e., from bottom to top, level by level).
    """
    if not root:
        return []

    result = deque()
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        current_level: List[int] = []

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            current_level.append(node.value)

            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        # Push the current level to the FRONT of the result list
        result.appendleft(current_level)

    return list(result)

    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Bottom level first!
    expected1 = [[9, 2, 10, 5], [7, 1], [12]]
    assert reverse_level_order(root1) == expected1, f"Test 1 failed: {reverse_level_order(root1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert reverse_level_order(None) == [], "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert reverse_level_order(TreeNode(42)) == [[42]], "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")

Medium Zigzag Traversal
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Zigzag Traversal

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are taking pictures of the family tree again, but this time you want to be fancy.

  • For the Grandparents (Level 1), you take the picture from Left to Right.
  • For the Parents (Level 2), you take the picture from Right to Left!
  • For the Kids (Level 3), you go back to Left to Right.

It's a Zigzag!

To do this, we DO NOT change how people wait in line. They still wait in the exact same Queue (from left to right).

The ONLY thing that changes is how we put them into the photo album.

If it's a "Left to Right" round, we just append them normally to the end of the page.

If it's a "Right to Left" round, we push them into the FRONT of the page (using appendleft()), so the first person we took a picture of ends up at the very back!

After every round, we just flip a switch to change directions for the next round.

🎯 Core Strategy

This builds perfectly upon the standard Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. We maintain the exact same queue logic for traversing the tree. We just change how we format the output for each level based on a toggle flag.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize queue = deque([root]), result = [].
  2. The Toggle: Initialize a boolean left_to_right = True. This acts as our directional switch.
  3. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  4. level_size = len(queue)
  5. current_level = deque() <-- Notice we use a deque for the current level! This is critical for $O(1)$ front insertions.
  6. Node Loop: Loop level_size times:
  7. Pop node from queue.
  8. The Magic:
  9. IF left_to_right: current_level.append(node.value) (normal order)
  10. ELSE: current_level.appendleft(node.value) (reverse order)
  11. Append children to the queue (always Left then Right, regardless of the zigzag direction).
  12. Append list(current_level) to result.
  13. Flip the Switch: left_to_right = not left_to_right.
  14. Return result.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
12
     /  \
    7    1
   / \  / \
  9  2 10  5

Initialization: queue = [12], result = [], left_to_right = True.

Level 1 (Top Level)

  • left_to_right = True
  • Pop 12. current_level.append(12). Queue: [7, 1].
  • current_level: [12]. Append to result.
  • Flip switch: left_to_right = False.

Level 2 (Middle Level)

  • left_to_right = False
  • Pop 7. current_level.appendleft(7). current_level is [7]. Queue: [1, 9, 2].
  • Pop 1. current_level.appendleft(1). current_level is [1, 7]. Queue: [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • current_level: [1, 7]. Append to result.
  • Flip switch: left_to_right = True.

Level 3 (Bottom Level)

  • left_to_right = True
  • Pop 9. append(9). current_level is [9].
  • Pop 2. append(2). current_level is [9, 2].
  • Pop 10. append(10). current_level is [9, 2, 10].
  • Pop 5. append(5). current_level is [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • current_level: [9, 2, 10, 5]. Append to result.
  • Flip switch: left_to_right = False.

Queue empty! Return result: [[12], [1, 7], [9, 2, 10, 5]].

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. Every node is visited exactly once. Checking the boolean flag and pushing to either end of a deque takes $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The primary queue holds at most $N/2$ nodes. The current_level deque holds at most $N/2$ values. The result list stores all $N$ values.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely handled by the initial if not root: check. Returns [].
  • Tree with missing children: As with all BFS patterns, it only adds children if they exist if node.left: queue.append(node.left). It doesn't break if a node only has one child.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def zigzag_traversal(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Returns the zigzag level order traversal of a binary tree's nodes' values.
    """
    if not root:
        return []

    result: List[List[int]] = []
    queue = deque([root])
    left_to_right = True

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        current_level = deque()

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            
            # The magic happens here!
            if left_to_right:
                current_level.append(node.value)
            else:
                current_level.appendleft(node.value)

            # Children are always added to the queue left-to-right
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        result.append(list(current_level))
        # Flip the direction for the next level
        left_to_right = not left_to_right

    return result

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    / \  / \
    #   9  2 10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Expected: 
    # L0: L->R [12]
    # L1: R->L [1, 7]
    # L2: L->R [9, 2, 10, 5]
    expected1 = [[12], [1, 7], [9, 2, 10, 5]]
    assert zigzag_traversal(root1) == expected1, f"Test 1 failed: {zigzag_traversal(root1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert zigzag_traversal(None) == [], "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert zigzag_traversal(TreeNode(42)) == [[42]], "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited once. `append` and `appendleft` on deque are O(1). 💾 Space: O(N) — The queue can hold up to N/2 nodes at the bottom level of the tree.
Easy Level Averages in a Binary Tree
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Level Averages in a Binary Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are still looking at your family tree, but instead of taking pictures, you want to find the AVERAGE age of each generation.

  • What's the average age of the Great-Grandparents?
  • What's the average age of the Grandparents?
  • What's the average age of the Parents?

Just like before, we use our Queue to line everyone up generation by generation.

When a generation is ready, instead of putting their names in a list, we just add up all their ages!

If the parents are 40 and 44, their total age is 84. Since there are 2 of them, the average is $84 / 2 = 42$.

We already know how many people are in the generation because we count them before we start (level_size = len(queue)). Easy!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a straightforward aggregation task built on the standard Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. Instead of storing an array of node values for each level, we maintain a running sum.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize queue = deque([root]), result = [].
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. level_size = len(queue) (This acts as our denominator for the average!).
  4. Initialize level_sum = 0.0.
  5. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  6. Pop node from queue.
  7. Add node.value to level_sum.
  8. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  9. Calculate Average: Append level_sum / level_size to result.
  10. Return result.

  • level_size = 1. level_sum = 0.0.
  • Pop 12. level_sum += 12. queue = [7, 1].
  • Calculate: $12.0 / 1 = 12.0$.
  • result = [12.0].

Level 2

  • level_size = 2. level_sum = 0.0.
  • Pop 7. level_sum += 7. queue = [1, 9, 2].
  • Pop 1. level_sum += 1. queue = [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • level_sum is now 8.0.
  • Calculate: $8.0 / 2 = 4.0$.
  • result = [12.0, 4.0].

Level 3

  • level_size = 4. level_sum = 0.0.
  • Pop 9, 2, 10, 5. Add them all to level_sum.
  • level_sum = $9 + 2 + 10 + 5 = 26.0$.
  • Calculate: $26.0 / 4 = 6.5$.
  • result = [12.0, 4.0, 6.5].

Queue is empty! Return result.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We traverse each node exactly once. Summing floats and division take $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The queue stores at most $N/2$ nodes.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely handled by if not root: return [].
  • Tree with negative values: E.g., a node with value -5. The float addition works identically.
  • Single Node: Properly handles a single-node tree, finding level_size = 1, and returning the value itself.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_level_averages(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[float]:
    """
    Returns the average value of nodes on each level of a binary tree.
    """
    if not root:
        return []

    result: List[float] = []
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        level_sum = 0.0

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level_sum += node.value

            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        # Calculate and store the average for this level
        result.append(level_sum / level_size)

    return result

    #   9  2 10  5

    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Expected: 
    # L0: 12.0
    # L1: (7+1)/2 = 4.0
    # L2: (9+2+10+5)/4 = 26/4 = 6.5
    expected1 = [12.0, 4.0, 6.5]
    assert find_level_averages(root1) == expected1, f"Test 1 failed: {find_level_averages(root1)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert find_level_averages(None) == [], "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert find_level_averages(TreeNode(42)) == [42.0], "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")

Easy Minimum Depth of a Binary Tree
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Minimum Depth of a Binary Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are climbing down a tree, starting from the very top (the root).

You want to find the fastest way to hit the ground (a leaf).

A leaf is a node that has NO children (no left, no right).

If you use Depth First Search (DFS), you might climb all the way down the deepest, longest branch first, taking forever just to realize there was a leaf right next to the root!

But if you use Breadth First Search (BFS), you check the entire Level 1 first.

Then you check the entire Level 2.

The very FIRST time you see a leaf node, you yell "I FOUND IT!" and stop immediately!

Because you are checking level by level, the first leaf you find is mathematically guaranteed to be the closest one to the root.

🎯 Core Strategy

This highlights the superpower of Tree Breadth First Search (BFS): finding the shortest path in an unweighted graph/tree. By traversing level by level, the first time we encounter our target condition (a leaf node), we can immediately return the current depth, short-circuiting the rest of the search.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return 0. Initialize queue = deque([root]). Initialize depth = 1.
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. level_size = len(queue)
  4. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  5. Pop node from queue.
  6. Leaf Check: Is it a leaf? if not node.left and not node.right:
  7. YES! The search is over. Return depth immediately.
  8. If not a leaf, append its children to the queue.
  9. Next Generation: After finishing the entire level, we haven't found a leaf, so we prepare to go deeper. depth += 1.
  10. If the queue somehow empties (which won't happen for a valid tree before hitting a leaf), return depth.

  • Pop 12.
  • Is 12 a leaf? No (it has children 7 and 1).
  • Push 7 and 1. Queue: [7, 1].
  • Loop finishes. depth becomes 2.

Level 2 (depth = 2)

  • level_size = 2.
  • Pop 7.
  • Is 7 a leaf? YES! (No left, no right).
  • RETURN depth (2) immediately!

We never even look at node 1, 10, or 5. The algorithm optimally terminates early.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$ in the absolute worst case (e.g., a completely balanced tree where we have to check all the way to the bottom, or a linked list). However, in the best case (a skewed tree with a leaf near the root), it runs in $O(1)$ time! This is vastly superior to DFS for this specific problem.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: return 0 handles this immediately.
  • Single Node: queue = [42], depth = 1. Pops 42. It has no children, so it's a leaf. Returns 1. Correct!
  • Tree with a single deep branch: E.g., 12 -> 7 -> 9 (no right children).
  • Depth 1: 12. Pushes 7.
  • Depth 2: 7. Pushes 9.
  • Depth 3: 9. Leaf! Returns 3. Correct.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def min_depth(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the minimum depth of a binary tree.
    """
    if not root:
        return 0

    queue = deque([root])
    depth = 1

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()

            # The very first time we see a leaf node, we return the depth!
            # Because BFS goes level by level, this is guaranteed to be the minimum.
            if not node.left and not node.right:
                return depth

            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        # Move to the next generation
        depth += 1

    return depth

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #         / \
    #        10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # 7 is a leaf at depth 2!
    assert min_depth(root1) == 2, f"Test 1 failed: {min_depth(root1)}"

    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    /      \
    #   9        5
    root2 = TreeNode(12)
    root2.left = TreeNode(7)
    root2.right = TreeNode(1)
    root2.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root2.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    assert min_depth(root2) == 3, f"Test 2 failed: {min_depth(root2)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert min_depth(None) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert min_depth(TreeNode(42)) == 1, "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — In the worst case, we check all nodes. But in the best case, we stop very early! 💾 Space: O(N) — The queue can hold up to N/2 nodes.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Level Order Successor

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are calling out the names of everyone in the family tree, level by level, left to right.

Someone asks you: "Hey, right after you call out 'Bob', who is the very next person you call?"

That next person is Bob's "Level Order Successor".

Because we are already using a Queue that perfectly lines everyone up in the exact order we call their names, this is incredibly easy!

We just pop people out of the line one by one.

The moment we pop "Bob", we stop!

Who is the next person we were going to call? It's simply the person standing at the very front of the line right now!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a clever variation of the Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. It demonstrates that the BFS queue inherently stores nodes in the exact Level Order sequence. We don't even need the inner for _ in range(level_size) loop because we don't care about isolating specific levels; we only care about the absolute, flattened sequence.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return None. Initialize queue = deque([root]).
  2. Continuous Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. Pop node from queue.
  4. Crucial Order: Append its children (Left then Right) to the queue BEFORE checking if we found the target. Why? Because if the target is the last node on Level 2, its successor is the first node on Level 3. We need Level 3 to be in the queue when we stop!
  5. Check Target: if node.value == target_value:
  6. YELL STOP! We found our target. Break out of the loop immediately.
  7. Get Successor: After breaking out of the loop, the successor is exactly queue[0] (the next person in line).
  8. If the queue is empty (meaning the target was the very last node in the tree, or wasn't found at all), return None.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation

     /  \
    7    1
   / \  / \
  9  2 10  5

Target: 1 (The last node of Level 2).

Initialization: queue = [12].

Iteration 1

  • Pop 12.
  • Push children 7, 1. Queue: [7, 1].
  • Is 12 == 1? No.

Iteration 2

  • Pop 7.
  • Push children 9, 2. Queue: [1, 9, 2].
  • Is 7 == 1? No.

Iteration 3

  • Pop 1.
  • Push children 10, 5. Queue: [9, 2, 10, 5]. (Notice how Level 3 is now in the queue!).
  • Is 1 == 1? YES! Break out of the loop.

Final Result

  • Queue is currently [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • Return queue[0], which is Node 9.
  • Node 9 is exactly the node that follows Node 1 in a level-order sequence!

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit nodes until we find the target. In the worst case (target is at the very end of the tree), we visit all $N$ nodes.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Target is the last node in the tree: e.g., Target is 5. We pop 5, push no children (queue becomes empty). We break. Returning queue[0] would crash, so we use return queue[0] if queue else None. Returns None. Correct!
  • Target is not in the tree: The loop exhausts the queue. queue is empty. Returns None. Correct!
  • Empty Tree: Handled by initial if not root: check. Returns None.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_successor(root: Optional[TreeNode], target_value: int) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    """
    Finds the level order successor of the given node in a binary tree.
    """
    if not root:
        return None

    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        # Notice we don't need `level_size` here! 
        # We don't care about generations, just the absolute ordering in the queue.
        node = queue.popleft()

        # Insert children BEFORE we check the target.
        # Why? Because if the target is the last node on Level 2, its successor
        # is the first node on Level 3. We need Level 3 to be in the queue!
        if node.left:
            queue.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            queue.append(node.right)

        if node.value == target_value:
            break

    # If the queue is not empty, the next person in line is the successor
    return queue[0] if queue else None

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    / \  / \
    #   9  2 10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Level order: 12, 7, 1, 9, 2, 10, 5
    
    res1 = find_successor(root1, 12)
    assert res1 and res1.value == 7, "Test 1 failed: Successor of 12 should be 7"

    res2 = find_successor(root1, 9)
    assert res2 and res2.value == 2, "Test 2 failed: Successor of 9 should be 2"

    # The tricky cross-level jump!
    res3 = find_successor(root1, 1)
    assert res3 and res3.value == 9, "Test 3 failed: Successor of 1 should be 9"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # Last node in tree
    res4 = find_successor(root1, 5)
    assert res4 is None, "Edge 1 failed: Successor of last node should be None"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — We visit nodes until we find the target. 💾 Space: O(N) — The queue holds up to N/2 nodes.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Connect Level Order Siblings

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine all the kids in a generation are holding hands from left to right.

The leftmost kid holds the hand of the kid next to them, and so on.

The rightmost kid doesn't have anyone to hold onto, so their hand just hangs empty (points to None).

We already know how to perfectly line up each generation using a Queue!

All we have to do is remember who the "Previous" kid was.

When we pull a kid out of the line, we tell the "Previous" kid to grab this new kid's hand (previous_node.next = current_node).

Then, the new kid becomes the "Previous" kid for the next time we pull someone out!

At the start of every new generation, we reset the "Previous" kid to None, so generations don't accidentally hold hands with each other.

🎯 Core Strategy

This problem requires us to link nodes using a .next pointer. Since the links only happen within the same level, Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) is the perfect tool. We maintain state within the inner level loop to connect adjacent nodes.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return None. Initialize queue = deque([root]).
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. level_size = len(queue).
  4. Reset State: Initialize previous_node = None. This ensures that the last node of Level 1 doesn't accidentally connect to the first node of Level 2.
  5. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  6. Pop current_node from queue.
  7. Make the Connection: If previous_node is not None (meaning this isn't the first node of the level):
  8. previous_node.next = current_node.
  9. Advance State: Update previous_node = current_node.
  10. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  11. Return the modified root.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

    7    1
   / \  / \
  9  2 10  5

Initialization: queue = [12].

Level 1 (Top Level)

  • level_size = 1.
  • previous_node = None.
  • Pop 12.
  • previous_node is None. Skip connection.
  • previous_node becomes 12.
  • Push 7, 1. Queue: [7, 1].
  • End of level. Node 12's next pointer naturally defaults to None.

Level 2 (Middle Level)

  • level_size = 2.
  • previous_node is RESET to None!
  • Iteration 1:
  • Pop 7.
  • previous_node is None. Skip connection.
  • previous_node becomes 7.
  • Push 9, 2. Queue: [1, 9, 2].
  • Iteration 2:
  • Pop 1.
  • previous_node is 7. CONNECT: 7.next = 1.
  • previous_node becomes 1.
  • Push 10, 5. Queue: [9, 2, 10, 5].
  • End of level. Node 1's next pointer remains None.

Level 3 (Bottom Level)

  • level_size = 4.
  • previous_node is RESET to None!
  • Pop 9. prev becomes 9.
  • Pop 2. CONNECT: 9.next = 2. prev becomes 2.
  • Pop 10. CONNECT: 2.next = 10. prev becomes 10.
  • Pop 5. CONNECT: 10.next = 5. prev becomes 5.
  • End of level. Node 5's next pointer remains None.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. Setting pointers takes $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes at the bottom level. (Note: The problem description on LeetCode sometimes asks for an $O(1)$ space solution using already established next pointers, but this standard BFS approach is $O(N)$ space and perfectly acceptable as the primary solution).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Handled by initial if not root: check.
  • Tree missing children: The BFS handles null children gracefully. If the tree is just 12 -> 7 -> 9 (a straight line leftwards), level_size is always 1, previous_node is always None when the single node is popped, so no connections are falsely made! All nodes correctly point to None.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None, next=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
        self.next = next

def connect_siblings(root: Optional[Node]) -> Optional[Node]:
    """
    Connects each node in a binary tree with its level order sibling.
    """
    if not root:
        return None

    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        
        # Reset previous_node at the start of every new level
        previous_node = None

        for _ in range(level_size):
            current_node = queue.popleft()

            # If there was a previous node on this level, link it to the current one
            if previous_node:
                previous_node.next = current_node
            
            # The current node becomes the previous node for the next iteration
            previous_node = current_node

            if current_node.left:
                queue.append(current_node.left)
            if current_node.right:
                queue.append(current_node.right)

    return root

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    def get_next_values(root):
        """Helper to collect 'next' pointer values for easy testing."""
        res = []
        curr = root
        while curr:
            level_head = curr
            level_res = []
            while level_head:
                level_res.append(level_head.value)
                level_head = level_head.next
            res.append(level_res)
            curr = curr.left
        return res

    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    / \  / \
    #   9  2 10  5
    root1 = Node(12)
    root1.left = Node(7)
    root1.right = Node(1)
    root1.left.left = Node(9)
    root1.left.right = Node(2)
    root1.right.left = Node(10)
    root1.right.right = Node(5)
    
    connected_root = connect_siblings(root1)
    
    # Let's verify the connections!
    assert connected_root.next is None, "12 -> None"
    assert connected_root.left.next == connected_root.right, "7 -> 1"
    assert connected_root.right.next is None, "1 -> None"
    assert connected_root.left.left.next == connected_root.left.right, "9 -> 2"
    assert connected_root.left.right.next == connected_root.right.left, "2 -> 10"
    assert connected_root.right.left.next == connected_root.right.right, "10 -> 5"
    assert connected_root.right.right.next is None, "5 -> None"

    # Using our helper
    expected1 = [[12], [7, 1], [9, 2, 10, 5]]
    assert get_next_values(connected_root) == expected1, "Helper traversal failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert connect_siblings(None) is None, "Edge 1: Empty tree"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited once. 💾 Space: O(N) — The queue can hold up to N/2 nodes at the bottom level of the tree.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Connect All Level Order Siblings

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine kids standing in lines for a school photo. In the last problem, we connected kids standing in the SAME row.

Now, the LAST kid in every row should also point to the FIRST kid of the NEXT row.

So everyone forms ONE long chain from top to bottom, left to right — like a single giant conga line winding through the tree!

To do this, we don't even care about which row someone is in. We just put everyone in our standard Queue.

As people pop out of the Queue one by one, we just tell the previous person who popped out to hold their hand. It's that simple!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a simplification of the standard Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. Since we want to connect all nodes in the exact order they are processed by BFS, we don't need to maintain state inside a level loop (level_size). We can just maintain a single global previous_node pointer across the entire while loop!

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return None. Initialize queue = deque([root]). Initialize prev = None.
  2. Continuous Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. Pop node from queue.
  4. Make the Connection: If prev is not None, connect it: prev.next = node.
  5. Advance State: Update prev = node. (Notice this does NOT reset at the end of a level!).
  6. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  7. Return the modified root.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. Connecting nodes takes $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue holds up to $N/2$ nodes at the bottom level.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: return None handles this safely.
  • Skewed Tree: (e.g., all left children). The queue will just contain one node at a time, and prev will correctly link them all into a straight line.
  • Tree with missing children: Handled gracefully. If node.left doesn't exist, it isn't pushed to the queue, meaning it won't interrupt the continuous sequence of valid nodes being processed.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right
        self.next = next


def connect_all_siblings(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
    if not root:
        return None

    queue = deque([root])
    prev = None

    while queue:
        node = queue.popleft()

        # Link previous node to current — regardless of level boundaries
        if prev:
            prev.next = node
        prev = node

        if node.left:
            queue.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            queue.append(node.right)

    return root


if __name__ == "__main__":
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    #    / \   \
    #   4   5   6
    root = TreeNode(1)
    root.left = TreeNode(2)
    root.right = TreeNode(3)
    root.left.left = TreeNode(4)
    root.left.right = TreeNode(5)
    root.right.right = TreeNode(6)

    connect_all_siblings(root)

    # Walk the chain: 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 -> None
    chain = []
    node = root
    while node:
        chain.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    assert chain == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], f"Test 1 failed: {chain}"

    # Edge: single node
    single = TreeNode(42)
    connect_all_siblings(single)
    assert single.next is None, "Test 2: single node"

    # Edge: empty tree
    assert connect_all_siblings(None) is None, "Test 3: empty"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — visit every node once. 💾 Space: O(N) — queue can hold up to N/2 nodes (last level).

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Right View of a Binary Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you're standing on the RIGHT side of a Christmas tree, looking at it from the side. You can only see the RIGHTMOST ornament on each row.

If a row has ornaments [4, 5, 6], you only see 6 because it's blocking 4 and 5 from your view.

Your goal is to return all the ornaments you can see from top to bottom.

Since we are already taking our pictures level by level (from left to right) using our Queue, the very LAST person we take a picture of on any given level is exactly the person standing on the far right!

We just need to save the very last person from every level.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a standard application of Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) where we only care about the last element processed in the inner level_size loop.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize queue = deque([root]). Initialize result = [].
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. level_size = len(queue)
  4. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times (for i in range(level_size)):
  5. Pop node from queue.
  6. Check for Last Node: If i == level_size - 1 (this is the very last node in the current level!):
  7. Append node.val to result.
  8. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  9. Return result.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation

     / \
    2   3
     \   \
      5   4

Initialization: queue = [1], result = [].

Level 1 (Top Level)

  • level_size = 1.
  • i = 0. Pop 1.
  • Is 0 == 1 - 1? Yes! (It's the last node). Append 1 to result.
  • Push children 2, 3. Queue: [2, 3].
  • result is [1].

Level 2 (Middle Level)

  • level_size = 2.
  • i = 0. Pop 2. Push child 5 (right child). Queue: [3, 5]. (Not the last node).
  • i = 1. Pop 3. Push child 4 (right child). Queue: [5, 4].
  • Is 1 == 2 - 1? Yes! (It's the last node). Append 3 to result.
  • result is [1, 3].

Level 3 (Bottom Level)

  • level_size = 2.
  • i = 0. Pop 5. Push no children. Queue: [4]. (Not the last node).
  • i = 1. Pop 4. Push no children. Queue: [].
  • Is 1 == 2 - 1? Yes! (It's the last node). Append 4 to result.
  • result is [1, 3, 4].
