🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. Checking the index and appending to an array are $O(1)$ operations.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes at the bottom level. The result array holds $H$ nodes (where $H$ is the height of the tree).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely returns [].
  • Skewed Left Tree: (e.g., 1 -> 2 -> 3 all left children). The code handles this perfectly! In this case, level_size is always 1, so i is always 0, which equals level_size - 1. The algorithm correctly realizes that if a level only has one node (even a left child), it is the rightmost node visible on that level! Returns [1, 2, 3].
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def right_side_view(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
    if not root:
        return []

    result = []
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)

        for i in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()

            # The last node in this level is the rightmost
            if i == level_size - 1:
                result.append(node.val)

            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    #      \   \
    #       5   4
    root = TreeNode(1)
    root.left = TreeNode(2)
    root.right = TreeNode(3)
    root.left.right = TreeNode(5)
    root.right.right = TreeNode(4)
    assert right_side_view(root) == [1, 3, 4], "Test 1"

    # Skewed left
    left_tree = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(3)))
    assert right_side_view(left_tree) == [1, 2, 3], "Test 2: skewed left"

    # Empty
    assert right_side_view(None) == [], "Test 3: empty"

    # Single
    assert right_side_view(TreeNode(42)) == [42], "Test 4: single"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — visit every node. 💾 Space: O(N) — queue can hold up to N/2 nodes.

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Look at each row of a tree. For each row, tell me the biggest number.

We just use our trusty Queue to look at the tree one row (level) at a time.

When we start looking at a new row, we grab a tiny notepad and write down "The biggest number I've seen so far is extremely small (negative infinity)."

As we look at each number in the row, we compare it to our notepad. If the number is bigger, we erase the notepad and write the new biggest number.

At the end of the row, we add whatever is on the notepad to our final list!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a straightforward aggregation problem using the Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize queue = deque([root]). Initialize result = [].
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. Initialize level_max = float('-inf'). This is crucial because nodes can have negative values!
  4. level_size = len(queue)
  5. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  6. Pop node from queue.
  7. Update Max: level_max = max(level_max, node.val).
  8. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  9. Append level_max to result.
  10. Return result.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

    3   2
   / \   \

Initialization: queue = [1], result = [].

Row 1

  • level_max = -inf.
  • Pop 1. level_max becomes max(-inf, 1) = 1.
  • Push 3, 2. Queue: [3, 2].
  • End row. result becomes [1].

Row 2

  • level_max = -inf.
  • Pop 3. level_max becomes max(-inf, 3) = 3. Push 5, 3.
  • Pop 2. level_max becomes max(3, 2) = 3. Push 9.
  • Queue: [5, 3, 9].
  • End row. result becomes [1, 3].

Row 3

  • level_max = -inf.
  • Pop 5. level_max becomes 5.
  • Pop 3. level_max remains 5.
  • Pop 9. level_max becomes 9.
  • Queue: [].
  • End row. result becomes [1, 3, 9].

Return [1, 3, 9].

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. Finding the max is an $O(1)$ operation per node.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue can hold up to $N/2$ nodes at the bottom level.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely returns [].
  • Negative Values: If a row is [-5, -10, -3], level_max initialized to 0 would incorrectly return 0. Initializing it to float('-inf') ensures it correctly captures -3.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional, List


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def largest_values(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> List[int]:
    if not root:
        return []

    result = []
    queue = deque([root])

    while queue:
        level_max = float('-inf')
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level_max = max(level_max, node.val)
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)
        result.append(level_max)

    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(5), TreeNode(3)), TreeNode(2, None, TreeNode(9)))
    assert largest_values(root) == [1, 3, 9], "Test 1"
    assert largest_values(TreeNode(-1)) == [-1], "Test 2: negative"
    assert largest_values(None) == [], "Test 3: empty"
    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) 💾 Space: O(N)
Medium Maximum Width of Binary Tree
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Maximum Width of Binary Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine building a binary tree using LEGO blocks on a massive grid.

The root is at position 0.

Every time you add a left child, it goes to 2 * parent_position.

Every time you add a right child, it goes to 2 * parent_position + 1.

Even if you skip adding some blocks (because they are None), the grid positions for the remaining blocks stay the same!

The "width" of a row is just the distance from the leftmost block in that row to the rightmost block, including all the empty spaces between them.

So, width = Rightmost Position - Leftmost Position + 1.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an advanced application of the Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. Instead of just storing nodes in our queue, we store tuples: (node, position_index).

  1. The Formula: For any node at index i, its left child is at 2*i and its right child is at 2*i + 1. This is the standard array representation of a binary tree.
  2. Initialization: Initialize queue = deque([(root, 0)]) and max_width = 0.
  3. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  4. level_size = len(queue)
  5. Prevent Overflow: Get the first_pos = queue[0][1]. We subtract this first_pos from every node's index on this level to "normalize" the indices to start at 0. This stops the integers from exploding to massive numbers in very deep, skewed trees.
  6. Node Loop: Loop level_size times:
  7. Pop (node, pos) from queue.
  8. Normalize: pos -= first_pos.
  9. Push children with calculated indices:
  10. Left child: queue.append((node.left, 2 * pos))
  11. Right child: queue.append((node.right, 2 * pos + 1))
  12. Calculate Width: By the end of the node loop, pos holds the normalized index of the last node processed. So, the width of the level is pos + 1.
  13. Update max_width = max(max_width, pos + 1).
  14. Return max_width.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
     / \
    3   2
   /     \
  5       9

Initialization: queue = [(1, 0)], max_width = 0.

Row 1

  • first_pos = 0.
  • Pop (1, 0). Normalized pos = $0 - 0 = 0$.
  • Push Left (3, 2*0 = 0).
  • Push Right (2, 2*0+1 = 1).
  • Queue: [(3, 0), (2, 1)].
  • max_width = $max(0, 0 + 1) = 1$.

Row 2

  • first_pos = 0. (First node is 3 at pos 0).
  • Pop (3, 0). Normalized pos = $0 - 0 = 0$.
  • Push Left (5, 2*0 = 0).
  • Pop (2, 1). Normalized pos = $1 - 0 = 1$.
  • Push Right (9, 2*1+1 = 3).
  • Queue: [(5, 0), (9, 3)].
  • max_width = $max(1, 1 + 1) = 2$.

Row 3

  • first_pos = 0. (First node is 5 at pos 0).
  • Pop (5, 0). Normalized pos = $0 - 0 = 0$. (No children).
  • Pop (9, 3). Normalized pos = $3 - 0 = 3$. (No children).
  • Queue: [].
  • max_width = $max(2, 3 + 1) = 4$.

Return 4. (The width spans positions 0, 1, 2, 3, which is a width of 4).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue holds up to $N/2$ node-index pairs.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely returns 0.
  • Deep Skewed Tree: E.g., a tree with only right children going down 100 levels. Without our pos -= first_pos trick, the index at level 100 would be $2^{100} - 1$, which is a ridiculously large number and might cause memory/performance issues in languages other than Python (Python handles arbitrarily large integers, but it's slow). With normalization, the first node of the level is always reset to index 0, preventing this overflow! Width remains 1.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def width_of_binary_tree(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    if not root:
        return 0

    max_width = 0
    queue = deque([(root, 0)])

    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        first_pos = queue[0][1]  # Normalize to prevent overflow

        for _ in range(level_size):
            node, pos = queue.popleft()
            pos -= first_pos  # Normalize
            if node.left:
                queue.append((node.left, 2 * pos))
            if node.right:
                queue.append((node.right, 2 * pos + 1))

        max_width = max(max_width, pos + 1)  # pos is the last position (0-indexed)

    return max_width


if __name__ == "__main__":
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     3   2
    #    /     \
    #   5       9
    root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(3, TreeNode(5)), TreeNode(2, None, TreeNode(9)))
    assert width_of_binary_tree(root) == 4, "Test 1: level 3 has positions 0 and 3"

    #     1
    #    /
    #   2
    #  /
    # 3
    skewed = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(2, TreeNode(3)))
    assert width_of_binary_tree(skewed) == 1, "Test 2: skewed"

    assert width_of_binary_tree(None) == 0, "Test 3: empty"
    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) 💾 Space: O(N)
Medium Maximum Level Sum of a Binary Tree
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Maximum Level Sum of a Binary Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine walking down the rows of an apple orchard. Some trees give you apples (positive numbers), but some are cursed and steal apples from you (negative numbers)!

As you walk through each row, you add up all the apples you gained (or lost).

At the end, you want to know: Which row number gave me the most apples?

If two rows gave you the exact same maximum number of apples, you prefer the row that you visited first (the smallest row number).

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an aggregation problem using the Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern. We calculate the sum for each level and keep track of the maximum sum and the level at which it occurred.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return 0.
  2. queue = deque([root])
  3. max_sum = float('-inf') (Crucial because all sums could theoretically be negative).
  4. max_level = 1 (The row we will return at the end).
  5. level = 0 (Our current row counter).
  6. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  7. Increment level += 1.
  8. Initialize level_sum = 0.
  9. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times (len(queue)):
  10. Pop node from queue.
  11. Add node.val to level_sum.
  12. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  13. Update Max: If level_sum > max_sum: (Note the strictly greater > sign, which naturally breaks ties by preferring the earlier level!)
  14. max_sum = level_sum
  15. max_level = level
  16. Return max_level.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
     / \
    7   0
   / \
  7  -8

Initialization: queue = [1], max_sum = -inf, max_level = 1, level = 0.

Row 1

  • level = 1. level_sum = 0.
  • Pop 1. level_sum becomes 1.
  • Push 7, 0. Queue: [7, 0].
  • Is level_sum (1) > max_sum (-inf)? Yes!
  • max_sum = 1, max_level = 1.

Row 2

  • level = 2. level_sum = 0.
  • Pop 7. level_sum becomes 7. Push 7, -8.
  • Pop 0. level_sum stays 7. Push nothing.
  • Queue: [7, -8].
  • Is level_sum (7) > max_sum (1)? Yes!
  • max_sum = 7, max_level = 2.

Row 3

  • level = 3. level_sum = 0.
  • Pop 7. level_sum becomes 7.
  • Pop -8. level_sum becomes -1.
  • Queue: [].
  • Is level_sum (-1) > max_sum (7)? No.

Return max_level, which is 2. (Row 2 has the highest sum: 7).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue holds up to $N/2$ nodes.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • All Negative Values: If the tree is just -100, max_sum starts at -inf, gets updated to -100, and returns level 1. This works perfectly because of -inf.
  • Tie-Breaker: If Row 1 sums to 5, and Row 2 sums to 5. level_sum > max_sum becomes 5 > 5, which is False. So max_level remains 1. This perfectly fulfills the requirement "return the smallest level x".
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def max_level_sum(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    if not root:
        return 0

    queue = deque([root])
    max_sum = float('-inf')
    max_level = 1
    level = 0

    while queue:
        level += 1
        level_sum = 0
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            node = queue.popleft()
            level_sum += node.val
            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        if level_sum > max_sum:
            max_sum = level_sum
            max_level = level

    return max_level


if __name__ == "__main__":
    root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(7, TreeNode(7), TreeNode(-8)), TreeNode(0))
    assert max_level_sum(root) == 2, "Test 1: level 2 has sum 7"

    assert max_level_sum(TreeNode(-100)) == 1, "Test 2: single negative"
    assert max_level_sum(TreeNode(1, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(1))) == 2, "Test 3: level 2 wins"
    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) 💾 Space: O(N)
Medium Even Odd Tree
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Even Odd Tree

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine a tree where the rows have strict rules about who can stand in them based on the row number:

  • Even Rows (0, 2, 4...): Only allow ODD numbers. And as you read the row from left to right, the numbers must be getting strictly bigger.
  • Odd Rows (1, 3, 5...): Only allow EVEN numbers. And as you read the row from left to right, the numbers must be getting strictly smaller.

Our job is to walk through the tree, row by row. If we see a single number that breaks the rules (wrong odd/even type, or going the wrong direction), we immediately blow the whistle and say False. If we check every row and everyone followed the rules, we say True!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a validation problem that relies on Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) to examine the tree level by level. At each level, we validate the two conditions: parity (odd/even) and monotonicity (strictly increasing/decreasing).

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return True (an empty tree doesn't violate rules).
  2. queue = deque([root])
  3. level = 0 (Zero-indexed levels).
  4. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  5. Initialize prev = None (used to check if values are strictly increasing/decreasing).
  6. Node Loop: Loop exactly len(queue) times:
  7. Pop node from queue.
  8. Validation:
  9. If level is even: Check that node.val is odd. Check that node.val > prev.
  10. If level is odd: Check that node.val is even. Check that node.val < prev.
  11. If any check fails, return False.
  12. Update prev = node.val.
  13. Append children to the queue (Left then Right).
  14. Increment level += 1.
  15. If the loop completes without returning False, return True.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
        /   \
      10     4
     /  \     \
    3    7     9

Initialization: queue = [1], level = 0.

Row 0 (Even Row)

  • level = 0. prev = None.
  • Pop 1.
  • Rule 1 (Odd Value): 1 % 2 != 0. Pass.
  • Rule 2 (Increasing): prev is None, so skip comparison.
  • prev = 1. Push 10, 4. Queue: [10, 4].
  • End of Row 0. level becomes 1.

Row 1 (Odd Row)

  • level = 1. prev = None.
  • Iteration 1: Pop 10.
  • Rule 1 (Even Value): 10 % 2 == 0. Pass.
  • Rule 2 (Decreasing): prev is None. Pass.
  • prev = 10. Push 3, 7. Queue: [4, 3, 7].
  • Iteration 2: Pop 4.
  • Rule 1 (Even Value): 4 % 2 == 0. Pass.
  • Rule 2 (Decreasing): Is 4 < prev (10)? Yes! Pass.
  • prev = 4. Push 9. Queue: [3, 7, 9].
  • End of Row 1. level becomes 2.

Row 2 (Even Row)

  • level = 2. prev = None.
  • Pop 3. Value is odd. prev becomes 3.
  • Pop 7. Value is odd. 7 > 3. Pass! prev becomes 7.
  • Pop 9. Value is odd. 9 > 7. Pass! prev becomes 9.
  • Queue is empty.

Return True!

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node at most once. The algorithm terminates early if it finds a violation.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue holds up to $N/2$ nodes.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Equal adjacent values: [3, 3] in an even row correctly returns False because the condition is strictly greater (node.val > prev).
  • Single Node: root = [2]. Level is 0 (even), but value is 2 (even). Instantly returns False.
  • Deep trees with early failure: By using BFS instead of DFS, if a rule is broken near the top of the tree, we return False immediately without needing to visit the thousands of nodes beneath it.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import Optional


class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.val = val
        self.left = left
        self.right = right


def is_even_odd_tree(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
    if not root:
        return True

    queue = deque([root])
    level = 0

    while queue:
        prev = None
        for _ in range(len(queue)):
            node = queue.popleft()

            # Check parity
            if level % 2 == 0:  # Even level → values must be odd
                if node.val % 2 == 0:
                    return False
                if prev is not None and node.val <= prev:
                    return False
            else:  # Odd level → values must be even
                if node.val % 2 == 1:
                    return False
                if prev is not None and node.val >= prev:
                    return False

            prev = node.val

            if node.left:
                queue.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                queue.append(node.right)

        level += 1

    return True


if __name__ == "__main__":
    #         1
    #       /   \
    #      10    4
    #     / \     \
    #    3   7    11
    root = TreeNode(1, TreeNode(10, TreeNode(3), TreeNode(7)), TreeNode(4, None, TreeNode(11)))
    assert is_even_odd_tree(root) == True, "Test 1"

    #         5
    #       /   \
    #      4     2
    #     / \
    #    3   3
    root2 = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(4, TreeNode(3), TreeNode(3)), TreeNode(2))
    assert is_even_odd_tree(root2) == False, "Test 2: 3,3 not strictly increasing"

    assert is_even_odd_tree(TreeNode(1)) == True, "Test 3: single odd"
    assert is_even_odd_tree(TreeNode(2)) == False, "Test 4: even at level 0"
    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) 💾 Space: O(N)

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: N-ary Tree Level Order Traversal

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine a family tree, but instead of everyone having exactly two children (left and right), people can have any number of children! Some might have 0, some might have 3, some might have 10.

We want to take a picture of this massive family, generation by generation.

We use the exact same strategy as before: line everyone up in a Queue.

The only difference is that when a parent gets out of the line, instead of just calling their left and right kids to join the back of the line, they call all of their children in order!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the fundamental Tree Breadth First Search (BFS) pattern, but generalized for N-ary trees.

Instead of explicitly checking if node.left: and if node.right:, we just iterate over the node.children array.

  1. Initialization: If the root is None, return []. Initialize queue = deque([root]). Initialize result = [].
  2. Level Loop: Loop while queue is not empty:
  3. level_size = len(queue)
  4. current_level = []
  5. Node Loop: Loop exactly level_size times:
  6. Pop node from queue.
  7. Add node.val to current_level.
  8. Push Children: Loop over node.children:
  9. Append each child to the queue.
  10. Append current_level to result.
  11. Return result.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
      / | \
     3  2  4
    / \
   5   6

Initialization: queue = [1], result = [].

Row 1 (Generation 1)

  • level_size = 1.
  • Pop 1. Add to current_level.
  • Loop over 1's children: [3, 2, 4].
  • Push 3, 2, 4 to queue.
  • queue is now [3, 2, 4].
  • End of loop. result becomes [[1]].

Row 2 (Generation 2)

  • level_size = 3.
  • Pop 3: Add to current_level.
  • Loop over 3's children: [5, 6].
  • Push 5, 6. Queue: [2, 4, 5, 6].
  • Pop 2: Add to current_level.
  • Loop over 2's children: []. (None).
  • Pop 4: Add to current_level.
  • Loop over 4's children: []. (None).
  • End of loop. current_level is [3, 2, 4].
  • result becomes [[1], [3, 2, 4]].

Row 3 (Generation 3)

  • level_size = 2.
  • Pop 5: No children.
  • Pop 6: No children.
  • Queue is empty [].
  • End of loop. current_level is [5, 6].
  • result becomes [[1], [3, 2, 4], [5, 6]].

Notice how the transition from Binary Tree to N-ary Tree just involves a simple for loop over the children array instead of hardcoded left/right checks:

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once, and appending to the queue takes $O(1)$ time per child. The sum of all children across all nodes is exactly $N-1$ (every node except the root is someone's child).
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The BFS queue holds up to the maximum width of the tree, which can be $O(N)$ in a very wide tree (e.g., a root with $N-1$ children).

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: return [] handles it.
  • Single Node: root = Node(42). Returns [[42]]. node.children is an empty list [], so the inner loop simply skips, and the queue empties gracefully.
  • Extremely Wide Tree: If the root has 1000 children, the algorithm easily pushes them all onto the queue in one go during the first iteration. The next iteration will have a level_size of 1000. It scales perfectly.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from collections import deque
from typing import List, Optional

class Node:
    def __init__(self, val=None, children=None):
        self.val = val
        self.children = children if children is not None else []

def levelOrder(root: 'Node') -> List[List[int]]:
    if not root:
        return []
    
    result = []
    queue = deque([root])
    
    while queue:
        level_size = len(queue)
        current_level = []
        
        for _ in range(level_size):
            node = queue.popleft()
            current_level.append(node.val)
            
            for child in node.children:
                queue.append(child)
                
        result.append(current_level)
        
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Test 1:
    #       1
    #     / | \
    #    3  2  4
    #   / \
    #  5   6
    root = Node(1, [
        Node(3, [Node(5), Node(6)]),
        Node(2),
        Node(4)
    ])
    assert levelOrder(root) == [[1], [3, 2, 4], [5, 6]], "Test 1 Failed"
    
    # Test 2: Empty tree
    assert levelOrder(None) == [], "Test 2 Failed"
    
    # Test 3: Single node
    assert levelOrder(Node(42)) == [[42]], "Test 3 Failed"
    
    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) - visit each node exactly once. 💾 Space: O(N) - queue can hold at most N nodes (the widest level).

Explorers 7 Problems
📖 COMPREHENSIVE THEORY & MENTAL MODELS▶

Pattern 12: Tree Depth First Search (DFS)

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you are exploring a giant maze.

Breadth First Search (BFS) is like sending a million clones of yourself to walk

down every possible path one step at a time.

Depth First Search (DFS) is like just being you. You pick a path, and you run

down it as fast and as far as you possibly can!

You keep going until you hit a dead end (a Leaf).

When you hit a dead end, you take one step backward, see if there is another path,

and run down that one instead.

To remember how to get back, you leave a trail of breadcrumbs.

In code, this trail of breadcrumbs is called Recursion (a function calling itself).

The computer's "Call Stack" remembers exactly where you left off at every fork

in the road, so you can easily backtrack!

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

The DFS pattern works by diving deep into the tree until it hits a leaf node, and then backtracking. It is almost always implemented using Recursion because the Call Stack naturally handles the backtracking logic for us.

When to use it:

  • The problem asks you to search from the Root to a Leaf.
  • You need to find all possible paths from top to bottom.
  • You need to aggregate values along a vertical path.
  • The problem involves finding the "Diameter" or "Maximum Path Sum" (which requires computing bottom-up from the leaves).

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Recipe: Standard DFS (Pre-order Traversal)

When you process the node BEFORE you visit its children, it's called Pre-order traversal. This is standard for "Root-to-Leaf" path problems.

  1. Base Case 1: if not root: return False
  2. Base Case 2 (Leaf): if not root.left and not root.right:
  3. Check if this path meets the condition (e.g. current_sum == target).
  4. Recursive Step:
  5. return dfs(root.left, updated_state) or dfs(root.right, updated_state)

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
Path SumDO subtract the current node's value from the target_sum as you go down. When you hit a leaf, check if target_sum == 0.DON'T keep a running total and pass it down unless you have to, subtracting is usually cleaner.
All PathsDO append the current node to a current_path list, and pop() it AFTER the recursive calls finish (Backtracking!).DON'T pass current_path.append() directly into the recursion. It mutates the single list for all branches. Pass a copy, or strictly append/pop.
Bottom-Up (Diameter)DO use Post-order traversal (process left child, process right child, THEN do logic on current node).DON'T try to compute the diameter from the top down. You need the heights of the subtrees first!

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(N)We visit every node in the tree exactly once.
SpaceO(H)The Recursion Call Stack takes up memory equal to the Height (H) of the tree. In a balanced tree, this is O(log N). In a skewed tree (a linked list), this is O(N).

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Forgetting to Backtrack: If you are storing the current path in a list, and you modify that list in-place, that modification will bleed into other branches! You MUST remove the node from the list when the function returns (e.g., current_path.pop()).
  2. Missing the Leaf Check: For root-to-leaf problems, you must explicitly check not node.left and not node.right. If you just check not node, you'll process a path ending in a node that only has one child (which is NOT a leaf).
  3. Global Variables: In Python, avoid global variables for counts or maximums. Instead, pass them as a mutable list [0] or use a class attribute self.max_val.

Easy Binary Tree Path Sum

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Binary Tree Path Sum

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are walking through a magical forest (a tree).

Every tree branch has a number on it.

You have a backpack with a target number, say 22.

As you walk down a path, you subtract the number you see from your backpack.

If the first branch says 5, your backpack now holds 17.

If you reach the very end of the path (a leaf node) and your backpack is exactly empty (0), you win!

But if you reach a leaf and your backpack isn't 0, that path was a loser, so you magically teleport backward (Backtracking) and try a different path!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the foundational Tree Depth First Search (DFS) pattern. We explore all the way down to a leaf before looking at other paths. We do this by recursively calling the function on the left and right children while passing down the updated state (the remaining sum needed).

  1. Base Case (Empty): If the root is None, return False. (A non-existent path can't equal the sum).
  2. Base Case (Leaf): If the current node is a leaf (no left, no right children):
  3. Check if root.value == target_sum. If it is, return True!
  4. Note: We check if it equals the current target_sum, which has been reduced by the parent nodes.
  5. Recursive Step: If it's not a leaf, recursively check the left and right subtrees.
  6. We subtract the current node's value from the target_sum before passing it down.
  7. return has_path_sum(root.left, target_sum - root.value) or has_path_sum(root.right, target_sum - root.value)

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
12
     /  \
    7    1
   /    / \
  9    10  5

Target Sum: 23

The Descent

  1. At Node 12:
  2. Is it a leaf? No.
  3. Recursively call left and right with target_sum = 23 - 12 = 11.
  4. At Node 7 (Left of 12):
  5. Target is 11.
  6. Is it a leaf? No.
  7. Recursively call left and right with target_sum = 11 - 7 = 4.
  8. At Node 9 (Left of 7):
  9. Target is 4.
  10. Is it a leaf? Yes!
  11. Does 9 == 4? No. Return False.

The Backtrack

  • We return False back up to Node 7. Node 7 checks its right child, which is None (returns False). Node 7 returns False back up to Node 12.
  • Now Node 12 explores its right child.
  1. At Node 1 (Right of 12):
  2. Target is 11. (Remember, this branch stems from Node 12!).
  3. Is it a leaf? No.
  4. Recursively call left and right with target_sum = 11 - 1 = 10.
  5. At Node 10 (Left of 1):
  6. Target is 10.
  7. Is it a leaf? Yes!
  8. Does 10 == 10? YES! Return True!
  • Node 10 returns True to Node 1. Node 1 returns True to Node 12. The final answer is True. (The recursion short-circuits via the or operator, so Node 5 is never checked).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$ in the worst case (where we have to visit every node).
  • Space Complexity: $O(H)$ where $H$ is the height of the tree. This is the space used by the recursion stack. In a balanced tree, it's $O(\log N)$. In the worst-case skewed tree, it's $O(N)$.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: if not root: immediately returns False.
  • Target met early but not at a leaf: If the path is 12 -> 1, and the target is 13, it doesn't accidentally return True at Node 1 unless Node 1 has no children. The problem explicitly asks for a root-to-leaf path sum. Our if not root.left and not root.right check enforces this.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def has_path_sum(root: Optional[TreeNode], target_sum: int) -> bool:
    """
    Returns True if the tree has a root-to-leaf path such that adding up all 
    the values along the path equals the given target_sum.
    """
    if not root:
        return False

    # Check if the current node is a leaf
    if not root.left and not root.right:
        # If it's a leaf, the remaining target must exactly match the leaf's value
        return root.value == target_sum

    # Recursively check the left and right subtrees, passing down the remaining sum needed
    return has_path_sum(root.left, target_sum - root.value) or \
           has_path_sum(root.right, target_sum - root.value)

# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    /    / \

    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Path: 12 -> 1 -> 10 == 23
    assert has_path_sum(root1, 23) == True, "Test 1 failed"
    
    # Path: 12 -> 7 -> 9 == 28
    assert has_path_sum(root1, 28) == True, "Test 2 failed"
    
    # Not a root-to-leaf path sum (12 -> 1 == 13, but 1 is not a leaf!)
    assert has_path_sum(root1, 13) == False, "Test 3 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert has_path_sum(None, 0) == False, "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert has_path_sum(TreeNode(42), 42) == True, "Edge 2: Single node matches"
    assert has_path_sum(TreeNode(42), 10) == False, "Edge 3: Single node doesn't match"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — In the worst case, we visit every node in the tree. 💾 Space: O(H) — Where H is the height of the tree, representing the recursion stack. (O(log N) for balanced trees, O(N) for skewed trees).
Medium All Paths for a Sum
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: All Paths for a Sum

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

This is just like the previous game where we walked through the magical forest trying to empty our backpack to exactly 0.

BUT this time, instead of just shouting "I won!" when you reach a leaf and hit 0, you have to write down the EXACT path you took to win.

And you have to find ALL the winning paths, not just one!

Because you are walking up and down branches, you keep a "current path" list on a clipboard.

When you step onto a branch, you write that number down on your clipboard.

When you hit a dead end and need to turn around (Backtracking), you ERASE that number from your clipboard before you step back up. This way, your clipboard always perfectly matches the path you are currently standing on!

🎯 Core Strategy

This introduces the concept of Backtracking alongside Tree Depth First Search (DFS). As we recursively traverse down the tree, we maintain the current path in an array. When we return from a recursive call, we must remove the node we just visited to keep the array clean for the next branch.

  1. Initialization: Initialize an empty list all_paths = [] to store the winning paths.
  2. Recursive Helper: Define find_paths_recursive(node, current_sum, current_path).
  3. Base Case: If node is None, return.
  4. Add to Path: Append the current node's value to current_path.
  5. Check for Winner: If it's a leaf node AND current_sum == node.value:
  6. We found a winner!
  7. CRITICAL STEP: Append a COPY of current_path to all_paths (e.g., list(current_path)). If we just append the reference, our future backtracking steps will erase the winning path we just saved!
  8. Explore: If it's not a winner, recursively call the left and right subtrees with current_sum - node.value.
  9. BACKTRACK: After exploring both subtrees, we are about to return to the parent node. We MUST remove the current node from current_path by calling current_path.pop().
  10. Call the helper with the root and return all_paths.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
12
     /  \
    7    1
   /    / \
  4    10  5

Target: 23

The Descent

  1. Node 12: path = [12]. Call Left(7) with target 11.
  2. Node 7: path = [12, 7]. Call Left(4) with target 4.
  3. Node 4: path = [12, 7, 4].
  4. Is Leaf? Yes. Does 4 == 4? Yes!
  5. Append COPY of [12, 7, 4] to all_paths.

The Backtrack

  • We finished Node 4. Backtrack: path.pop(). path is now [12, 7].
  • Return to Node 7. Node 7 has no right child.
  • We finished Node 7. Backtrack: path.pop(). path is now [12].
  • Return to Node 12. Call Right(1) with target 11.

Exploring the Right Side

  1. Node 1: path = [12, 1]. Call Left(10) with target 10.
  2. Node 10: path = [12, 1, 10].
  3. Is Leaf? Yes. Does 10 == 10? Yes!
  4. Append COPY of [12, 1, 10] to all_paths.
  5. Finished Node 10. Backtrack: path.pop(). path is [12, 1].
  6. Return to Node 1. Call Right(5) with target 10.
  7. Node 5: path = [12, 1, 5].
  8. Is Leaf? Yes. Does 5 == 10? No.
  9. Finished Node 5. Backtrack: path.pop(). path is [12, 1].
  10. Finished Node 1. Backtrack: path.pop(). path is [12].

Traversal complete! all_paths contains [[12, 7, 4], [12, 1, 10]].

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N^2)$. In the worst-case scenario (e.g., every single root-to-leaf path equals the target sum), we have to copy the current_path for every single leaf node. Creating a copy of an array of length $H$ takes $O(H)$ time. With $N/2$ leaves, this approaches $O(N \log N)$ for balanced trees, and $O(N^2)$ for skewed trees.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N \log N)$. The recursion stack takes $O(H)$ space. The all_paths array will store the copies of the paths. If there are many valid paths, storing them all can take significant space.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Forgetting to copy the array: If you just use all_paths.append(current_path), then as your recursion progresses, it modifies that exact same list object in memory. By the time the algorithm finishes, current_path will be empty [], and all_paths will look like [[], [], []]. Using list(current_path) or current_path.copy() prevents this.
  • Empty Tree: Safely handled by the initial if not node: check. Returns [].
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_paths(root: Optional[TreeNode], target_sum: int) -> List[List[int]]:
    """
    Finds all root-to-leaf paths where each path's sum equals the target_sum.
    """
    all_paths: List[List[int]] = []

    def find_paths_recursive(node: Optional[TreeNode], current_sum: int, current_path: List[int]):
        if not node:
            return

        # 1. Add the current node to the path
        current_path.append(node.value)

        # 2. Check if we reached a leaf AND the sum matches
        if not node.left and not node.right and current_sum == node.value:
            # We found a winner! Add a COPY of the path.
            all_paths.append(list(current_path))
        else:
            # 3. If not a leaf, keep going down
            find_paths_recursive(node.left, current_sum - node.value, current_path)
            find_paths_recursive(node.right, current_sum - node.value, current_path)

        # 4. BACKTRACK! We are about to go back UP the tree, so remove this node.
        current_path.pop()

    find_paths_recursive(root, target_sum, [])
    return all_paths

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    /    / \
    #   4    10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(4)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Target = 23. Paths: 12->7->4 (23) and 12->1->10 (23)
    expected1 = [[12, 7, 4], [12, 1, 10]]
    assert find_paths(root1, 23) == expected1, f"Test 1 failed: {find_paths(root1, 23)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert find_paths(None, 0) == [], "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert find_paths(TreeNode(42), 42) == [[42]], "Edge 2: Single node matches"
    assert find_paths(TreeNode(42), 10) == [], "Edge 3: Single node doesn't match"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N^2) — In the worst case (where every path is a winner), copying the path takes O(N) time for each of the O(N) leaves. 💾 Space: O(N log N) — The recursion stack is O(log N) for balanced trees, but storing all paths can take O(N * log N) space.
Medium Sum of Path Numbers
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Sum of Path Numbers

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine every node in the tree is a single digit (0-9).

As you walk down a path from the top of the tree to a leaf, you write down the numbers you see.

If you see a 1, then a 7, then a 3, you just formed the number 173.

Your job is to find ALL the numbers formed by every possible path to the bottom, and add them all together!

How do we build the number as we walk down?

Math! If you currently have the number 17, and you step on a 3, you don't add 3 to 17 (that would be 20). You multiply 17 by 10 (which makes it 170), and THEN add 3 (which makes it 173).

Formula: current_number = (current_number * 10) + node.value

When you hit a leaf, you return that fully built number.

When branches split, you just add the total from the left branch and the total from the right branch!

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an elegant Tree Depth First Search (DFS) application where state is passed down the tree, and the aggregated results are passed up.

  1. Helper Function: We define a recursive helper find_sum(node, path_sum) that takes the current node and the number built so far.
  2. Base Case (Empty): If the node is None, return 0.
  3. State Update: Calculate the new number: path_sum = 10 * path_sum + node.value.
  4. Base Case (Leaf): Is this a leaf node? (if not node.left and not node.right:)
  5. If yes, we have finished building this specific number. Return path_sum!
  6. Recursive Step: If it's not a leaf, we need to collect the numbers from both branches. Return the sum of the left subtree PLUS the sum of the right subtree.
  7. return find_sum(node.left, path_sum) + find_sum(node.right, path_sum)
  8. Initialization: Start the recursion from the root with a starting sum of 0: return find_sum(root, 0).

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
     / \
    7   9
       / \
      2   9

The DFS Process

  1. At Node 1:
  2. Incoming path_sum = 0.
  3. New path_sum = $10 * 0 + 1 = 1$.
  4. Not a leaf. Recurse Left and Right with path_sum = 1.
  5. At Node 7 (Left of 1):
  6. Incoming path_sum = 1.
  7. New path_sum = $10 * 1 + 7 = 17$.
  8. Is a leaf! Return 17.
  9. At Node 9 (Right of 1):
  10. Incoming path_sum = 1.
  11. New path_sum = $10 * 1 + 9 = 19$.
  12. Not a leaf. Recurse Left and Right with path_sum = 19.
  13. At Node 2 (Left of 9):
  14. Incoming path_sum = 19.
  15. New path_sum = $10 * 19 + 2 = 192$.
  16. Is a leaf! Return 192.
  17. At Node 9 (Right of 9):
  18. Incoming path_sum = 19.
  19. New path_sum = $10 * 19 + 9 = 199$.
  20. Is a leaf! Return 199.

Aggregating Back Up

  • Node 9 (right of 1) receives 192 from left and 199 from right. Returns 192 + 199 = 391.
  • Node 1 receives 17 from left and 391 from right. Returns 17 + 391 = 408.

Final Answer: 408.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. The math operations (* 10 + value) take $O(1)$ time.
  • Space Complexity: $O(H)$ where $H$ is the tree height, representing the recursion stack. $O(\log N)$ for balanced, $O(N)$ for skewed.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely handled by if not node: return 0.
  • Node value is 0: e.g., a path is 1 -> 0 -> 2.
  • Node 1: path_sum = 1.
  • Node 0: path_sum = $10 * 1 + 0 = 10$.
  • Node 2: path_sum = $10 * 10 + 2 = 102$.
  • Handled perfectly via the math formula!
  • Single Node: root = [5]. path_sum becomes 5. It's a leaf, so it returns 5. Correct.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def sum_numbers(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the total sum of all the numbers represented by all root-to-leaf paths.
    """
    def find_sum(node: Optional[TreeNode], path_sum: int) -> int:
        if not node:
            return 0

        # Calculate the number formed so far
        path_sum = 10 * path_sum + node.value

        # If it's a leaf, return the fully formed number
        if not node.left and not node.right:
            return path_sum

        # Recursively find the sums from the left and right branches and add them together
        return find_sum(node.left, path_sum) + find_sum(node.right, path_sum)

    return find_sum(root, 0)

    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     7   9
    #        / \
    #       2   9
    root1 = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(9)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(9)
    
    # Path 1: 1 -> 7 = 17
    # Path 2: 1 -> 9 -> 2 = 192
    # Path 3: 1 -> 9 -> 9 = 199
    # Total = 17 + 192 + 199 = 408
    assert sum_numbers(root1) == 408, f"Test 1 failed: {sum_numbers(root1)}"

    #       4
    #      / \
    #     9   0
    #    / \
    #   5   1
    root2 = TreeNode(4)
    root2.left = TreeNode(9)
    root2.right = TreeNode(0)
    root2.left.left = TreeNode(5)
    root2.left.right = TreeNode(1)
    
    # Paths: 495 + 491 + 40 = 1026
    assert sum_numbers(root2) == 1026, f"Test 2 failed: {sum_numbers(root2)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert sum_numbers(None) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert sum_numbers(TreeNode(5)) == 5, "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited once. 💾 Space: O(H) — The recursion stack goes as deep as the tree height.
Medium Path With Given Sequence
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Path With Given Sequence

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

You are walking down a path in the forest, and you have a treasure map.

The map says: "Walk exactly on the numbers: 1, then 9, then 9".

If you step on a 1, great! You check the map, and the next number should be 9.

If the next branch says 5, you know immediately this is the wrong path! You don't even need to walk to the end of it; you can turn around right away.

If you step on 1, then 9, then 9, AND you are at a leaf (the end of a path), you found the treasure!

To keep track of where you are on the map, you carry a pointer called sequence_index. Every time you step on a correct number, sequence_index goes up by 1.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an efficient Tree Depth First Search (DFS) implementation with early exit. We don't need to blindly explore the whole tree. If a path deviates from the sequence at any point, we prune that branch immediately.

  1. Base Case (Empty/Invalid): If root is None or sequence is empty, return False.
  2. Recursive Helper: Define find_path_recursive(node, sequence, sequence_index).
  3. Early Exits (Pruning):
  4. If node is None, return False.
  5. If sequence_index is too large (out of bounds), return False.
  6. If node.value != sequence[sequence_index], the number doesn't match! Return False immediately.
  7. Win Condition: If the number matches, we ask: Is this the very end of the map AND the end of the tree?
  8. if sequence_index == len(sequence) - 1 and not node.left and not node.right:
  9. Return True!
  10. Recursive Step: If it's not the end yet, keep walking down both the left and right branches, passing sequence_index + 1 so they look for the next number.
  11. return find_path_recursive(node.left, ...) or find_path_recursive(node.right, ...)

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
     / \
    7   9
       / \
      2   9

Target Sequence: [1, 9, 9]

The Search

  1. Node 1 (Index 0):
  2. Does 1 match seq[0] (which is 1)? Yes!
  3. Is it the last index and a leaf? No.
  4. Recurse Left and Right with index = 1.
  5. Node 7 (Left of 1) (Index 1):
  6. Does 7 match seq[1] (which is 9)? NO!
  7. Early Exit! Return False immediately. We don't explore under 7.
  8. Node 9 (Right of 1) (Index 1):
  9. Does 9 match seq[1] (which is 9)? Yes!
  10. Is it the last index and a leaf? No.
  11. Recurse Left and Right with index = 2.
  12. Node 2 (Left of 9) (Index 2):
  13. Does 2 match seq[2] (which is 9)? NO!
  14. Early Exit! Return False.
  15. Node 9 (Right of 9) (Index 2):
  16. Does 9 match seq[2] (which is 9)? Yes!
  17. Is it the last index (2 == 3-1)? Yes.
  18. Is it a leaf? Yes.
  19. Return True!

Node 9 returns True to its parent, which propagates up to the root. Final answer: True.

📊 Visual Diagram

Here is how the algorithm aggressively prunes bad paths (like Node 7 and Node 2):

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$ in the worst case (e.g., all paths perfectly match the sequence up to the leaves, but fail at the very end). However, due to early exit pruning, average time complexity is much better.
  • Space Complexity: $O(H)$ for the recursion stack, where $H$ is the height of the tree.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Sequence is longer than any path: Safely handles this because when it reaches a leaf, index won't equal len(sequence) - 1, so it won't return True. It will recurse into None children and return False.
  • Sequence is shorter than the path: E.g., Tree is 1 -> 9 -> 2, Sequence is [1, 9].
  • At node 9, index matches, but node is not a leaf. It recurses to node 2 with index 2.
  • At node 2, index >= seq_len triggers our out-of-bounds check if sequence_index >= seq_len: return False. It correctly rejects the path!
  • Empty Sequence or Tree: if not root or not sequence: return False catches these immediately.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional, List

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_path(root: Optional[TreeNode], sequence: List[int]) -> bool:
    """
    Returns True if the sequence is present as a root-to-leaf path.
    """
    if not root or not sequence:
        return False

    def find_path_recursive(node: Optional[TreeNode], sequence: List[int], sequence_index: int) -> bool:
        if not node:
            return False

        seq_len = len(sequence)

        # 1. Early exit if the index is out of bounds or the number doesn't match
        if sequence_index >= seq_len or node.value != sequence[sequence_index]:
            return False

        # 2. If it matches, check if it's the very last number AND a leaf node
        if sequence_index == seq_len - 1 and not node.left and not node.right:
            return True

        # 3. Otherwise, keep going down the tree, looking for the next number
        return find_path_recursive(node.left, sequence, sequence_index + 1) or \
               find_path_recursive(node.right, sequence, sequence_index + 1)

    return find_path_recursive(root, sequence, 0)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     7   9
    #        / \
    #       2   9
    root1 = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(9)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(9)
    
    assert find_path(root1, [1, 9, 9]) == True, "Test 1 failed"
    assert find_path(root1, [1, 7]) == True, "Test 2 failed"
    
    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # Matches part of the path, but doesn't end at a leaf
    assert find_path(root1, [1, 9]) == False, "Edge 1: Doesn't end at leaf"
    
    # Sequence is longer than the path
    assert find_path(root1, [1, 7, 3]) == False, "Edge 2: Sequence too long"
    
    assert find_path(None, [1, 2]) == False, "Edge 3: Empty tree"
    assert find_path(TreeNode(1), []) == False, "Edge 4: Empty sequence"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — In the worst case, we check all nodes. But often we exit early if the sequence breaks. 💾 Space: O(H) — The recursion stack is O(H) for the height of the tree.
Medium (Advanced) Count Paths for a Sum
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Count Paths for a Sum

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Remember the trick where we used a magical notebook (Hash Map) to store our Running Totals in an array?

This is the EXACT same trick, but instead of an array, it's a tree!

The paths don't have to start at the root, and they don't have to end at a leaf. They just have to go straight down.

As we walk down a branch, we keep a Running Total.

If the Target is 8, and our Running Total is 10, we check our magical notebook:

"Did I ever have a Running Total of 2 higher up on this EXACT same path?"

If yes, that means the numbers between that old spot and our current spot add up exactly to 8!

BUT, there is a catch. When we hit a dead end and backtrack to try a different branch, we MUST erase our Running Total from the notebook! We can't let the left branch's totals accidentally get used by the right branch!

🎯 Core Strategy

This marries the Subarray Sum Equals K (Prefix Sum) technique with Tree Depth First Search (DFS) and Backtracking.

  1. Global/Shared State: Initialize a Hash Map prefix_sums = {0: 1}. (Base case: a path perfectly matches the target from the very beginning).
  2. Recursive DFS: Define dfs(node, current_sum).
  3. Update Sum: current_sum += node.value.
  4. Check Notebook: Check if current_sum - target_sum exists in prefix_sums. If it does, add that frequency to our path_count.
  5. Add to Notebook: Add the current current_sum to prefix_sums (increment by 1).
  6. Recurse: Recursively calculate the path counts for the left and right subtrees and add them to path_count.
  7. BACKTRACK (CRITICAL): Before returning from this node, DECREMENT the current_sum in prefix_sums by 1. We are stepping back up the tree, so this sum is no longer available to other parallel branches!

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
12
     /  \
    7    1
   /    / \
  4    10  5

Target: 11

Initialization: prefix = {0: 1}.

Down the Left Side

  1. Node 12: current_sum = 12.
  2. needed = 12 - 11 = 1. Not in prefix.
  3. prefix becomes {0: 1, 12: 1}.
  4. Recurse Left.
  5. Node 7: current_sum = 19.
  6. needed = 19 - 11 = 8. Not in prefix.
  7. prefix becomes {0: 1, 12: 1, 19: 1}.
  8. Recurse Left.
  9. Node 4: current_sum = 23.
  10. needed = 23 - 11 = 12. Wait, 12 IS in prefix! (Frequency is 1).
  11. This means the path from after the node that gave 12 (Node 12 itself) down to this node (Node 7 -> Node 4) equals 11! 7 + 4 = 11.
  12. path_count += 1.
  13. prefix becomes {0: 1, 12: 1, 19: 1, 23: 1}.

Backtracking

  • Finished Node 4. Backtrack: prefix[23] -= 1. prefix is {0: 1, 12: 1, 19: 1}.
  • Finished Node 7. Backtrack: prefix[19] -= 1. prefix is {0: 1, 12: 1}.
  • Back at Node 12. Recurse Right.

Down the Right Side

  1. Node 1: current_sum = 13.
  2. needed = 13 - 11 = 2. Not in prefix.
  3. prefix becomes {0: 1, 12: 1, 13: 1}.
  4. Recurse Left.
  5. Node 10: current_sum = 23.
  6. needed = 23 - 11 = 12. Wait, 12 IS in prefix! (Frequency is 1).
  7. The path 1 -> 10 = 11.
  8. path_count += 1.
  9. prefix becomes {0: 1, 12: 1, 13: 1, 23: 1}.

Total path_count is 2.

📊 Visual Diagram

Notice how the backtracking prevents Node 10 from falsely seeing the 23 that was generated by Node 4 on the other side of the tree:

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once. Looking up the needed sum in the hash map is $O(1)$. This is vastly superior to the brute-force $O(N^2)$ approach where we start a new DFS from every node.
  • Space Complexity: $O(N)$. The hash map can store up to $N$ distinct prefix sums if all values in a skewed tree are positive. The recursion stack also takes $O(H)$ space.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Negative Values: The hash map handles negative values flawlessly. The current_sum might dip up and down, but the math current - needed = target always holds true regardless of signs.
  • Path starts at Root: The initialization prefix_sums = {0: 1} ensures that if current_sum perfectly equals target_sum, then current_sum - target_sum = 0. The map looks up 0, finds 1, and correctly registers the path!
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def count_paths(root: Optional[TreeNode], target_sum: int) -> int:
    """
    Finds the total number of paths in the tree where the sum of nodes equals 
    target_sum.
    """
    # Base case: a prefix sum of 0 exists 1 time before we start
    prefix_sums = {0: 1}

    def dfs(node: Optional[TreeNode], current_sum: int) -> int:
        if not node:
            return 0

        current_sum += node.value
        path_count = 0

        # 1. Did we see a previous sum that leaves exactly target_sum?
        needed = current_sum - target_sum
        if needed in prefix_sums:
            path_count += prefix_sums[needed]

        # 2. Add the current sum to our notebook
        prefix_sums[current_sum] = prefix_sums.get(current_sum, 0) + 1

        # 3. Go down the left and right branches
        path_count += dfs(node.left, current_sum)
        path_count += dfs(node.right, current_sum)

        # 4. BACKTRACK! Remove the current sum as we go back up the tree
        prefix_sums[current_sum] -= 1

        return path_count

    return dfs(root, 0)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       12
    #      /  \
    #     7    1
    #    /    / \
    #   4    10  5
    root1 = TreeNode(12)
    root1.left = TreeNode(7)
    root1.right = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(4)
    root1.right.left = TreeNode(10)
    root1.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Target = 11. Paths: (7 -> 4) and (1 -> 10)
    assert count_paths(root1, 11) == 2, f"Test 1 failed: {count_paths(root1, 11)}"

    # Target = 12. Path: (12)
    assert count_paths(root1, 12) == 1, "Test 2 failed"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert count_paths(None, 0) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty tree"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited exactly once, and Hash Map lookups are O(1). 💾 Space: O(N) — The Hash Map can store up to N distinct prefix sums (if the tree is a straight line), and the recursion stack can also go O(N) deep.
Hard (Advanced) Tree Diameter
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Tree Diameter

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine stretching a string from one leaf of the tree as far across the tree as possible to another leaf.

The length of this string is the "Diameter" of the tree.

You might think: "Oh, it's just the distance from the furthest leaf on the left to the furthest leaf on the right of the ROOT!"

But wait! What if the left branch is extremely short, but the right branch is MASSIVE and branches out into its own two giant sub-branches?

The longest string might be completely inside the right branch, never even touching the root!

To solve this, we can't just check from the top down. We have to work BOTTOM-UP.

Every node asks its left child: "How tall are you?"

And asks its right child: "How tall are you?"

The node then says: "If I stretch my string from the bottom of my left child, through me, down to the bottom of my right child, the string would be exactly left_tall + right_tall + 1 nodes long!"

Every single node calculates this, and we just remember the biggest number we see.

To answer its own parent, the node passes up its OWN height: max(left_tall, right_tall) + 1.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is a classic Post-order Traversal using Tree Depth First Search (DFS). "Post-order" means we process the children before we process the parent node.

  1. Global Variable: Initialize a variable max_diameter = 0.
  2. Recursive Helper: Define calculate_height(node).
  3. Base Case: If node is None, its height is 0.
  4. Post-order Step (Ask Children):
  5. left_height = calculate_height(node.left)
  6. right_height = calculate_height(node.right)
  7. Process Parent (Calculate Diameter):
  8. The diameter of the tree passing through the current node is: left_height + right_height + 1. (Note: Some variations, like LeetCode, ask for the number of EDGES instead of nodes, which is just left_height + right_height).
  9. Update our record: max_diameter = max(max_diameter, current_diameter).
  10. Return to Parent (Calculate Height):
  11. The height of the current node to give to its parent is the tallest of its two branches plus itself: return max(left_height, right_height) + 1.
  12. Call the helper on the root and return max_diameter.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
     / \
    2   3
       / \
      5   6
     /     \
    7       8

Initialization: max_diameter = 0.

  1. Leaf Nodes (7, 8):
  2. Node 7: left=0, right=0. Diameter: 0+0+1=1. max_diameter=1. Returns max(0,0)+1 = 1.
  3. Node 8: left=0, right=0. Diameter: 0+0+1=1. max_diameter=1. Returns max(0,0)+1 = 1.
  4. Node 5:
  5. Left (7) returned 1. Right (None) returned 0.
  6. Diameter passing through 5: 1 + 0 + 1 = 2. max_diameter=2.
  7. Returns height: max(1, 0) + 1 = 2.
  8. Node 6:
  9. Left (None) returned 0. Right (8) returned 1.
  10. Diameter passing through 6: 0 + 1 + 1 = 2. max_diameter=2.
  11. Returns height: max(0, 1) + 1 = 2.
  12. Node 3:
  13. Left (5) returned 2. Right (6) returned 2.
  14. Diameter passing through 3: 2 + 2 + 1 = 5. max_diameter=5.
  15. Returns height: max(2, 2) + 1 = 3.
  16. Node 2 (Leaf):
  17. Returns height 1.
  18. Node 1 (Root):
  19. Left (2) returned 1. Right (3) returned 3.
  20. Diameter passing through 1: 1 + 3 + 1 = 5. max_diameter=5.

The max diameter was found passing through node 3 and node 1. Answer: 5 (nodes 7->5->3->6->8).

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once during the post-order traversal.
  • Space Complexity: $O(H)$ where $H$ is the tree height. This is the memory used by the recursion stack.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Empty Tree: Safely handled by if not node: return 0. The helper is called, returns 0, and the initial max_diameter = 0 is returned.
  • Single Node: calculate_height returns 1, current_diameter becomes 0 + 0 + 1 = 1. max_diameter becomes 1. Returns correctly.
  • Longest Path completely in one subtree: This is exactly why we use a global max_diameter variable instead of just combining the root's left and right heights. Node 3 will correctly calculate a diameter of 5, which will be safely saved in max_diameter even if the root's diameter was smaller.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_diameter(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the diameter of a binary tree (represented as the maximum number of nodes).
    """
    max_diameter = 0

    def calculate_height(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        nonlocal max_diameter
        
        if not node:
            return 0

        # POST-ORDER: Ask the children first
        left_height = calculate_height(node.left)
        right_height = calculate_height(node.right)

        # Do the math for the current node
        current_diameter = left_height + right_height + 1
        
        # Update the global record if this is the longest string we've seen
        max_diameter = max(max_diameter, current_diameter)

        # Tell our parent how tall we are
        return max(left_height, right_height) + 1

    calculate_height(root)
    return max_diameter

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    #    / \
    #   4   5
    root1 = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right = TreeNode(3)
    root1.left.left = TreeNode(4)
    root1.left.right = TreeNode(5)
    
    # Path: 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 (4 nodes)
    # OR 5 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 (4 nodes)
    assert find_diameter(root1) == 4, f"Test 1 failed: {find_diameter(root1)}"

    # Diameter completely contained in the right subtree
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    #        / \
    #       5   6
    #      /     \
    #     7       8
    #    /         \
    #   9           10
    root2 = TreeNode(1)
    root2.left = TreeNode(2)
    root2.right = TreeNode(3)
    root2.right.left = TreeNode(5)
    root2.right.right = TreeNode(6)
    root2.right.left.left = TreeNode(7)
    root2.right.left.left.left = TreeNode(9)
    root2.right.right.right = TreeNode(8)
    root2.right.right.right.right = TreeNode(10)
    
    # Path: 9 -> 7 -> 5 -> 3 -> 6 -> 8 -> 10 (7 nodes)
    assert find_diameter(root2) == 7, f"Test 2 failed: {find_diameter(root2)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    assert find_diameter(None) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty tree"
    assert find_diameter(TreeNode(1)) == 1, "Edge 2: Single node"

    print("All tests passed!")
⏱ Time: O(N) — Every node is visited once. 💾 Space: O(H) — The recursion stack is bounded by the height of the tree.
Hard (Advanced) Maximum Path Sum
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Maximum Path Sum

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

This is just like finding the longest string across the tree (Tree Diameter), but instead of counting the number of nodes, we want the path with the HIGHEST SCORE.

Every node has a score (some are positive, some are negative).

A node asks its left child: "What is the highest score I can get if I walk down your branch?"

And it asks its right child the same thing.

If a child returns a NEGATIVE score (like -10), the parent says: "Ew, no thanks! I'm just not going to walk down your branch at all!"

So we replace any negative scores with a 0 (meaning we just ignore that branch entirely and stop our path there).

The score of the path going THROUGH the current node is: left_score + right_score + node's own score.

We keep track of the absolute highest score we ever see.

Then, to answer its OWN parent, the node can only pick ONE path to pass up (you can't walk down both branches and then go back up to the parent without retracing your steps).

So it passes up: max(left_score, right_score) + node's own score.

🎯 Core Strategy

This is an advanced application of Post-order Traversal using Tree Depth First Search (DFS), where we filter out negative contributions.

  1. Global Variable: Initialize max_sum = -infinity (to handle trees with all negative numbers).
  2. Recursive Helper: Define calculate_max_path_sum(node).
  3. Base Case: If node is None, return 0.
  4. Post-order Step (Ask Children, Filter Negatives):
  5. Ask left child: left_sum = max(calculate_max_path_sum(node.left), 0)
  6. Ask right child: right_sum = max(calculate_max_path_sum(node.right), 0)
  7. Process Parent (Calculate Global Max):
  8. The maximum path sum passing through the current node is: current_max_sum = left_sum + right_sum + node.value.
  9. Update our record: max_sum = max(max_sum, current_max_sum).
  10. Return to Parent (Return Branch Max):
  11. The node returns the best single continuous line down its subtree: return max(left_sum, right_sum) + node.value.
  12. Call the helper on the root and return max_sum.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Tree:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
1
      / \
     2   3
    /     \
   4       5
  / \     / \
 -1 -2   -3 -4

Initialization: max_sum = -infinity.

  1. Leaf Node -1:
  2. Left=0, Right=0. current = -1. max_sum = -1. Returns max(0,0)-1 = -1.
  3. Leaf Node -2:
  4. Left=0, Right=0. current = -2. max_sum = -1. Returns max(0,0)-2 = -2.
  5. Node 4:
  6. Left returned -1. We take max(-1, 0) = 0.
  7. Right returned -2. We take max(-2, 0) = 0.
  8. current = 0 + 0 + 4 = 4. max_sum = 4.
  9. Returns max(0, 0) + 4 = 4.
  10. Leaves -3 and -4:
  11. Similar to above, they return -3 and -4.
  12. Node 5:
  13. Left returned -3 -> becomes 0.
  14. Right returned -4 -> becomes 0.
  15. current = 0 + 0 + 5 = 5. max_sum = 5.
  16. Returns max(0, 0) + 5 = 5.
  17. Node 2:
  18. Left (4) returned 4 -> 4. Right is None -> 0.
  19. current = 4 + 0 + 2 = 6. max_sum = 6.
  20. Returns max(4, 0) + 2 = 6.
  21. Node 3:
  22. Left is None -> 0. Right (5) returned 5 -> 5.
  23. current = 0 + 5 + 3 = 8. max_sum = 8.
  24. Returns max(0, 5) + 3 = 8.
  25. Root Node 1:
  26. Left (2) returned 6. Right (3) returned 8.
  27. current = 6 + 8 + 1 = 15. max_sum = 15.
  28. Returns max(6, 8) + 1 = 9.

Final Answer: 15.

🛑 Edge Cases & Complexity

Complexity

  • Time Complexity: $O(N)$. We visit every node exactly once during the post-order traversal.
  • Space Complexity: $O(H)$ where $H$ is the tree height. This is the memory used by the recursion stack.

Edge Cases Handled Safely

  • Tree with ONLY negative numbers: E.g., [-10, -20, -30].
  • Node -20 returns -20. Node -30 returns -30.
  • Root -10 filters these to 0. current = 0 + 0 - 10 = -10.
  • Because max_sum was initialized to -infinity, it correctly updates to -10 instead of falsely returning 0.
  • Empty Tree: Handled by if not root: return 0.
⚡ Python 3.12+ Implementation 
from typing import Optional
import math

class TreeNode:
    def __init__(self, value=0, left=None, right=None):
        self.value = value
        self.left = left
        self.right = right

def find_maximum_path_sum(root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
    """
    Finds the path with the maximum sum in a given binary tree.
    """
    if not root:
        return 0

    max_sum = -math.inf

    def calculate_max_path_sum(node: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        nonlocal max_sum
        
        if not node:
            return 0

        # POST-ORDER: Ask the children first, but IGNORE them if they are negative!
        left_sum = max(calculate_max_path_sum(node.left), 0)
        right_sum = max(calculate_max_path_sum(node.right), 0)

        # The maximum path sum passing through the current node
        current_max_sum = left_sum + right_sum + node.value
        
        # Update the global maximum
        max_sum = max(max_sum, current_max_sum)

        # To the parent, we can only return ONE branch (either left or right) plus ourselves
        return max(left_sum, right_sum) + node.value

    calculate_max_path_sum(root)
    return int(max_sum)

# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# TEST CASES
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────
if __name__ == "__main__":
    # ✅ Normal cases
    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    root1 = TreeNode(1)
    root1.left = TreeNode(2)
    root1.right = TreeNode(3)
    
    # Path: 2 -> 1 -> 3 (Sum = 6)
    assert find_maximum_path_sum(root1) == 6, f"Test 1 failed: {find_maximum_path_sum(root1)}"

    #       1
    #      / \
    #     2   3
    #    /     \
    #   4       5
    #  / \     / \
    # -1 -2   -3 -4
    root2 = TreeNode(1)
    root2.left = TreeNode(2)
    root2.right = TreeNode(3)
    root2.left.left = TreeNode(4)
    root2.right.right = TreeNode(5)
    root2.left.left.left = TreeNode(-1)
    root2.left.left.right = TreeNode(-2)
    root2.right.right.left = TreeNode(-3)
    root2.right.right.right = TreeNode(-4)
    
    # We ignore the negative leaves. 
    # Max path: 4 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 5 = 15
    assert find_maximum_path_sum(root2) == 15, f"Test 2 failed: {find_maximum_path_sum(root2)}"

    # 🔲 Edge cases
    # All negative numbers
    root3 = TreeNode(-10)
    root3.left = TreeNode(-20)
    root3.right = TreeNode(-30)
    # The max is just -10 itself
    assert find_maximum_path_sum(root3) == -10, f"Test 3 failed: {find_maximum_path_sum(root3)}"

    assert find_maximum_path_sum(None) == 0, "Edge 1: Empty tree"

    print("All tests passed!")

Pattern 13: Graphs

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you are exploring a giant city using a map.

The city has buildings (Nodes), and roads connecting those buildings (Edges).

Unlike a family tree, which always flows from top to bottom without crossing over,

a city is chaotic!

A road can go from Building A to Building B, but another road can go from Building B

right back to Building A! This is called a Cycle.

If you try to explore the city without a plan, you might just walk back and forth

between A and B forever.

To prevent this, you carry a magical red marker.

Every time you enter a building, you put a big red "X" on the door.

If you ever walk down a road and see a building that already has a red "X" on it,

you say "I've already been here!" and turn around.

This red "X" is called a Visited Set.

🧩 Core Idea & Pattern Detection

Graphs are just Trees with Cycles and multiple interconnected components.

You can traverse them using DFS (Recursion) or BFS (Queue), but you MUST maintain a visited set to avoid infinite loops.

When to use it:

  • The problem asks about "Connected Components" (e.g. Number of Islands/Provinces).
  • The problem involves scheduling or dependencies (e.g. "Course B requires Course A"). This usually requires Topological Sort.
  • The problem asks about connecting nodes or finding redundant edges (e.g. Union Find).

🔧 Algorithmic Anatomy

Concept 1: The Adjacency List

Before traversing a graph, you often need to build it. We use a Hash Map where the Key is a node, and the Value is a list of its neighbors.

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
graph = {i: [] for i in range(num_nodes)}
for u, v in edges:
    graph[u].append(v)
    graph[v].append(u) # Only if undirected!

Concept 2: Traversal with a Visited Set (DFS)

⚡ PYTHON Implementation 
def dfs(node):
    if node in visited:
        return
    visited.add(node)
    for neighbor in graph[node]:
        dfs(neighbor)

Concept 3: Union Find (Disjoint Set)

Used to instantly check if two nodes are already connected, or to detect cycles in an undirected graph.

100%

🛑 Per-Variant DOs and DON'Ts

VariantDODON'T
DFS/BFS TraversalDO add nodes to the visited set immediately when you push them to the Queue or enter the DFS function.DON'T forget that a Graph might be disconnected! You often need an outer for loop over all nodes to ensure you visit every component.
Topological SortDO count the "in-degree" (number of incoming edges) for every node. Start with nodes that have an in-degree of 0.DON'T use a standard visited set for Cycle Detection in directed graphs; you need a path_visited set to track the CURRENT path!
Union FindDO use Path Compression in your find function (parent[x] = find(parent[x])) to keep the tree flat.DON'T forget to initialize the parent array such that every node is its own parent at the start (parent = {i: i}).

⏱️ Complexity Analysis

AspectComplexityWhy
TimeO(V + E)We visit every Vertex (Node) and traverse every Edge exactly once.
SpaceO(V + E)Storing the Adjacency List takes V + E space. The visited set takes O(V).

⚠️ Common Pitfalls

  1. Infinite Loops: If you forget your visited set, or forget to add nodes to it, a cycle like A -> B -> A will run until the computer crashes with a Stack Overflow.
  2. Disconnected Graphs: In Trees, starting from the Root guarantees you can reach every node. In Graphs, nodes might be isolated islands! Always wrap your traversal in an outer loop: for node in range(n): if node not in visited: dfs(node).
  3. Directed vs Undirected: When building your Adjacency List, pay close attention to the problem description. If the road is one-way, only graph[u].append(v). If it's two-way, you MUST also graph[v].append(u).

Medium Number of Provinces (Connected Components)
LeetCode ↗ ▶

🚶‍♂️ Walkthrough: Number of Provinces

👶 Explain Like I'm 5

Imagine you have a map of cities.

Some cities have roads connecting them. If City A is connected to City B, and City B is connected to City C, they all belong to the same "Province".

But what if City D and City E are connected to each other, but have NO roads leading to A, B, or C? Then D and E form a SECOND Province.

Your job is to count how many completely separate Provinces there are.

How do we do this? We just pick a city, say City A, and start exploring!

We put a red "X" (visited) on City A, then we walk down the road to City B and put an "X" on it, then to City C and put an "X" on it.

Once we hit a dead end, we know we have fully explored Province 1!

Then we look at our list of all cities.

"Is City B visited?" Yes. "City C?" Yes.

"What about City D?" No! City D doesn't have an "X".

That means City D is in a brand new Province!

So we increment our Province count, start exploring from City D, and repeat until every single city has an "X".

🎯 Core Strategy

This is the foundational Connected Components algorithm using Graph Depth First Search (DFS).

  1. State Tracking: n is the number of cities. We use a visited set to keep track of which cities we've already explored. provinces = 0.
  2. Recursive DFS Helper: dfs(city) explores all cities connected to a starting city.
  3. Loop through all possible neighbor indices from 0 to n-1.
  4. If is_connected[city][neighbor] == 1 AND neighbor is NOT in visited:
  5. Mark it visited: visited.add(neighbor).
  6. Recursively call dfs(neighbor) to continue exploring from there.
  7. Outer Loop: We loop through every city from 0 to n-1. This is the crucial step that prevents us from stopping after the first component.
  8. If the city is NOT in visited:
  9. We found an unexplored node! This means we found a new province. Increment provinces += 1.
  10. Add city to visited.
  11. Call dfs(city) to explore its entire component.
  12. Return provinces.

🏃‍♂️ Step-by-Step Execution (Dry Run)

Example Input Matrix:

⚡ TEXT Implementation 
0  1  2  (Cities)
   0 [1, 1, 0]  (City 0 connected to 0 and 1)
   1 [1, 1, 0]  (City 1 connected to 0 and 1)
   2 [0, 0, 1]  (City 2 only connected to itself)

Initialization: visited = set(), provinces = 0.

Outer Loop - Iteration 0

  • city = 0. Is it in visited? No.
  • provinces += 1 (Now provinces = 1).
  • visited.add(0). (Now visited = {0}).
  • Call dfs(0):
  • Check neighbors of City 0:
  • Neighbor 0: Connected? Yes. Visited? Yes. Skip.
  • Neighbor 1: Connected? Yes! Visited? No.
  • visited.add(1). (Now {0, 1}).
  • Call dfs(1):
  • Check neighbors of City 1:
  • Neighbor 0: Connected? Yes. Visited? Yes. Skip.
  • Neighbor 1: Connected? Yes. Visited? Yes. Skip.
  • Neighbor 2: Connected? No. Skip.
  • dfs(1) finishes.
  • Neighbor 2: Connected? No. Skip.
  • dfs(0) finishes.

Outer Loop - Iteration 1

  • city = 1. Is it in visited? Yes! (It was found during dfs(0)).
  • Skip!

Outer Loop - Iteration 2

  • city = 2. Is it in visited? No!
  • provinces += 1 (Now provinces = 2).
  • visited.add(2). (Now visited = {0, 1, 2}).
  • Call dfs(2):
  • Check neighbors of City 2:
  • Neighbor 0: Connected? No. Skip.
  • Neighbor 1: Connected? No. Skip.
  • Neighbor 2: Connected? Yes. Visited? Yes. Skip.
  • dfs(2) finishes.

Loop finishes. Return provinces (which is 2).
